alkene-structure.why: CnH2n+2 is the alkane (fully saturated) formula. Alkenes have one fewer degree of saturation, so they follow CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: In ethylene (H2C=CH2), the C=C bond is made up of:
options: one sigma bond and one pi bond
alkene-structure.why: A double bond always consists of one sigma bond (head-on overlap) and one pi bond (side-by-side overlap of p orbitals); you cannot have two sigma bonds between the same two atoms.

alkene-structure.q: A carbon-carbon double bond is shorter than a carbon-carbon single bond between the same two types of carbons.
alkene-structure.why: The additional pi bond in a double bond pulls the two carbons closer together, shortening the bond compared to a single (sigma-only) bond.

alkene-structure.q: How many sigma bonds are present in ethylene, H2C=CH2 (including the C-C sigma bond)?
alkene-structure.why: Ethylene has one C-C sigma bond and four C-H sigma bonds (5 total), plus one pi bond that is not counted as a sigma bond.

alkene-structure.q: Cis and trans isomers of an alkene exist because rotation around the C=C bond is restricted.
alkene-structure.why: Rotating one carbon relative to the other would require breaking the pi bond's side-by-side p-orbital overlap, so geometric (cis/trans) isomers are locked in place at room temperature.

alkene-structure.q: A compound with the molecular formula C5H10 and no rings has a degree of unsaturation of:
alkene-structure.why: Degree of unsaturation = (2(5)+2-10)/2 = (12-10)/2 = 1, consistent with one double bond and no ring.

alkene-structure.q: Which suffix in IUPAC nomenclature indicates the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond?
alkene-structure.why: The suffix -ene specifically designates a double bond in the parent chain, as in propene or 2-butene.

alkene-structure.q: According to general alkene stability trends, which alkene is typically the most stable?
alkene-structure.why: More substituted alkenes are stabilized by additional alkyl groups donating electron density (hyperconjugation) into the pi system, so tetrasubstituted alkenes are typically the most stable.

alkene-structure.q: E/Z nomenclature (rather than simple cis/trans) is needed when:
options: the alkene has a plane of symmetry
the alkene is part of a ring
alkene-structure.why: Cis/trans only works cleanly when it's obvious which groups are 'similar'; when each carbon carries two different substituents, CIP priority rules assign E (opposite, higher priorities) or Z (same side, higher priorities) unambiguously.

alkene-structure.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a compound with molecular formula C6H10?
alkene-structure.why: DoU = (2×6+2-10)/2 = 2, which could correspond to two double bonds, one ring plus one double bond, or one triple bond.

alkene-structure.q: A compound with a degree of unsaturation of 2 could contain one triple bond instead of two double bonds or a ring plus a double bond.
alkene-structure.why: A triple bond itself counts as two degrees of unsaturation (two pi bonds), so DoU=2 is consistent with one triple bond, two double bonds, two rings, or one ring plus one double bond.

alkene-structure.q: For CIP priority at an alkene carbon bearing both a chlorine atom and a methyl group, which substituent receives higher priority?
options: it depends on the rest of the molecule only
alkene-structure.why: CIP priority is assigned first by atomic number at the point of attachment; chlorine (Z=17) outranks a carbon-based methyl group (Z=6) regardless of what else is in the molecule.

alkene-structure.q: Geometric (cis/trans) isomerism is possible for an alkene only when:
options: each double-bond carbon bears two different substituents
there are at least three carbons total
alkene-structure.why: If either alkene carbon has two identical substituents, there is no distinct 'other side' to compare, so no cis/trans isomerism exists; each carbon needs two different groups.

alkene-structure.q: The pi bond of an alkene forms from the side-by-side overlap of:
options: an s orbital and a p orbital
two unhybridized p orbitals perpendicular to the sp2 plane
alkene-structure.why: Each sp2 carbon retains one unhybridized p orbital oriented perpendicular to the plane of the three sp2 orbitals; side-by-side overlap of these two p orbitals creates the pi bond.

alkene-structure.q: Alkenes are generally more chemically reactive than alkanes because the pi electrons are held less tightly and are more exposed than sigma electrons.
alkene-structure.why: Pi electrons sit above and below the molecular plane, farther from the nuclei and more accessible to electrophiles, making the C=C pi bond a reactive site compared to the strong, low-energy C-C and C-H sigma bonds in alkanes.

alkene-structure.q: For the same number of carbons, how does the molecular formula of an alkyne compare to that of an alkene?
options: alkyne has two more hydrogens than the alkene
alkyne and alkane have the same formula
alkyne has two fewer hydrogens than the alkene, CnH2n-2
alkene-structure.why: A triple bond contributes two degrees of unsaturation versus one for a double bond, removing two additional hydrogens, so alkynes follow CnH2n-2 while alkenes follow CnH2n.

alkene-structure.q: Why is trans-2-butene more stable (lower in energy) than cis-2-butene?
options: the cis methyls crowd each other
cis has a longer bond length
trans has more degrees of unsaturation
alkene-structure.why: In the cis isomer, the two methyl groups point to the same side of the double bond and crowd each other, raising the molecule's energy; in trans they point to opposite sides, minimizing steric clash.

alkene-structure.q: What is the degree of unsaturation of a monoterpene with molecular formula C10H16?
alkene-structure.why: DoU = (2×10+2-16)/2 = 3, consistent with, for example, one ring and two double bonds, a common pattern in monoterpenes.

alkene-structure.q: A six-membered ring containing three double bonds (like benzene) has a degree of unsaturation of 4.
alkene-structure.why: One ring contributes 1 and each of the three pi bonds contributes 1, for a total DoU of 1+3=4, matching benzene's formula C6H6: (2×6+2-6)/2=4.

alkene-structure.q: A double bond positioned at the bridgehead carbon of a small bicyclic ring system is typically extremely unstable or impossible to form because:
options: bridgehead carbons cannot bond to hydrogen
the ring prevents a planar sp2 carbon
pi bonds cannot exist in rings
alkene-structure.why: An sp2 alkene carbon needs its three attached groups and itself to lie in one plane; in small fused or bridged ring systems the bridgehead geometry can't twist into that planar arrangement without severe strain (this limitation is summarized by Bredt's rule).

alkene-structure.q: Why can a small ring like cyclohexene easily be cis but trans-cyclohexene is essentially impossible to isolate?
options: the ring is too small for trans
alkene-structure.why: Placing the ring's two connecting chains on opposite faces of the double bond (trans) in a small ring requires bond angles far from ideal, introducing enormous strain; only larger rings (roughly 8+ membered) can accommodate a stable trans-cycloalkene.

alkene-structure.q: Free rotation around a C=C double bond does not occur at room temperature because doing so would require:
options: breaking a sigma bond, which needs very little energy
alkene-structure.why: Rotating one carbon 90° relative to the other misaligns the two p orbitals so they can no longer overlap, effectively breaking the pi bond; this costs far more energy (~260 kJ/mol) than is available from ordinary thermal motion.

alkene-structure.q: In an alkene, the two double-bond carbons and the four atoms directly attached to them all lie approximately in a single plane.
alkene-structure.why: Because each alkene carbon is sp2 hybridized, its three sigma-bonded groups (including the other alkene carbon) are arranged trigonally in one plane, making the whole six-atom C=C unit planar.

alkene-structure.q: A smaller magnitude (less exothermic) heat of hydrogenation for an alkene indicates that alkene is:
options: less stable, higher in energy to begin with
more stable, lower in energy to begin with
alkene-structure.why: Hydrogenation converts all alkene isomers to the same alkane product, so the isomer that starts out lower in energy (more stable) releases less heat upon hydrogenation.

alkene-structure.q: Ranking by stability, which alkene substitution pattern is generally most stable?
alkene-structure.why: Alkene stability generally increases with the number of alkyl substituents directly attached to the double-bond carbons, due to increased hyperconjugative and inductive electron donation into the pi system; tetrasubstituted alkenes are the most stable of these options.

addition-reactions.q: In an addition reaction across a C=C double bond, the pi bond is:
options: Broken, and two new sigma bonds form
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions break the reactive pi bond and add two new groups, one to each former alkene carbon.

addition-reactions.q: Which step typically starts an electrophilic addition to an alkene?
options: The alkene acts as an electrophile
A proton is removed from the alkene
addition-reactions.why: Alkenes are electron-rich at the pi bond and act as nucleophiles toward an incoming electrophile, forming a carbocation (or similar) intermediate.

addition-reactions.q: Which of these is a classic electrophile added across an alkene in a halogenation (addition) reaction?
addition-reactions.why: Br₂ is polarized by the approaching alkene and forms a bromonium ion intermediate, a classic electrophilic addition across the double bond.

addition-reactions.q: In a general addition reaction, what happens to the alkene's degree of unsaturation?
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions convert the pi bond into two new sigma bonds to the added atoms, removing one degree of unsaturation from the starting alkene.

addition-reactions.q: Addition reactions to alkenes increase the molecule's degree of unsaturation.
addition-reactions.why: Addition reactions consume the pi bond, converting an alkene (or alkyne) into a more saturated product, which decreases the degree of unsaturation, not increases it.

addition-reactions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene (addition of H2) typically requires a catalyst such as:
addition-reactions.why: H2 doesn't react with alkenes on its own at a useful rate; a transition metal catalyst (commonly Pt, Pd, or Ni) adsorbs H2 and the alkene on its surface, allowing the addition to occur.

addition-reactions.q: What is the product of adding Br2 across ethylene (H2C=CH2)?
addition-reactions.why: Br2 adds across the double bond, putting one bromine on each former alkene carbon, giving the vicinal dihalide 1,2-dibromoethane.

addition-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene adds an H atom and an OH group across the former double bond.
addition-reactions.why: Hydration is the addition of water (formally H and OH) across the pi bond, converting the alkene into an alcohol.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of Br2 or Cl2 to an alkene is an example of what general reaction category?
addition-reactions.why: The electron-rich pi bond of the alkene attacks the electrophilic halogen, and both halogen atoms end up added to the former double-bond carbons, making this an electrophilic addition.

addition-reactions.q: The gradual disappearance of the orange-brown color when Br2 is added to an unknown compound is commonly used as a qualitative test for the presence of:
options: a halogen already in the molecule
a carbon-carbon pi bond (alkene or alkyne)
addition-reactions.why: Colored Br2 is consumed as it adds across a reactive pi bond, turning colorless; alkanes lack this reactive pi bond and don't decolorize Br2 without light or heat.

addition-reactions.q: The addition of H2 across a carbon-carbon double bond is called hydrogenation.
addition-reactions.why: Hydrogenation specifically refers to the addition of molecular hydrogen (H2) across a multiple bond, typically with a metal catalyst.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of a hydrogen halide (HX) across an alkene's double bond produces:
addition-reactions.why: HX adds H to one carbon and the halogen X to the other, converting the alkene directly into an alkyl halide.

addition-reactions.q: The electrophilic addition of Br2 to an alkene proceeds through which key intermediate?
addition-reactions.why: The alkene's pi electrons attack one bromine of Br2, displacing bromide and forming a three-membered ring bromonium ion in which bromine bridges both former alkene carbons, before bromide attacks from the opposite face.

addition-reactions.q: Hydroboration-oxidation (BH3 then H2O2/NaOH) converts an alkene into an alcohol with what regiochemistry?
options: always on a ring carbon only
addition-reactions.why: Boron, the less electronegative, bulkier atom, adds preferentially to the less hindered (less substituted) carbon, and after oxidation that carbon ends up bearing the OH, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

addition-reactions.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration gives the Markovnikov alcohol without the carbocation rearrangements sometimes seen in acid-catalyzed hydration because the mechanism proceeds through:
options: direct SN2 attack by water on the alkene carbon
addition-reactions.why: Mercury bridges both alkene carbons in a cyclic mercurinium ion; the positive character is delocalized rather than concentrated on one carbon, so water attacks the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov) without a true carbocation able to rearrange.

addition-reactions.q: Addition of Br2 to an alkene gives anti (opposite-face) stereochemistry because the bridged bromonium ion is attacked by bromide from the face opposite the bromonium ring.
addition-reactions.why: Since the first bromine already blocks one face as part of the bromonium ion, the incoming bromide ion must attack from the backside, giving net anti addition of the two bromines.

addition-reactions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene over a metal surface delivers the two hydrogen atoms with what stereochemistry?
addition-reactions.why: Both the alkene and H2 adsorb onto the same flat metal surface, so both hydrogen atoms are transferred to the same face of the double bond, giving syn addition.

addition-reactions.q: Why does bromine water (or Br2/CCl4) turn from colored to colorless when shaken with an alkene?
options: the alkene dissolves the bromine without reacting
Br2 is consumed, forming a colorless dibromide
the alkene reduces Br2 to HBr gas
addition-reactions.why: The addition reaction chemically consumes Br2, converting it into a colorless vicinal dibromide, which is why the test solution loses its color as the reaction proceeds.

addition-reactions.q: Hydroboration-oxidation follows Markovnikov's rule, placing OH on the more substituted carbon.
addition-reactions.why: Hydroboration-oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: boron adds to the less substituted, less hindered carbon due to steric factors (not carbocation stability), and OH ends up there after oxidation.

addition-reactions.q: The acid-catalyzed addition of water across an alkene's double bond is called:
addition-reactions.why: Acid catalysis protonates the alkene to form a carbocation, which water then attacks, adding H and OH across the former double bond in a process called acid-catalyzed hydration.

addition-reactions.q: Which reagent adds H and Br across a double bond with Markovnikov selectivity via a carbocation intermediate?
addition-reactions.why: Without peroxides, HBr adds through a polar (ionic) mechanism: the alkene is protonated to form the more stable carbocation, which is then captured by bromide, giving the Markovnikov product.

addition-reactions.q: Why doesn't hydroboration-oxidation give the carbocation-rearrangement products sometimes seen with acid-catalyzed hydration?
options: concerted syn addition, so no carbocation forms
Boron is too unreactive to add to alkenes at all
hydroboration only works on alkynes, not alkenes
oxidation always occurs before boron can add
addition-reactions.why: In hydroboration, boron and hydrogen add to the same face of the double bond simultaneously in one transition state, so there's no discrete carbocation intermediate available to undergo a hydride or alkyl shift.

addition-reactions.q: What is the overall stereochemical outcome when an alkene undergoes catalytic hydrogenation, and why?
options: anti addition, because the two hydrogens approach from opposite faces of the metal surface
syn addition, because both hydrogens add from the catalyst surface
no defined stereochemistry, because the mechanism is radical-based
anti addition, because a bridged intermediate forms like in halogenation
addition-reactions.why: Since the alkene binds flat against the catalyst surface and both hydrogens are transferred from that same surface, they must end up added to the same face, producing syn addition.

addition-reactions.q: Bromine addition can be used to chemically distinguish alkenes from alkanes because alkanes do not readily react with Br2 in the dark at room temperature, while alkenes do.
addition-reactions.why: Alkanes require light or heat to undergo a slow radical halogenation, whereas alkenes rapidly and visibly decolorize Br2 at room temperature via fast electrophilic addition, making the color change a useful diagnostic test.

addition-reactions.q: What is the correct order of key mechanistic steps in the ionic (non-radical) addition of HX to an alkene?
options: nucleophile attacks first, then protonation occurs
halide ion attacks the alkene directly in one step with no intermediate
protonation first gives a carbocation, then halide attacks
the alkene is first oxidized, then protonated
addition-reactions.why: In the standard two-step mechanism, the pi bond acts as a nucleophile toward the acidic H of HX, forming the more stable carbocation in the rate-determining first step, after which halide ion rapidly captures that carbocation.

addition-reactions.q: In the ionic addition of HX to an alkene, what determines the rate-determining step?
options: the final product stability has no bearing on rate at all
halide attack on the carbocation is always rate-determining
the reaction has no discernible rate-determining step
addition-reactions.why: Generating the carbocation requires breaking the pi bond and is the higher-activation-energy step; the subsequent capture of that carbocation by halide ion is fast, so the first step controls the overall rate.

addition-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an alkene can give rearranged (unexpected) products because the reaction proceeds through a carbocation intermediate that can undergo hydride or alkyl shifts.
addition-reactions.why: Because a genuine carbocation forms during acid-catalyzed hydration, it is free to rearrange to a more stable carbocation (via a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift) before water attacks, sometimes giving a product with the OH in an unexpected position.

addition-reactions.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration avoids the rearranged products possible in simple acid-catalyzed hydration because the mechanism proceeds through:
options: a bridged mercurinium ion with delocalized positive charge
a fully localized, long-lived carbocation just like acid hydration
direct nucleophilic substitution with no intermediate at all
addition-reactions.why: Because the mercurinium ion delocalizes the positive charge across a three-membered ring rather than placing it entirely on one carbon, there's no free carbocation available to rearrange before water attacks the more substituted carbon.

addition-reactions.q: How does the degree of alkyl substitution on an alkene generally affect its rate of electrophilic addition (e.g., with HX or Br2)?
options: more substituted alkenes react more slowly because they are more stable and less reactive
more substituted alkenes react faster, being more electron-rich
substitution has no effect on the rate of addition
only terminal alkenes undergo electrophilic addition at a useful rate
addition-reactions.why: Additional alkyl groups donate electron density into the pi system (making it a better nucleophile toward electrophiles) and stabilize the developing positive charge in the transition state, so more substituted alkenes typically react faster in electrophilic additions.

addition-reactions.q: Halogenation of an alkene gives anti addition, while catalytic hydrogenation gives syn addition. What accounts for this mechanistic difference?
options: halogenation and hydrogenation actually proceed through the identical intermediate
hydrogenation always occurs in two completely separate, unrelated steps years apart
halogenation goes via a bridged halonium ion, hydrogenation via a metal surface
anti addition only happens with gases, and syn addition only happens with liquids
addition-reactions.why: The bromonium/chloronium ion intermediate in halogenation blocks one face, forcing backside (anti) attack by the halide, whereas in hydrogenation both H atoms come from the same catalyst surface onto the same (syn) face — different intermediates give different stereochemical outcomes.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov addition places the new H (or nucleophile, depending on convention) on the carbon that is:
markovnikov.why: Markovnikov’s rule: the electrophile (often H⁺) adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already, placing the nucleophile on the more substituted (more stable-cation) carbon.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov addition (e.g., via radical HBr addition) places Br on the:
options: Same carbon as in Markovnikov addition
markovnikov.why: Radical mechanisms form the more stable radical at the more substituted carbon, so Br ends up on the less substituted carbon — opposite of the ionic Markovnikov outcome.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov’s rule is best explained mechanistically by:
options: Formation of the more stable carbocation
Steric hindrance of the nucleophile alone
markovnikov.why: In ionic (non-radical) addition, the proton adds to give whichever carbon leads to the more stable carbocation — i.e., the more substituted one — and the nucleophile then attacks that cation.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule states that when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds preferentially to the carbon that:
options: already has the fewest hydrogens attached
already has the most hydrogens attached
markovnikov.why: Markovnikov's original empirical rule: the H of HX ends up on the carbon that already bears more hydrogens, while X ends up on the more substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule was originally formulated as an empirical observation about reaction outcomes before the carbocation mechanism was understood.
markovnikov.why: Vladimir Markovnikov proposed the rule in 1865 based on observed patterns in addition reactions, decades before carbocation intermediates and their stability were used to explain why the rule holds.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product when HCl adds to propene (CH3-CH=CH2)?
markovnikov.why: Protonation occurs at the terminal CH2 carbon to generate the more stable secondary carbocation, which chloride then captures, giving 2-chloropropane as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr to an alkene is observed specifically under which condition?
options: with excess HBr and no catalyst
markovnikov.why: Peroxides generate bromine radicals that initiate a radical chain addition mechanism, which adds Br first and gives the opposite (anti-Markovnikov) regiochemistry compared to the normal ionic pathway.

markovnikov.q: When HBr adds to propene in the presence of peroxides, the major product is 1-bromopropane rather than 2-bromopropane.
markovnikov.why: Under radical (peroxide) conditions, bromine adds first to the terminal carbon to generate the more stable secondary radical, placing Br at the end of the chain — the anti-Markovnikov product, 1-bromopropane.

markovnikov.q: Acid-catalyzed (Markovnikov) hydration of 2-methylpropene (isobutylene) gives which alcohol as the major product?
markovnikov.why: Protonation generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the central carbon, which water then attacks, giving tert-butanol as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: In determining the Markovnikov product, which carbocation is more stable and therefore favored as the reaction intermediate?
options: it doesn't matter, they're equally stable
secondary carbocation (compared to a primary option)
markovnikov.why: Carbocation stability increases with substitution (methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary) due to hyperconjugation and inductive donation from neighboring alkyl groups, so the reaction favors forming the more substituted, more stable carbocation.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov selectivity with peroxides works equally well for HCl, HBr, and HI.
markovnikov.why: Only HBr undergoes an efficient radical chain addition; the bond energetics for HCl and HI make the necessary radical propagation steps unfavorable, so anti-Markovnikov addition is essentially unique to HBr among the hydrogen halides.

markovnikov.q: The term 'Markovnikov addition' is named after:
markovnikov.why: Vladimir Markovnikov, a 19th-century Russian chemist, first described the regiochemical pattern now named after him.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product of HBr addition (no peroxides) to 1-methylcyclohexene?
options: Br ends up on C2, away from the methyl group
Br ends up on C1, bearing the methyl group
Br adds to both carbons equally
No reaction occurs because the alkene is in a ring
markovnikov.why: Protonation of the ring double bond occurs at C2 to place the positive charge on C1 (already bearing a methyl group), forming the more stable tertiary carbocation; bromide then attacks C1, so Br and the methyl end up on the same carbon.

markovnikov.q: What is the major product of HI addition to 2-methyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3?
options: 2-iodo-2-methylbutane (I on the more substituted, tertiary carbon)
markovnikov.why: Protonating the less substituted alkene carbon generates the more stable tertiary carbocation at the other carbon; iodide then attacks that tertiary center, giving 2-iodo-2-methylbutane as the Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's rule can be restated in mechanistic terms as: the electrophile's positively polarized atom adds to whichever carbon generates the more stable carbocation intermediate.
markovnikov.why: This mechanistic restatement explains the empirical rule: reaction proceeds through the lower-energy transition state, which is the pathway that forms the more stable (typically more substituted) carbocation.

markovnikov.q: For a terminal alkene CH2=CHR reacting with HX under normal ionic conditions, the halogen X ends up mainly on:
options: neither carbon; X leaves as HX unreacted
the internal carbon bearing R (the more substituted carbon)
markovnikov.why: Protonation at the terminal CH2 carbon generates the more stable carbocation at the internal, more substituted carbon, which halide then attacks, placing X on that more substituted carbon.

markovnikov.q: How does the regiochemistry of hydroboration-oxidation compare to Markovnikov's rule?
options: it is anti-Markovnikov: OH ends up on the less substituted carbon
it gives a random mixture with no preference
it only works on alkynes, not alkenes
markovnikov.why: Because hydroboration proceeds through steric control (boron adding to the less hindered carbon) rather than carbocation stability, the resulting alcohol has OH on the less substituted carbon — the opposite of the typical Markovnikov outcome.

markovnikov.q: Oxymercuration-demercuration of an alkene installs the new OH group following which regiochemical pattern?
options: anti-Markovnikov orientation (OH on the less substituted carbon)
Markovnikov orientation (OH on the more substituted carbon)
OH always ends up on a terminal carbon regardless of substitution
no defined pattern; products are random
markovnikov.why: Water attacks the more substituted carbon of the bridged mercurinium ion, where positive character is greater, giving the same overall Markovnikov regiochemistry as acid-catalyzed hydration, but without carbocation rearrangement.

markovnikov.q: In the anti-Markovnikov radical addition of HBr, a bromine radical (not a hydrogen atom) is the species that adds first, attaching to the terminal carbon.
markovnikov.why: The radical chain begins when a bromine radical adds to the less hindered terminal carbon, generating the more stable internal (secondary or tertiary) carbon radical, which then abstracts H from HBr — this order is why Br ends up terminal.

markovnikov.q: What intermediate determines the regiochemistry of anti-Markovnikov radical addition of HBr?
markovnikov.why: Radical addition proceeds by bromine radical adding to generate the most stable carbon radical (paralleling how ionic mechanisms favor the most stable carbocation), which dictates where Br ultimately attaches.

markovnikov.q: Why does ordinary HBr addition (no peroxides present) give the Markovnikov product rather than the anti-Markovnikov one?
options: HBr is simply incapable of anti-Markovnikov addition under any conditions
anti-Markovnikov addition requires light, which is always present
HBr only reacts with alkynes, not alkenes, without peroxides
without a radical initiator, the ionic carbocation path dominates
markovnikov.why: The radical chain mechanism needs peroxides (or similar initiators) to generate the initial bromine radical; absent that, the alkene reacts through the conventional polar mechanism, which is governed by carbocation stability and gives the Markovnikov outcome.

markovnikov.q: Addition of HCl to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, (CH3)3C-CH=CH2, can give a rearranged product in addition to the expected one because:
options: the secondary carbocation shifts a methyl to become tertiary
HCl never reacts with this alkene
the methyl groups block all possible addition
the secondary carbocation is already the most stable possible intermediate here
markovnikov.why: Protonation gives a secondary carbocation adjacent to a carbon bearing three methyl groups; a methyl group can shift over (1,2-shift) to generate a more stable tertiary carbocation, leading to a rearranged chloride product alongside the 'simple' Markovnikov product.

markovnikov.q: Why does a tertiary carbocation intermediate lead to the Markovnikov product being favored over one from a secondary carbocation?
options: tertiary carbocations are actually less stable, so they form more slowly but give better yields
tertiary carbocations are better stabilized by hyperconjugation and induction
tertiary carbocations are not real intermediates, just a convenient theoretical tool
secondary and tertiary carbocations are always equally stable
markovnikov.why: More alkyl groups attached to the cationic carbon donate electron density through hyperconjugation and induction, lowering the energy of the carbocation and the transition state leading to it, which channels the reaction toward the product derived from the more stable intermediate.

markovnikov.q: Radical (anti-Markovnikov) addition of HBr proceeds via the more stable free radical intermediate, in direct analogy to how the ionic mechanism proceeds via the more stable carbocation.
markovnikov.why: Both mechanisms are governed by the same underlying principle — the reaction pathway that generates the lower-energy reactive intermediate (radical or cation) is favored — they just differ in which species (radical vs. cation) and which atom (Br vs. H) adds first.

markovnikov.q: In peroxide-mediated (anti-Markovnikov) HBr addition, what species initiates the radical chain?
options: a bromide anion formed by simple ionization of HBr
a proton (H+) generated from the peroxide
a bromine radical from peroxide plus HBr
a carbocation formed directly from the peroxide
markovnikov.why: Peroxides undergo weak O-O bond homolysis to generate alkoxy radicals, which abstract a hydrogen atom from HBr to generate a bromine radical; this bromine radical is what adds to the alkene to begin the chain.

markovnikov.q: Markovnikov's original rule (H goes to the carbon with more H's already) becomes ambiguous or insufficient in which situation, revealing why the carbocation-stability explanation is actually needed?
options: never; the simple rule always works perfectly for every alkene
only for symmetrical alkenes, which have no regiochemistry question at all
only when no acid catalyst is present
for complex alkenes, counting H's doesn't identify the stabler cation
markovnikov.why: The simple 'more H's' heuristic can fail to clearly distinguish outcomes for more complex or highly substituted alkenes; the mechanistic version — protonate to form the more stable carbocation — is the general and reliable explanation underlying the empirical rule.

markovnikov.q: Why is anti-Markovnikov addition essentially unique to HBr among the hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), rather than occurring readily with HCl or HI too?
options: the radical chain steps are selective for Br but not Cl or I
HCl and HI simply don't exist as reagents
HCl and HI are too unreactive to add to alkenes by any mechanism
anti-Markovnikov addition actually works equally well for all four halides
markovnikov.why: The bond dissociation energies involved make each step of the HBr radical chain reasonably exothermic and selective, while the analogous steps for HCl are too exothermic and unselective and for HI are endothermic, so a clean radical chain mechanism practically only works for HBr.

markovnikov.q: Anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry from a radical mechanism is a special case associated with HBr addition; it does not apply to ordinary acid-catalyzed hydration or to halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) reactions under typical conditions.
markovnikov.why: Hydration and halogenation (Br2/Cl2 addition) proceed through cationic or bridged-ion intermediates that follow normal Markovnikov-type (most stable intermediate) selectivity; the radical chain pathway that flips the regiochemistry is essentially unique to peroxide-mediated HBr addition.

markovnikov.q: Comparing HBr addition to 2-methyl-1-butene with and without peroxides, what regiochemical difference is expected?
options: no difference; both conditions give the identical major product
without peroxides, Br goes to C2; with peroxides, to C1
without peroxides, Br ends up on C1; with peroxides, Br ends up on C2
peroxides prevent the reaction from occurring at all
markovnikov.why: The ionic pathway is governed by carbocation stability, favoring Br at the more substituted carbon (C2); the radical pathway is governed by radical stability formed by Br adding first to the terminal carbon (C1), flipping the regiochemistry.

markovnikov.q: Rank the following carbocations from least to most stable, which underlies the reasoning behind Markovnikov's rule:
options: tertiary less than secondary less than primary less than methyl
secondary less than methyl less than tertiary less than primary
methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary
all carbocations are equally stable regardless of substitution
markovnikov.why: Carbocation stability increases with the number of alkyl groups attached to the cationic carbon because each alkyl group donates electron density via hyperconjugation and the inductive effect, giving the order methyl less than primary less than secondary less than tertiary.

alkynes.q: A terminal alkyne’s C–H is unusually acidic (pKa ~25) because:
options: There is no acidity difference from alkanes
alkynes.why: sp hybrid orbitals have 50% s-character (vs. 25% for sp³), holding the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilizing the conjugate base — more s-character, more acidic.

alkynes.q: How many pi bonds are in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: A triple bond is 1 sigma bond plus 2 pi bonds.

alkynes.q: Compared to an alkene, an alkyne undergoing addition of 2 equivalents of HX can ultimately give what kind of product?
options: Only a single addition is ever possible
A geminal dihalide (both halogens on the same carbon) after two additions
alkynes.why: The first HX addition (following Markovnikov) gives a vinyl halide; a second addition of HX to that alkene gives a geminal dihalide, both halogens on the same, more substituted carbon.

alkynes.q: What is the hybridization of each carbon in a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: Each alkyne carbon forms two sigma bonds (linear, 180°) using sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridized p orbitals to form the two pi bonds of the triple bond.

alkynes.q: What is the approximate bond angle around each carbon of a terminal or internal alkyne?
alkynes.why: sp-hybridized carbons arrange their two sigma bonds linearly, 180° apart, giving alkynes their characteristic straight, rod-like geometry at the triple bond.

alkynes.q: Alkynes are generally somewhat less reactive than alkenes toward many electrophilic addition reactions because the sp carbons hold their pi electrons more tightly.
alkynes.why: Alkyne pi electrons are held closer to the carbon nuclei due to the higher s-character (more electronegative character) of sp carbons, making the alkyne pi bond somewhat less available to electrophiles compared to the more loosely held pi electrons of an alkene.

alkynes.q: What is the general molecular formula for an acyclic alkyne with one triple bond and n carbons?
alkynes.why: A triple bond counts as two degrees of unsaturation, removing four hydrogens relative to the saturated alkane (CnH2n+2), giving CnH2n-2.

alkynes.q: A terminal alkyne is defined by having the triple bond:
options: in the middle of a long carbon chain
at the end of the chain, with one triple-bond carbon bonded directly to a hydrogen
alkynes.why: In a terminal alkyne, such as HC≡C-CH3 (propyne), one sp carbon of the triple bond is bonded to a hydrogen atom rather than to another carbon, placing the triple bond at the very end of the chain.

alkynes.q: In an internal alkyne, both triple-bond carbons are bonded to other carbons rather than to hydrogen.
alkynes.why: An internal alkyne, like 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), has the triple bond flanked on both sides by carbon substituents, distinguishing it from a terminal alkyne, which has a triple-bond C-H.

alkynes.q: Addition of exactly 1 equivalent of Br2 to an internal alkyne gives what kind of product?
options: a saturated alkane with four bromines
a tetrahalide with no unsaturation remaining
a dihaloalkene, with one degree of unsaturation still remaining
alkynes.why: Just as with alkenes, Br2 adds across one of the two pi bonds of the triple bond first, converting the alkyne into a dihalogenated alkene; a second equivalent of Br2 would be needed to fully saturate it into a tetrahalide.

alkynes.q: Which IUPAC suffix indicates a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: The suffix -yne is used specifically to denote a triple bond in the parent chain, as in ethyne (acetylene) or 2-butyne.

alkynes.q: How many sigma bonds exist directly between the two carbon atoms of a carbon-carbon triple bond?
alkynes.why: A triple bond is composed of exactly one sigma bond (from head-on sp-sp orbital overlap) plus two pi bonds (from two pairs of unhybridized p orbitals); there is never more than one sigma bond between any two directly bonded atoms.

alkynes.q: Why is the C-H bond of a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25) considerably more acidic than a similar C-H bond in an alkene or alkane?
options: the alkyne C-H bond is longer and weaker
alkynes have more hydrogens overall, diluting the charge
the sp carbanion has more s-character, stabilizing the charge
terminal alkynes contain an oxygen atom that withdraws electron density
alkynes.why: An sp orbital has 50% s character, versus 33% for sp2 and 25% for sp3; more s character means the lone pair sits closer to and is better stabilized by the positively charged nucleus, making the conjugate base (acetylide ion) more stable and the C-H more acidic.

alkynes.q: Given the approximate pKa values: alkane C-H ~50, alkene C-H ~44, alkyne C-H ~25, water ~15.7, which of these four is the most acidic?
alkynes.why: A lower pKa means a stronger acid; water at pKa ~15.7 is far more acidic than even a terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25), even though the alkyne C-H is unusually acidic compared to other hydrocarbon C-H bonds.

alkynes.q: Which of the following bases is commonly strong enough to fully deprotonate a terminal alkyne C-H?
alkynes.why: Since the conjugate acid of amide ion, ammonia (pKa ~38), is a much weaker acid than a terminal alkyne (pKa ~25), sodium amide is a strong enough base to completely deprotonate terminal alkynes to form acetylide ions; hydroxide (conjugate acid water, pKa ~15.7) is not strong enough.

alkynes.q: The acetylide ion formed by deprotonating a terminal alkyne is a good nucleophile that can be used in SN2 reactions with primary alkyl halides to form a new carbon-carbon bond.
alkynes.why: Acetylide ions are strong, relatively unhindered carbanion-like nucleophiles that readily displace halide from primary (unhindered) alkyl halides via SN2, a classic method for extending carbon chains and building larger alkynes.

alkynes.q: Acid/Hg2+-catalyzed (Markovnikov) hydration of a terminal alkyne proceeds through an unstable enol intermediate that then converts into what final functional group?
alkynes.why: Markovnikov addition of water places OH on the more substituted alkyne carbon, generating an enol, which rapidly tautomerizes (favoring the more stable keto form) into a ketone.

alkynes.q: Anti-Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne via hydroboration-oxidation ultimately yields what functional group?
alkynes.why: Boron adds to the less substituted terminal carbon; oxidation replaces boron with OH there, giving an enol with OH on the terminal carbon, which tautomerizes to an aldehyde rather than a ketone.

alkynes.q: Treating an alkyne with excess H2 and a Pt (or Pd/Ni) catalyst results in complete reduction to the corresponding alkane.
alkynes.why: With an unrestricted (non-poisoned) metal catalyst and excess H2, both pi bonds of the triple bond are hydrogenated in sequence, first to the alkene and then fully to the alkane.

alkynes.q: Partial hydrogenation of an internal alkyne using Lindlar's catalyst (Pd poisoned with lead and quinoline) gives predominantly which product?
alkynes.why: Lindlar's catalyst delivers both hydrogens to the same face of the triple bond (syn addition) and is deliberately poisoned to stop after adding just one equivalent of H2, giving the cis alkene selectively.

alkynes.q: Reduction of an internal alkyne with sodium metal in liquid ammonia (Na/NH3, a dissolving-metal reduction) gives predominantly which product?
options: no reaction; Na/NH3 does not reduce alkynes
alkynes.why: The Na/NH3 dissolving-metal mechanism proceeds through a vinyl radical/anion intermediate that equilibrates to the more stable, less crowded trans geometry before picking up a second electron and proton, giving the trans alkene selectively — complementary to Lindlar's cis selectivity.

alkynes.q: Mechanistically, why does Lindlar's catalyst stop at the cis-alkene stage rather than continuing on to the fully saturated alkane?
options: the cis-alkene is simply the only possible product from any hydrogenation of a triple bond
the poisoned catalyst adds H2 to the alkyne but is far less active toward the alkene
Lindlar's catalyst only works on terminal alkynes
the reaction is run with insufficient H2 gas to go any further
alkynes.why: Lead and quinoline additives reduce the catalytic activity of Pd just enough that it can still deliver H2 syn across a triple bond but is much less effective at further adsorbing and reducing the resulting alkene, letting the reaction be stopped cleanly at the cis-alkene stage.

alkynes.q: Mechanistically, why does dissolving-metal (Na/NH3) reduction of an internal alkyne favor the trans alkene rather than the cis?
options: the mechanism is identical to catalytic hydrogenation, which also favors trans products
trans alkenes are formed because Na/NH3 is a poor reducing agent that barely reacts
the vinyl radical anion adopts the more stable trans-like geometry
the alkyne first converts to a cis alkene, which then isomerizes under basic conditions
alkynes.why: Unlike the concerted syn delivery on a catalyst surface, the dissolving-metal mechanism proceeds stepwise through a radical anion intermediate that has time to adopt the thermodynamically preferred, less strained trans-like arrangement before being fully reduced, giving the trans alkene as the major product.

alkynes.q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of an unsymmetrical internal alkyne can give a mixture of two different ketones, because water can add with its oxygen ending up on either of the two different triple-bond carbons.
alkynes.why: Unless the internal alkyne is symmetrical, Markovnikov addition of water is not perfectly selective for one carbon over the other when both are similarly substituted, so both possible enol/ketone regiochemistries can form, giving a mixture of ketone products.

alkynes.q: When a terminal alkyne reacts with 2 equivalents of HBr (no peroxides), Markovnikov addition occurs in both steps. What is the final product?
options: a 1,2-dibromide with one Br on each of the original terminal alkyne carbons
a vicinal dihalide alkene still containing a double bond
an alkane with no halogens at all
a geminal dihalide, with both bromine atoms ending up on the same (internal, more substituted) carbon
alkynes.why: The first HBr addition follows Markovnikov's rule, putting Br on the more substituted carbon to form a bromoalkene; the second HBr addition again follows Markovnikov's rule on that bromoalkene, placing the second Br on the very same carbon, yielding a geminal dihalide.

alkynes.q: Why does the initial product of acid-catalyzed alkyne hydration (an enol) not survive as the final isolated product?
options: the enol tautomerizes to the more stable keto form
the enol is actually more stable than the corresponding ketone and is isolated unchanged
enols are never formed in alkyne hydration in the first place
the enol immediately polymerizes into a completely different product class
alkynes.why: Keto-enol tautomerization is a fast, acid- or base-catalyzed equilibrium that overwhelmingly favors the keto form because a C=O pi bond is significantly more stable than a C=C-OH arrangement, so the enol formed transiently from alkyne hydration converts essentially completely to the ketone.

alkynes.q: Terminal alkynes, but not internal alkynes, give an aldehyde product from hydroboration-oxidation, because boron selectively adds to the less hindered, terminal carbon of the triple bond.
alkynes.why: Only a terminal alkyne has a CH-bearing end carbon available for boron's steric preference to place OH there after oxidation, generating a terminal enol that tautomerizes to an aldehyde; internal alkynes lack a terminal position and instead give ketones.

alkynes.q: Ranking carbon-carbon bond lengths and relative bond strengths from a single bond to a triple bond, which statement is correct?
options: triple bonds are the longest and weakest of the three
triple bonds are the shortest and strongest
all three bond types have essentially identical length and strength
double bonds are shorter than triple bonds
alkynes.why: More shared electron pairs (three bonding pairs in a triple bond) pull the bonded atoms closer together and require more energy to break, and the increased s-character of sp orbitals further shortens the sigma bond, making triple bonds the shortest and strongest, followed by double, then single bonds.

alkynes.q: Why does a carbon-carbon triple bond contain two mutually perpendicular pi bonds rather than one larger pi bond?
options: because triple bonds actually only have one pi bond, just like double bonds
because the two pi bonds merge into a single circular orbital around the bond axis
each sp carbon has two perpendicular p orbitals that overlap separately
because nitrogen atoms are required to form the second pi bond
alkynes.why: sp hybridization uses only one s and one p orbital, leaving two p orbitals unhybridized and oriented perpendicular to each other; each of these forms its own independent pi bond with the matching p orbital on the other sp carbon, giving two distinct, perpendicular pi bonds plus the one sigma bond.

alkynes.q: Treating a symmetrical internal alkyne, such as 2-butyne (CH3-C≡C-CH3), with H2O/H2SO4/HgSO4 gives what outcome, and why?
options: a mixture of two different ketones, because the molecule isn't symmetrical enough to favor one over the other
no reaction at all, because symmetrical alkynes cannot undergo hydration
an alcohol with no carbonyl group formed
a single ketone (2-butanone), since symmetry makes either addition give the same product
alkynes.why: Because both triple-bond carbons of 2-butyne carry identical methyl substituents, it doesn't matter which carbon water's oxygen ends up on — both regiochemical outcomes converge on the same single ketone product (2-butanone), avoiding the mixture problem seen with unsymmetrical internal alkynes.

conjugated-systems.q: Two double bonds separated by two sp3 carbons are described as what?
conjugated-systems.why: Their p orbitals never meet, so each double bond behaves as though the other were not there.

conjugated-systems.q: Two double bonds alternating with a single bond are described as what?
conjugated-systems.why: Every carbon in the run is sp2 and the p orbitals overlap continuously.

conjugated-systems.q: Two double bonds sharing a carbon are described as what?
conjugated-systems.why: The shared carbon is sp, and the two pi systems are perpendicular, so they cannot interact.

conjugated-systems.q: Which arrangement is the most stable?
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugated > isolated > cumulated. Only the conjugated arrangement earns delocalization energy.

conjugated-systems.q: Which arrangement is the least stable?
conjugated-systems.why: A cumulated diene has an sp carbon holding two perpendicular pi systems, and is strained relative to the alternatives.

conjugated-systems.q: Hydrogenating but-1-ene releases about how much energy?
conjugated-systems.why: Two isolated double bonds should therefore release about twice that, roughly 254 kJ/mol.

conjugated-systems.q: Buta-1,3-diene releases about 239 kJ/mol on hydrogenation. What does that show?
options: It is about 15 kJ/mol more stable
It is much less stable than expected
conjugated-systems.why: It gives out less energy reaching the same kind of product, so it started lower down. That difference is the delocalization energy.

conjugated-systems.q: How long is the C2-C3 bond of buta-1,3-diene?
conjugated-systems.why: Shorter than an ordinary C-C single bond at 1.54 A, because the pi system is delocalized and the bond has partial double-bond character.

conjugated-systems.q: What does the s in s-cis stand for?
conjugated-systems.why: It describes the conformation about the SINGLE bond joining the two double bonds, not a double-bond geometry.

conjugated-systems.q: Can s-cis and s-trans interconvert at room temperature?
options: Only with an acid catalyst present
conjugated-systems.why: They are conformations about a single bond, so rotation is free. cis and trans across a double bond cannot interconvert without breaking the pi bond.

conjugated-systems.q: Which conformation of a conjugated diene is more stable?
conjugated-systems.why: In s-cis the terminal hydrogens crowd each other, so it sits slightly higher in energy.

conjugated-systems.q: Which conformation does the Diels-Alder reaction require?
conjugated-systems.why: The two ends of the diene must reach the two ends of the dienophile at once, which only s-cis allows.

conjugated-systems.q: Why is a diene locked s-trans unreactive in a Diels-Alder?
options: It is far too electron-poor to react
Its ends cannot reach the dienophile
conjugated-systems.why: The requirement is geometric, not electronic. No amount of electron-donating substitution fixes it.

conjugated-systems.q: Where does the positive charge sit in an allylic cation?
conjugated-systems.why: Draw both resonance forms: the charge appears at the termini and never in the middle.

conjugated-systems.q: Why are allylic and benzylic cations unusually stable?
options: They are sterically protected from attack
Their charge is delocalized by conjugation
conjugated-systems.why: An empty p orbital next to a pi system conjugates with it, which is the same delocalization you draw as resonance.

conjugated-systems.q: Which of these can conjugate with an adjacent pi bond?
options: Only another pi bond can do this
A lone pair, empty p orbital or radical
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugation needs a p orbital that can align, and all of these provide one.

conjugated-systems.q: Roughly how much stabilization does conjugation provide in buta-1,3-diene?
conjugated-systems.why: Measured as the gap between its heat of hydrogenation and that of two isolated double bonds.

conjugated-systems.q: What is propa-1,2-diene commonly called?
conjugated-systems.why: It is the simplest cumulated diene, with an sp central carbon.

conjugated-systems.q: Why can the two pi systems of an allene not conjugate?
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugation needs p orbitals aligned closely enough to overlap. At right angles they cannot.

conjugated-systems.q: Penta-1,4-diene is an example of which arrangement?
conjugated-systems.why: One sp3 carbon sits between the two double bonds, breaking the conjugation.

conjugated-systems.q: Which hybridization do the carbons of a conjugated diene have?
conjugated-systems.why: Every carbon in the conjugated run is sp2, which is what lets the p orbitals line up.

conjugated-systems.q: What is the central carbon of an allene hybridized as?
conjugated-systems.why: Two double bonds to one carbon means two sigma bonds and two pi systems, which is sp.

conjugated-systems.q: What does the shortened C2-C3 bond of butadiene tell you?
options: The pi system is delocalized over it
conjugated-systems.why: A formally single bond with partial double-bond character is direct evidence for delocalization.

conjugated-systems.q: Why is cyclopentadiene unusually reactive as a diene?
conjugated-systems.why: It never has to pay the rotation penalty, and it dimerizes on standing as a result.

conjugated-systems.q: Conjugation is best described as what, in orbital terms?
conjugated-systems.why: It is the orbital picture of the same delocalization you draw with resonance structures.

conjugated-systems.q: How does an allylic radical compare to an ordinary alkyl radical?
conjugated-systems.why: Its half-filled p orbital conjugates with the adjacent pi bond, spreading the unpaired electron.

conjugated-systems.q: Which is NOT evidence for delocalization in buta-1,3-diene?
conjugated-systems.why: The formula is the same as for an isolated diene. The other three all report on the electrons.

conjugated-systems.q: What happens to reactivity along a conjugated system?
conjugated-systems.why: The termini carry the charge, the odd electron, or the largest orbital coefficients.

conjugated-systems.q: Why is conjugation relevant to allylic bromination?
options: It blocks the position from attack
conjugated-systems.why: Abstracting an allylic hydrogen leaves a resonance-delocalized radical, which makes that abstraction much easier.

conjugated-systems.q: Which sequence gives the correct stability order?
conjugated-systems.why: Conjugation stabilizes; cumulation destabilizes relative to having the double bonds apart.

diene-addition.q: Adding one equivalent of HBr to buta-1,3-diene gives how many products?
diene-addition.why: The intermediate is an allylic cation with two reactive ends, so bromide has two places to attack.

diene-addition.q: What kind of intermediate forms when HBr protonates buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Protonating C1 puts the charge next to the remaining double bond, so it delocalizes.

diene-addition.q: In the 1,2-addition product from buta-1,3-diene, where is the double bond?
diene-addition.why: 3-bromobut-1-ene keeps a terminal CH2= group.

diene-addition.q: In the 1,4-addition product from buta-1,3-diene, where is the double bond?
diene-addition.why: 1-bromobut-2-ene has the double bond in the middle of the chain, disubstituted.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,2-addition product of HBr and buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures C2, the carbon carrying most of the positive charge.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,4-addition product of HBr and buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures C4, at the far end of the delocalized system.

diene-addition.q: At about -80 C, which product dominates?
diene-addition.why: Roughly 80:20 in favor of 1,2. Cold and irreversible means the rates decide.

diene-addition.q: At about 40 C, which product dominates?
diene-addition.why: Roughly 15:85 in favor of 1,4. Warm and reversible means the stabilities decide.

diene-addition.q: Why does bromide attack C2 faster than C4?
options: More positive charge sits on C2
C4 is not electrophilic at all here
diene-addition.why: The resonance form with charge on C2 is secondary and the other is primary, so the better form puts more charge on C2.

diene-addition.q: Why is the 1,4-product more stable?
diene-addition.why: Alkene stability rises with substitution, and the 1,4-product's double bond is internal and disubstituted.

diene-addition.q: What does 1,4-addition also get called?
diene-addition.why: You will meet the same name in enolate chemistry, for the same reason.

diene-addition.q: In the term 1,4-addition, what do the numbers refer to?
options: The number of new bonds formed
diene-addition.why: They describe where the two new groups landed relative to the starting diene, not the product's own numbering.

diene-addition.q: Warming the pure 1,2-product with a trace of HBr gives a 15:85 mixture. What does that prove?
diene-addition.why: Bromide can leave again and regenerate the allylic cation, so the system re-equilibrates.

diene-addition.q: How many resonance forms describe the allylic cation from buta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Charge on C2 in one and on C4 in the other, with C3 never carrying it.

diene-addition.q: Which resonance form of that cation is the major contributor?
diene-addition.why: A secondary carbocation is more stable than a primary one, so it describes more of the real intermediate.

diene-addition.q: Protonating 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene at C1 gives which cation?
diene-addition.why: The charge lands on C2, which bears two methyls and the chain.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,2-product from HBr and 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures the tertiary carbon, leaving the terminal alkene intact.

diene-addition.q: What is the 1,4-product from HBr and 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene?
diene-addition.why: Bromide captures the far end, and the alkene moves inward to become trisubstituted.

diene-addition.q: Why is penta-1,3-diene a poor example for comparing 1,2 and 1,4 products?
options: It does not react with HBr at all
diene-addition.why: With a methyl at each end of the allylic cation, capturing at either end gives the same compound.

diene-addition.q: Which carbon of the allylic cation never carries positive charge?
diene-addition.why: Neither resonance form places charge on the middle carbon of the three-carbon system.

diene-addition.q: Is the double bond moving in 1,4-addition a rearrangement?
options: No, it is the other resonance form being captured
No, and the double bond does not actually move
diene-addition.why: Nothing shifts. The intermediate was already delocalized, and capture at the far end simply fixes the other form.

diene-addition.q: What is the first step of HBr addition to a conjugated diene?
options: The proton adds to a terminal carbon
diene-addition.why: The pi system is nucleophilic and takes the proton, which generates the allylic cation.

diene-addition.q: Why is protonation at a terminal carbon preferred?
diene-addition.why: Protonating an inner carbon would give a cation that cannot delocalize into the remaining double bond.

diene-addition.q: What would you change to favor the kinetic product?
diene-addition.why: Cold conditions prevent the products from reverting, so the first-formed ratio is frozen in.

diene-addition.q: What would you change to favor the thermodynamic product?
diene-addition.why: Warming allows bromide to leave again, so the mixture can re-equilibrate into the deeper well.

diene-addition.q: How does 1,2-addition to a diene compare to ordinary alkene addition?
options: It is the same mechanism with a delocalized cation
It is an entirely different mechanism
diene-addition.why: Protonation then capture, exactly as for a simple alkene. The only difference is that the cation is allylic.

diene-addition.q: Both products from buta-1,3-diene and HBr have which formula?
diene-addition.why: One HBr adds across the system, so both are isomers of the same formula.

diene-addition.q: Which statement about the two products is correct?
options: They are different compounds with the same formula
diene-addition.why: They are constitutional isomers, differing in where the Br and the double bond sit.

diene-addition.q: What makes an intermediate capable of giving two products?
diene-addition.why: A localized cation has one electrophilic carbon; a delocalized one has two.

diene-addition.q: Where does conjugate addition reappear later in the course?
diene-addition.why: A nucleophile adding to the far end of a conjugated enone is the same idea with a different intermediate.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What is the kinetic product?
options: The one with the most new bonds
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Lower transition state, smaller activation energy. It need not be the most stable product available.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What is the thermodynamic product?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Lower in energy once formed. It need not be the one that forms fastest.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What must be true for thermodynamic control to operate?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: The system can only settle into the most stable product if it is able to leave the others.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What conditions favor kinetic control?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Low temperature stops anything climbing back out, so the first-formed ratio is frozen in.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What conditions favor thermodynamic control?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Warming supplies the energy to reverse the step, so the system can explore and settle in the deepest well.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Kinetics is about which of these?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: How high the hill is on the way out. Thermodynamics is how deep the valley is when you land.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Thermodynamics is about which of these?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Stability of the product, which is a separate question from how fast it forms.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Does the lower barrier always lead to the more stable product?
options: Only when the reaction is reversible throughout
No, and the interesting cases are when it does not
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: When they coincide there is nothing to discuss. The distinction matters precisely when they do not.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What does raising the temperature actually change?
options: Which of the products is intrinsically more stable
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Stability and rates are properties of the system. Temperature decides whether the system is allowed to find out.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A stated temperature of -78 C usually signals what?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: An unusually low temperature is there to stop the reaction reversing, which freezes in the faster-formed product.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Which enolate does LDA at -78 C give?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: A bulky base removes the most accessible proton fastest, and the cold prevents equilibration.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Which enolate do warm equilibrating conditions give?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: The more substituted, more stable enolate, because the system can now re-equilibrate into it.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Why can a sulfonic acid group be installed on a ring and later removed?
options: It never really attaches to the ring at all
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Most electrophilic aromatic substitutions cannot be undone; sulfonation can, which makes it useful as a blocking group.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Zaitsev's more substituted alkene is which kind of product?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: It is the more stable alkene. The Hofmann product from a bulky base is the kinetic outcome instead.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A bulky base giving the less substituted alkene is which kind of outcome?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Sterics make the less hindered proton faster to remove, so the faster route wins.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Product A forms faster; product B is more stable. Cold and irreversible, what do you get?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Rates decide, and B's extra stability is irrelevant because nothing will ever visit it.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Product A forms faster; product B is more stable. Warm and reversible, what do you get?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Both keep forming and reverting, so the mixture drains into the deeper well.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: B is more stable but its formation is irreversible. Does heating help?
options: Only in the presence of a catalyst
Yes, prolonged heating steadily gives more B
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Without a way back, you simply get more of the faster product, faster.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: In the diene case, which route has the lower barrier?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Bromide attacks C2, which carries more positive charge, so that route is faster.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: In the diene case, which product sits in the deeper well?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Its alkene is internal and more substituted, so it is the more stable of the two.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Why does warming the diene mixture invert the ratio?
options: Bromide can leave again and re-equilibrate
The charge distribution in the cation shifts
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Nothing about the mechanism or the intermediate changes. What changes is what the products can do afterwards.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What is the Diels-Alder endo product an example of?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: It is the faster route despite being the more crowded arrangement, thanks to a secondary orbital interaction.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What does the endo rule show about the word kinetic?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: The endo transition state is more crowded and still faster, so kinetic cannot be read as less hindered.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: A reaction is run at high temperature but its first step cannot reverse. Which control applies?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Reversibility, not temperature, is the actual requirement. Heat without a way back changes nothing.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Which question should you ask first when predicting the major product?
options: Which of the two products is more stable overall
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: That question determines which of the two comparisons you should even be making.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What is the activation energy usually written as?
options: Delta G for the overall step
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: The double dagger marks the transition state. Delta G without it refers to the overall change.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Two products form from a common intermediate. What does that make possible?
options: Only one possible outcome, whatever the conditions
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: A branch point is what lets conditions select between outcomes.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: Which is NOT a case of kinetic versus thermodynamic control?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: SN2 stereochemistry is fixed by the geometry of backside attack, not by a competition between two product wells.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: If a reaction gives one product cold and another warm, what can you infer?
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Reversibility is what lets the warm run reach a different answer from the same intermediate.

kinetic-thermodynamic.q: What does it mean that a product is trapped under kinetic control?
options: It cannot revert to starting material
It cannot be purified by ordinary means
kinetic-thermodynamic.why: Once formed it stays, so the product ratio simply records which route was faster.

diels-alder.q: The Diels-Alder is classified as which kind of reaction?
diels-alder.why: Four pi electrons from the diene and two from the dienophile.

diels-alder.q: What is the product of a Diels-Alder reaction?
diels-alder.why: Two new sigma bonds close a six-membered ring, and one pi bond survives in the middle.

diels-alder.q: How many new sigma bonds form?
diels-alder.why: Three pi bonds go in; two sigma bonds and one pi bond come out, which is why the reaction is downhill.

diels-alder.q: Is there an intermediate in a Diels-Alder reaction?
diels-alder.why: Every bond breaks and forms in one step through a single cyclic transition state.

diels-alder.q: Why does the Diels-Alder never give rearranged products?
options: The reaction conditions are always mild
There is no carbocation to rearrange
diels-alder.why: With no intermediate there is nothing to shift, nothing to lose stereochemistry and nothing whose stability to compare.

diels-alder.q: Which conformation must the diene adopt?
diels-alder.why: Both ends of the diene must reach both ends of the dienophile at once.

diels-alder.q: What is the commonest reason a Diels-Alder fails?
diels-alder.why: It is a geometric requirement, and no amount of electronic tuning fixes it.

diels-alder.q: Why is cyclopentadiene exceptionally reactive?
diels-alder.why: It pays no rotation penalty, and dimerizes on standing as a result.

diels-alder.q: How is cyclopentadiene stored and prepared for use?
options: As the dimer, cracked by distillation
Frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen
diels-alder.why: It dimerizes at room temperature via a Diels-Alder, and the retro reaction on heating gives it back.

diels-alder.q: What makes a good dienophile?
diels-alder.why: They lower its LUMO, bringing it closer to the diene's HOMO.

diels-alder.q: What makes a good diene?
diels-alder.why: They raise its HOMO, narrowing the gap to the dienophile's LUMO.

diels-alder.q: Which pairing is fastest?
diels-alder.why: Mismatching them in this direction brings the interacting orbitals closest in energy.

diels-alder.q: Maleic anhydride is a classic what?
diels-alder.why: Two carbonyls flank its double bond, which pulls the LUMO down sharply.

diels-alder.q: Why does ethene react only under forcing conditions?
options: It is simply too stable to react at all
diels-alder.why: Nothing lowers its LUMO, so the orbital gap to the diene stays wide.

diels-alder.q: Two substituents cis on the dienophile end up how in the product?
diels-alder.why: Both bonds form on the same face in one step, so nothing can rotate and the relationship is preserved.

diels-alder.q: Two substituents trans on the dienophile end up how in the product?
diels-alder.why: The same suprafacial addition preserves trans just as it preserves cis.

diels-alder.q: What does stereospecific mean here?
options: Only one stereoisomer of the dienophile can react
The starting geometry determines the product geometry
diels-alder.why: Change the stereochemistry of the starting material and you get a predictably different stereochemistry in the product.

diels-alder.q: Which product is favored when the dienophile bears a substituent?
diels-alder.why: The endo transition state benefits from a secondary orbital interaction, making it faster.

diels-alder.q: Why is the endo product favored despite being more crowded?
options: It is in fact the less crowded arrangement
A secondary orbital interaction lowers its barrier
diels-alder.why: The substituent's pi system interacts favorably with the developing pi system of the diene.

diels-alder.q: The endo product is which kind of product?
diels-alder.why: It forms faster, which is a useful corrective to reading kinetic as less hindered.

diels-alder.q: What is a retro-Diels-Alder?
options: The reverse reaction, splitting the ring
A Lewis-acid catalyzed version of it
diels-alder.why: Heating a suitable cyclohexene sends it back to a diene and a dienophile.

diels-alder.q: Why is the retro-Diels-Alder useful in synthesis planning?
options: It removes stereocenters from the target
diels-alder.why: Mentally cutting a six-membered ring at that disconnection is one of the most productive moves in retrosynthesis.

diels-alder.q: How many pi electrons does the diene contribute?
diels-alder.why: Two double bonds, two pi electrons each. The dienophile brings two more.

diels-alder.q: How many pi electrons does the dienophile contribute?
diels-alder.why: One double or triple bond. Four plus two is the [4+2] in the name.

diels-alder.q: Can an alkyne serve as a dienophile?
diels-alder.why: It contributes two pi electrons just as an alkene does, and the extra pi bond survives into the product.

diels-alder.q: Where does the new double bond sit in the product?
options: Between the diene's former C2 and C3
diels-alder.why: The two terminal carbons form the new sigma bonds, and the central bond becomes the alkene.

diels-alder.q: Why is the reaction thermodynamically favorable?
diels-alder.why: Sigma bonds are stronger, so trading two pi bonds for two sigma bonds releases energy.

diels-alder.q: What does concerted mean?
options: All bonds break and form in one step
diels-alder.why: One transition state, no intermediate, and every consequence of that follows.

diels-alder.q: Does the Diels-Alder need a catalyst?
options: Yes, it always needs a strong acid
No, though Lewis acids can accelerate it
diels-alder.why: The bond arithmetic already favors it; a Lewis acid can lower the dienophile's LUMO further and speed it up.

diels-alder.q: Which diene cannot do a Diels-Alder at all?
options: One locked s-trans in a ring
diels-alder.why: It can never reach the conformation where both ends point the same way.

uv-vis.q: What transition does UV-Vis spectroscopy probe in an organic molecule?
uv-vis.why: A pi to pi-star transition, promoting an electron across the frontier orbital gap.

uv-vis.q: A bigger HOMO-LUMO gap means absorption at which wavelength?
uv-vis.why: A bigger gap needs a higher energy photon, and higher energy means shorter wavelength.

uv-vis.q: A smaller HOMO-LUMO gap means absorption at which wavelength?
uv-vis.why: Less energy is needed, and lower energy light has a longer wavelength.

uv-vis.q: What happens to the HOMO-LUMO gap as conjugation extends?
uv-vis.why: More p orbitals give more molecular orbitals over a similar range, so the highest occupied rises and the lowest empty falls.

uv-vis.q: Approximately where does ethene absorb?
uv-vis.why: A single isolated double bond absorbs well below 200 nm, which is inconvenient for ordinary instruments.

uv-vis.q: Approximately where does buta-1,3-diene absorb?
uv-vis.why: Conjugating two double bonds moves the absorption into the accessible range.

uv-vis.q: Approximately where does hexa-1,3,5-triene absorb?
uv-vis.why: Three conjugated double bonds, and the trend continues upward.

uv-vis.q: Approximately where does beta-carotene absorb?
uv-vis.why: Eleven conjugated double bonds put it past 400 nm and into the visible region.

uv-vis.q: How many conjugated double bonds does beta-carotene have?
uv-vis.why: Enough to bring its absorption into the visible, which is why it is colored at all.

uv-vis.q: What is a chromophore?
options: The group responsible for the absorption
uv-vis.why: In organic UV-Vis it is usually the conjugated pi system.

uv-vis.q: Why does beta-carotene look orange?
options: You see the light it does not absorb
It emits orange light after absorbing
uv-vis.why: It removes blue light around 450 nm, and what reaches your eye is the complementary color.

uv-vis.q: Why are most organic compounds colorless?
options: They are transparent in the solid state
uv-vis.why: Without a long conjugated system the gap is too wide, so absorption stays in the ultraviolet.

uv-vis.q: What is the Beer-Lambert law?
uv-vis.why: Absorbance equals molar absorptivity times concentration times path length.

uv-vis.q: In A = ecl, what does e represent?
uv-vis.why: A constant for that compound at that wavelength, measuring how strongly it absorbs.

uv-vis.q: In A = ecl, what does l represent?
uv-vis.why: Conventionally 1 cm for a standard cuvette.

uv-vis.q: Why is UV-Vis quantitative?
options: It counts the molecules present directly
uv-vis.why: The Beer-Lambert relationship makes it the standard way to follow a concentration while a reaction runs.

uv-vis.q: Typical molar absorptivity for a conjugated system is roughly what?
uv-vis.why: Conjugated systems absorb strongly, which is part of why the technique is sensitive.

uv-vis.q: Two isomers: one absorbs at 227 nm, one below 200 nm. Which is conjugated?
uv-vis.why: Conjugation narrows the gap, so the conjugated isomer absorbs at the longer wavelength.

uv-vis.q: What does a UV-Vis spectrum NOT tell you?
uv-vis.why: It reports on conjugation and amount, but nothing about position or connectivity. Pair it with NMR for that.

uv-vis.q: Roughly where does the visible region begin?
uv-vis.why: Below about 400 nm is ultraviolet, so a compound absorbing past that point can appear colored.

uv-vis.q: Why does an isolated alkene appear invisible to a routine UV-Vis instrument?
options: It does not absorb at all
It absorbs below the accessible range
It absorbs only in the infrared region
uv-vis.why: A single C=C absorbs below about 200 nm, which ordinary instruments do not reach comfortably.

uv-vis.q: Do alkyl substituents on a pi system shift lambda-max?
uv-vis.why: The effect is smaller than adding a double bond, but systematic enough that empirical rules exist.

uv-vis.q: Which technique best reports the extent of conjugation?
uv-vis.why: Each technique answers a different question, and this is the one UV-Vis answers sharply.

uv-vis.q: Which technique names functional groups?
uv-vis.why: IR reports on bond vibrations, which are characteristic of particular groups.

uv-vis.q: Why does UV-Vis sit in the conjugation chapter?
options: It is the oldest of the techniques
uv-vis.why: It turns the chapter's central claim into a number you can read off an instrument.

uv-vis.q: What is absorbance?
uv-vis.why: Read off the instrument, and proportional to concentration by Beer-Lambert.

uv-vis.q: Extending conjugation by one double bond does what to lambda-max?
uv-vis.why: Each additional conjugated double bond narrows the gap further and pushes absorption to longer wavelength.

uv-vis.q: What kind of orbital is the LUMO in a conjugated alkene?
uv-vis.why: The transition is pi to pi-star, so the empty orbital involved is the pi antibonding one.

uv-vis.q: Retinal, the visual pigment, works because of what?
uv-vis.why: Extended conjugation brings its absorption into the visible, which is what makes vision possible.

uv-vis.q: Can UV-Vis distinguish two conjugated isomers of the same length?
options: Often poorly, since it reports conjugation not position
Only if the compounds are colored
uv-vis.why: It answers one question sharply and says little about connectivity, so NMR does the placing.

alcohol-reactions.q: Why can’t OH⁻ typically leave directly from an alcohol in a substitution reaction?
options: OH⁻ is too strong a base
