alcohol-reactions.why: Hydroxide is a strong base (poor leaving group); alcohols are typically first protonated (or converted to a better leaving group like a tosylate) before substitution/elimination.

alcohol-reactions.q: Protonating an alcohol with strong acid converts –OH into:
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation turns the leaving group into neutral H₂O, which is a much weaker base (and thus a far better leaving group) than OH⁻.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent is commonly used to convert an alcohol into a good leaving group (a tosylate) without disturbing its stereochemistry?
options: Tosyl chloride (TsCl) with a mild base
alcohol-reactions.why: TsCl converts the OH into OTs, a weak-base, excellent leaving group, via a mechanism that doesn’t touch the stereocenter’s configuration (unlike acid-catalyzed substitution, which can invert or racemize it).

alcohol-reactions.q: Which mechanism does tert-butanol follow when it reacts with concentrated HCl to form tert-butyl chloride?
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary carbocations are stable enough to form, so the reaction proceeds through ionization (loss of water) followed by chloride capture, a classic SN1 pathway.

alcohol-reactions.q: Primary alcohols react with HBr via an SN1 mechanism because primary carbocations form easily.
alcohol-reactions.why: Primary carbocations are highly unstable, so primary alcohols instead react with HX through SN2, with the protonated alcohol acting as the leaving group while bromide attacks from the backside.

alcohol-reactions.q: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl chloride with the least risk of carbocation rearrangement?
alcohol-reactions.why: SOCl2 reacts through a chlorosulfite intermediate without generating a free carbocation, avoiding the hydride or alkyl shifts that can occur in purely acid-catalyzed routes.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a primary alcohol with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in dichloromethane gives:
alcohol-reactions.why: PCC is an anhydrous, mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage because there is no water present to hydrate the aldehyde into the gem-diol needed for further oxidation.

alcohol-reactions.q: To oxidize a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid, the best choice is:
alcohol-reactions.why: Strong aqueous Cr(VI) oxidants hydrate the intermediate aldehyde into a gem-diol, which is then readily oxidized further to the carboxylic acid; PCC and Swern conditions are anhydrous and stop at the aldehyde.

alcohol-reactions.q: Oxidizing a secondary alcohol with any chromium(VI) reagent (PCC, Jones, etc.) produces:
options: No reaction; secondary alcohols resist oxidation
alcohol-reactions.why: Secondary alcohols have only one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon; removing it gives a ketone, which has no further C-H bond to remove, so oxidation stops there regardless of the specific Cr(VI) reagent.

alcohol-reactions.q: Tertiary alcohols can be oxidized to ketones using PCC.
alcohol-reactions.why: Oxidation by these reagents requires removing a C-H bond from the carbinol carbon; a tertiary carbinol carbon has no such hydrogen, so tertiary alcohols resist this kind of oxidation entirely.

alcohol-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-butanol gives mainly:
alcohol-reactions.why: Zaitsev's rule favors the more stable, more substituted alkene; in the E1 mechanism the carbocation loses a proton preferentially toward the more substituted side, forming the more stable double bond.

alcohol-reactions.q: Put the steps of acid-catalyzed (E1) dehydration of an alcohol in the correct order.
options: Loss of a proton, protonation of OH, loss of water
Protonation, loss of water, then loss of a proton
Loss of water, loss of a proton, protonation of OH
Protonation of OH, loss of a proton, loss of water
alcohol-reactions.why: The OH must first be protonated to become a good leaving group (water), which then departs to generate a carbocation; a base finally removes a beta-proton to form the alkene.

alcohol-reactions.q: Dehydration rates for alcohols under acid catalysis follow the order 3 degrees > 2 degrees > 1 degree primarily because:
options: Primary alcohols have stronger O-H bonds
More substituted carbocations are more stable and form faster
Steric hindrance speeds up primary alcohol dehydration
alcohol-reactions.why: The rate-limiting step is carbocation formation; hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from additional alkyl groups stabilize more substituted carbocations, lowering the activation energy for their formation.

alcohol-reactions.q: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of a secondary alcohol can give a rearranged alkene product that would not be predicted from simply removing a proton adjacent to the original carbinol carbon.
alcohol-reactions.why: Because the mechanism passes through a carbocation intermediate, a hydride or alkyl shift can occur before the proton is lost, shifting the position of the resulting double bond or even the carbon skeleton.

alcohol-reactions.q: Adding sodium metal to ethanol produces:
options: No reaction; alcohols do not react with Na
alcohol-reactions.why: Alcohols are weak acids; the reactive Na metal reduces the O-H proton, releasing H2 gas and leaving behind the sodium alkoxide salt.

alcohol-reactions.q: In a Williamson ether synthesis starting from an alcohol, the first step is usually to:
options: Oxidize the alcohol to a ketone
alcohol-reactions.why: The alkoxide, not the neutral alcohol, is the nucleophile needed to perform SN2 displacement on the alkyl halide partner, so a strong, non-nucleophilic base like NaH is used first to form it.

alcohol-reactions.q: Fischer esterification combines an alcohol with a carboxylic acid under acid catalysis to form:
alcohol-reactions.why: Acid catalyzes nucleophilic attack of the alcohol on the protonated carbonyl; after loss of water from the resulting tetrahedral intermediate, the ester is formed. The overall process is reversible.

alcohol-reactions.q: A vicinal diol treated with acid can undergo a pinacol rearrangement, which proceeds by:
options: A simple SN2 substitution of one OH by the other
Direct elimination with no carbocation intermediate at all
Loss of water, a 1,2-shift, then loss of a proton
Radical coupling of the two oxygens
alcohol-reactions.why: One OH is protonated and leaves as water to form a carbocation; a neighboring alkyl or hydride group migrates to stabilize the positive charge, and loss of a proton from the resulting species gives the ketone product.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a vicinal (1,2-) diol with periodic acid (HIO4) results in:
options: No reaction; HIO4 only cleaves alkenes
alcohol-reactions.why: Periodic acid selectively cleaves the carbon-carbon bond between two adjacent hydroxyl groups, converting each carbinol carbon into a carbonyl (an aldehyde or ketone depending on substitution).

alcohol-reactions.q: Alcohols are generally slightly weaker acids than water.
alcohol-reactions.why: The alkyl group attached to the oxygen is electron-donating relative to hydrogen, which destabilizes the alkoxide conjugate base somewhat compared to hydroxide, making most simple alcohols a bit less acidic than water.

alcohol-reactions.q: Compared to methanol, tert-butanol is:
options: Less acidic (higher pKa), owing to alkyl donation
More acidic (lower pKa), because of steric relief on ionization
Equally acidic; alkyl substitution does not affect alcohol pKa
More acidic because tertiary carbons stabilize negative charge better
alcohol-reactions.why: The added alkyl groups push electron density onto the already-negative alkoxide oxygen, destabilizing the anion (and hindering its solvation), which raises the pKa relative to methanol.

alcohol-reactions.q: Adding a Grignard reagent (R-MgBr) to an alcohol results in:
options: Nucleophilic addition to give a new, larger alcohol
Simple acid-base protonation that destroys the Grignard reagent
An SN2 substitution that gives an ether
No reaction, since Grignards do not react with alcohols
alcohol-reactions.why: The O-H of an alcohol is acidic enough to protonate the strongly basic, carbanion-like Grignard reagent, quenching it as an alkane before it can perform any useful addition chemistry.

alcohol-reactions.q: Swern oxidation (DMSO and oxalyl chloride, then base) converts a primary alcohol to an aldehyde while avoiding:
options: Any stereochemical change at the carbinol carbon
The need for a final aqueous work-up
alcohol-reactions.why: Like PCC, Swern conditions contain no water, so the aldehyde product cannot be hydrated into the gem-diol that aqueous Cr(VI) systems go on to oxidize; it also avoids toxic chromium reagents.

alcohol-reactions.q: The Lucas test (HCl/ZnCl2) distinguishes primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols based on how quickly a cloudy alkyl chloride layer forms.
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary alcohols react almost instantly because their carbocation is highly stabilized, secondary alcohols take several minutes, and primary alcohols show little change at room temperature, so the reaction rate reveals the alcohol's class.

alcohol-reactions.q: In the Lucas test, a tertiary alcohol shows:
options: No visible change even after heating
Cloudiness only after five to ten minutes
A color change from orange to green
Immediate cloudiness or a separate layer
alcohol-reactions.why: Tertiary alcohols ionize very quickly under these acidic conditions because the resulting carbocation is highly stabilized, so the insoluble alkyl chloride forms almost immediately.

alcohol-reactions.q: Converting an alcohol to a TMS (trimethylsilyl) ether before carrying out a reaction elsewhere in the molecule is done primarily to:
options: Temporarily mask the OH from other reagents
Make the molecule more acidic overall
Oxidize the alcohol in a controlled, reversible way
alcohol-reactions.why: Protecting groups like TMS ethers are easily installed and later removed (for example with mild acid or fluoride), letting chemists carry out reactions elsewhere in a molecule without interference from a free -OH.

alcohol-reactions.q: The reaction of a secondary alcohol with PBr3 proceeds through:
options: An SN1 mechanism with a free carbocation, racemizing the product
An SN2-like mechanism with backside attack by bromide, inverting configuration
Simple proton transfer with no bond-breaking at carbon
alcohol-reactions.why: PBr3 first converts the OH into a good leaving group, and bromide then displaces it in a single concerted backside attack, giving clean inversion rather than the racemization seen with carbocation intermediates.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating a chiral secondary alcohol with PBr3 gives the alkyl bromide with inverted stereochemistry at that carbon.
alcohol-reactions.why: Because PBr3 operates through a concerted SN2-type displacement without a free carbocation, bromide must attack from the side opposite the leaving group, inverting the configuration.

alcohol-reactions.q: Treating that same chiral secondary alcohol with concentrated HBr alone (simple acid-catalyzed substitution) tends to give a racemized, or partially racemized, product.
alcohol-reactions.why: Protonation of the OH followed by loss of water generates a planar carbocation that can be attacked by bromide from either face, scrambling the stereochemistry relative to the clean inversion seen with PBr3.

alcohol-reactions.q: Among methanol, isopropanol, and tert-butanol, which dehydrates fastest when heated with strong acid?
options: They all dehydrate at the same rate
alcohol-reactions.why: Acid-catalyzed dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate; tert-butanol forms the most stable (tertiary) carbocation most readily, so it reacts fastest, while methanol has no adjacent carbon to form a double bond with at all.

ether-chemistry.q: Why are ethers generally unreactive under basic conditions?
options: There is no good leaving group
The C–O bond is too strong to ever break
Ethers react only with other ethers
ether-chemistry.why: Like alcohols, ethers need protonation (acidic conditions) to turn the alkoxide oxygen into a viable leaving group (neutral alcohol) before cleavage.

ether-chemistry.q: Strong acid cleavage of an ether (e.g., with HI) proceeds through what kind of mechanism for a secondary/tertiary carbon?
ether-chemistry.why: Protonated ethers at secondary/tertiary centers tend to cleave via SN1 (carbocation pathway), while primary centers favor SN2.

ether-chemistry.q: Why are ethers often used as solvents for reactions involving strong nucleophiles/bases (like Grignard reagents)?
options: They are highly reactive and participate directly
They are unreactive yet coordinate cations
Ethers decompose readily under these conditions
ether-chemistry.why: Ethers lack an acidic proton and don’t have a good leaving group under neutral/basic conditions, so they tolerate strongly basic/nucleophilic reagents while still solvating them through the oxygen’s lone pairs.

ether-chemistry.q: Why do ethers generally have lower boiling points than alcohols of similar molecular weight?
options: Ethers are always smaller molecules than alcohols
Ethers have stronger London dispersion forces
Ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, unlike alcohols
ether-chemistry.why: Alcohols can hydrogen-bond to one another through their O-H groups, which raises their boiling points substantially; ethers lack an O-H bond, so they only experience weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces between molecules.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethers can act as hydrogen bond acceptors (through their oxygen lone pairs) but not as hydrogen bond donors.
ether-chemistry.why: An ether oxygen has lone pairs that can accept a hydrogen bond from an O-H or N-H elsewhere, but since ethers have no O-H or N-H of their own, they cannot donate a hydrogen bond.

ether-chemistry.q: Heating methyl propyl ether with excess concentrated HI cleaves the ether to give propanol plus which alkyl halide?
options: A mixture of both in equal amounts
No cleavage occurs; ethers are inert to HI
ether-chemistry.why: Once the ether oxygen is protonated, iodide attacks via SN2 at the less hindered, less sterically crowded methyl carbon rather than the propyl carbon, giving methyl iodide and propanol (which can react further with excess acid).

ether-chemistry.q: Treating tert-butyl methyl ether with excess HI gives:
options: A mixture of tert-butyl and methyl iodide in equal amounts
No reaction, since tertiary ethers resist acidic cleavage
ether-chemistry.why: The tertiary carbon can ionize readily to form a stable carbocation (SN1-like pathway), so iodide captures that carbocation, leaving methanol as the other fragment rather than forming a methyl cation.

ether-chemistry.q: An unsymmetrical ether with one primary alkyl group and one tertiary alkyl group is treated with HBr. The major products are expected to be:
options: The primary bromide and the tertiary alcohol
Both carbons are substituted with equal probability
The tertiary bromide and the primary alcohol
Neither C-O bond breaks under these conditions
ether-chemistry.why: The tertiary carbon can ionize to a stable carbocation far more easily than the primary carbon can undergo a slow SN2 displacement, so cleavage occurs preferentially at the tertiary center, releasing the primary alcohol intact.

ether-chemistry.q: Treating anisole (methyl phenyl ether) with HI cleaves it to give phenol and methyl iodide, with the aryl-oxygen bond remaining completely intact.
ether-chemistry.why: Breaking the aryl-oxygen bond would require either an unstable aryl cation (no SN1 pathway) or backside attack on a planar, sp2 aromatic carbon (no SN2 pathway), so cleavage instead occurs exclusively at the methyl carbon.

ether-chemistry.q: Why is the Williamson ether synthesis generally a poor method for making an ether from a tertiary alkyl halide?
options: Tertiary alkyl halides are never soluble in the reaction solvent
Alkoxides cannot act as nucleophiles toward tertiary carbons
Tertiary halides spontaneously hydrolyze before the alkoxide can react
The strongly basic alkoxide promotes E2 elimination instead of SN2 substitution on the tertiary halide
ether-chemistry.why: A bulky, basic alkoxide approaching a hindered tertiary carbon strongly favors removing a beta-hydrogen (E2) over performing a backside SN2 attack, so elimination products dominate instead of the desired ether.

ether-chemistry.q: To cleanly synthesize an unsymmetrical ether via the Williamson method, you should generally:
options: Use the alkoxide from the more hindered alcohol paired with the less hindered (often primary) alkyl halide
Use the alkoxide from the less hindered alcohol paired with a tertiary alkyl halide
It never matters which partner is the alkoxide versus the halide
Always use two different tertiary components for best yield
ether-chemistry.why: Because the alkyl halide is the electrophile undergoing SN2 attack, choosing one that is primary (or otherwise unhindered) avoids competing elimination, regardless of how bulky the alkoxide nucleophile itself is.

ether-chemistry.q: Crown ethers such as 18-crown-6 are useful in organic synthesis mainly because they:
options: React covalently with alkyl halides to form new ethers
Bind metal cations and solubilize their salts
ether-chemistry.why: The ring of oxygen atoms in a crown ether can wrap around a metal cation of the right size, effectively dissolving otherwise poorly soluble ionic salts in nonpolar solvents.

ether-chemistry.q: 18-Crown-6 binds K+ more selectively than it binds Na+ because its cavity size is a better match for the potassium ion.
ether-chemistry.why: Crown ethers show size selectivity: 18-crown-6's ring cavity closely matches the ionic radius of K+, giving tighter binding than with the smaller Na+ ion, which fits less snugly.

ether-chemistry.q: Dissolving KF with 18-crown-6 in a nonpolar organic solvent makes fluoride a much more effective nucleophile because:
options: The crown ether reduces the overall negative charge on fluoride
Crown ethers convert fluoride into a stronger base but weaker nucleophile
The crown ether sequesters the potassium cation, leaving a more 'naked,' poorly ion-paired fluoride anion
The crown ether reacts with fluoride to form a more reactive complex
ether-chemistry.why: Normally F- is tightly ion-paired with its counter-cation and poorly solvated in nonpolar media, dampening its reactivity; encapsulating K+ inside the crown ether frees the anion to act as a much more potent, less hindered nucleophile.

ether-chemistry.q: Diethyl ether was historically used as a general anesthetic in surgery.
ether-chemistry.why: Diethyl ether was one of the earliest general anesthetics used in medicine, though it was eventually replaced by safer, less flammable agents.

ether-chemistry.q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is a commonly used ether solvent mainly because it:
options: Is a strong acid that activates electrophiles
Reacts readily with Grignard reagents to improve yields
Coordinates metal centers while staying unreactive
ether-chemistry.why: THF's oxygen lone pairs coordinate to metal cations (helping stabilize organometallic reagents in solution) while its ring is chemically unreactive toward most nucleophiles and bases, making it a versatile, widely used solvent.

ether-chemistry.q: Old bottles of diethyl ether that have been stored for a long time can become dangerous to distill because they slowly form explosive peroxides through reaction with atmospheric oxygen.
ether-chemistry.why: Autoxidation at the carbon next to the ether oxygen slowly generates peroxide and hydroperoxide species that can concentrate and detonate, especially when the ether is evaporated or distilled, which is why old ether stocks are handled with caution.

ether-chemistry.q: Why does peroxide formation (autoxidation) occur preferentially at the carbon directly attached to the ether oxygen?
options: The adjacent oxygen stabilizes the resulting radical
That carbon has the most hydrogens available statistically
The oxygen atom itself is directly oxidized first
Ether oxygens catalyze peroxide formation only at the far end of the chain
ether-chemistry.why: Removing a hydrogen from the carbon next to the ether oxygen gives a radical that is stabilized by overlap with a lone pair on oxygen, making that particular C-H bond especially susceptible to slow radical autoxidation by atmospheric O2.

ether-chemistry.q: Which characteristic infrared absorption is commonly used to help identify an ether functional group?
options: A broad O-H stretch around 3300 cm-1
A strong C-O stretch around 1050-1150 cm-1
A sharp C=O stretch around 1715 cm-1
ether-chemistry.why: Ethers lack the O-H and C=O groups that dominate alcohol and carbonyl spectra, so their most diagnostic IR feature is the strong C-O single bond stretch in the 1050-1150 cm-1 region.

ether-chemistry.q: Heating diethyl ether with a large excess of concentrated HI eventually gives, as the final organic products:
options: One equivalent of ethyl iodide and one of ethanol
Diethyl ether is unreactive toward HI even in excess
ether-chemistry.why: With excess strong acid and heat, both C-O bonds of the symmetrical ether are eventually cleaved by iodide via SN2, first releasing ethanol (which itself then reacts further with HI) and ultimately converting both ethyl groups into ethyl iodide.

ether-chemistry.q: Protonation of an ether's oxygen atom by a strong acid forms:
ether-chemistry.why: Adding a proton to the ether oxygen gives it three bonds plus a formal positive charge, a species called an oxonium ion, which makes the adjacent C-O bonds much easier to break.

ether-chemistry.q: Unlike alcohols, simple ethers have no O-H bond and therefore cannot be oxidized to aldehydes, ketones, or carboxylic acids under standard laboratory oxidation conditions.
ether-chemistry.why: Reagents like PCC or Jones reagent oxidize by removing the O-H hydrogen along with a C-H hydrogen from the carbinol carbon; since ethers have no O-H to begin with, this pathway simply is not available to them.

ether-chemistry.q: Grignard reagents generally fail to form well, or are ineffective, when prepared in purely hydrocarbon solvents like hexane mainly because:
options: No ether lone pairs coordinate the magnesium
Hydrocarbons react violently with magnesium metal
Hydrocarbon solvents are too polar for Grignard chemistry
Grignard reagents require an acidic solvent to initiate
ether-chemistry.why: Ether solvents donate electron density from their oxygen lone pairs to the electrophilic magnesium center, which helps stabilize and solubilize the highly reactive organomagnesium species; nonpolar hydrocarbons cannot offer this coordination.

ether-chemistry.q: Vinyl (enol) ethers are hydrolyzed much more readily under mild aqueous acid than ordinary dialkyl ethers because:
options: Vinyl ethers contain an extra oxygen atom that dialkyl ethers lack
Protonation gives a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion
The C-O bond in a vinyl ether is a double bond, which is intrinsically weaker
Vinyl ethers are actually esters in disguise
ether-chemistry.why: Protonating the alkene carbon of a vinyl ether produces a cation stabilized by resonance donation from the adjacent oxygen (an oxocarbenium ion); water then adds and loss of the alcohol gives a carbonyl compound, a much faster pathway than the harsh conditions needed to cleave a saturated dialkyl ether.

ether-chemistry.q: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) is best classified as a:
ether-chemistry.why: THF is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbons, making it a saturated cyclic ether rather than an open-chain one.

ether-chemistry.q: IUPAC nomenclature typically names simple ethers as alkoxy-substituted alkanes, such as calling CH3-O-CH2CH3 'methoxyethane.'
ether-chemistry.why: Rather than using a standalone 'ether' suffix, the preferred IUPAC approach treats the shorter alkyl-oxygen unit as an alkoxy substituent on the longer parent chain, giving names like methoxyethane for ethyl methyl ether.

ether-chemistry.q: Ethers are generally poor nucleophiles themselves in most reactions, but their oxygen lone pairs make them good Lewis bases, able to form a stable complex with a Lewis acid such as BF3.
options: False, ethers cannot interact with Lewis acids at all
False, only alcohols can coordinate to Lewis acids
True, but only aromatic ethers can do this
True, an ether-BF3 complex (an 'etherate') is a well-known, stable adduct
ether-chemistry.why: The ether oxygen's lone pair can donate into the empty orbital of a Lewis acid like BF3, forming a stable donor-acceptor (Lewis acid-base) adduct, such as the BF3 etherate commonly used as a mild Lewis acid catalyst.

ether-chemistry.q: Small ethers like diethyl ether show modest but real solubility in water, higher than a comparably sized pure hydrocarbon would have.
ether-chemistry.why: Although ethers cannot donate hydrogen bonds, their oxygen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules, giving small ethers noticeably greater water solubility than alkanes of similar size.

ether-chemistry.q: Ether cleavage reactions are typically carried out with HI or HBr rather than HCl mainly because:
options: Iodide and bromide are better nucleophiles
HCl cannot protonate an ether oxygen at all
HI and HBr are weaker acids, which favors cleavage
Chloride ions are too large to attack the ether carbon
ether-chemistry.why: After the ether oxygen is protonated, the halide ion must still act as the nucleophile (or cation-trapping species) that displaces the alcohol; iodide and bromide are considerably more nucleophilic than chloride, making the overall cleavage much faster and more practical.

ether-chemistry.q: Why do simple dialkyl ethers typically require a strong acid and prolonged heating to be cleaved, while esters hydrolyze readily with just dilute aqueous base at room temperature?
options: Esters contain more carbon atoms, making them inherently more reactive
An ester has an electrophilic carbonyl; an ether has none
Ethers are aromatic and therefore unreactive
Esters are ionic compounds, unlike ethers
ether-chemistry.why: A base can attack an ester's carbonyl carbon directly because the resulting tetrahedral intermediate is stabilized by the carbonyl oxygen and can expel a leaving group; an ether has no such electrophilic carbon, so it must first be protonated by strong acid before any C-O bond becomes breakable.

epoxides.q: Epoxides are much more reactive than regular ethers because:
epoxides.why: The ~60° bond angles in the three-membered ring are far from ideal, so opening the ring relieves substantial strain, driving reactivity.

epoxides.q: Under basic conditions, a nucleophile opens an epoxide by attacking:
options: The less substituted carbon (SN2-like, backside attack)
epoxides.why: Basic/neutral conditions favor an SN2-like mechanism — backside attack at the less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: Under acidic conditions, a nucleophile opens an epoxide preferentially at the:
options: Less substituted carbon only, same as base
The oxygen atom itself is attacked
epoxides.why: Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring-opening more SN1-like, so the nucleophile attacks the carbon that better stabilizes positive charge — the more substituted one — unlike the SN2-like base-catalyzed case.

epoxides.q: Epoxides are most commonly synthesized in the laboratory from alkenes using:
epoxides.why: Peroxyacids like mCPBA deliver an oxygen atom directly across the carbon-carbon double bond in a single concerted step, converting the alkene into an epoxide.

epoxides.q: Epoxidation of an alkene with a peroxyacid proceeds with syn (same-face) addition of the oxygen atom.
epoxides.why: The peroxyacid transfers its oxygen to both alkene carbons simultaneously from one face in a single concerted step (often pictured as a 'butterfly' transition state), so the new C-O bonds form on the same side of the original double bond.

epoxides.q: Epoxidizing cis-2-butene with mCPBA gives, as the major (and only) product:
options: A racemic mixture of two chiral epoxides
A mixture of cis and trans epoxide diastereomers
No epoxide forms from cis alkenes
epoxides.why: Syn addition preserves the original cis relationship of the two methyl groups, and the resulting epoxide has an internal mirror plane, making it a single achiral meso compound rather than a mixture of enantiomers.

epoxides.q: Epoxidizing trans-2-butene with mCPBA gives, as the product:
options: A mixture of four different diastereomers
epoxides.why: Syn addition to the trans alkene produces a chiral epoxide (no internal mirror plane); because the peroxyacid can approach either face of the planar alkene with equal likelihood, both enantiomers form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

epoxides.q: Regardless of whether the conditions are acidic or basic, nucleophilic ring-opening of an epoxide occurs through:
options: A radical mechanism with no stereochemical preference
Attack that always occurs with complete racemization
epoxides.why: In both the basic and acidic mechanisms, the nucleophile approaches from the side opposite the breaking C-O bond, so the carbon under attack is inverted even though the overall regiochemistry (which carbon is attacked) differs between the two conditions.

epoxides.q: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of cyclohexene oxide gives predominantly trans-1,2-cyclohexanediol rather than the cis diastereomer.
epoxides.why: Water attacks the protonated epoxide from the face opposite the ring oxygen (backside attack), so the two new OH groups end up anti to each other, giving the trans diol rather than the cis one.

epoxides.q: Reducing an unsymmetrical epoxide with excess LiAlH4 places the new hydrogen mainly on:
options: The more hindered carbon regardless of sterics
Neither carbon; LiAlH4 does not reduce epoxides
The less hindered carbon, leaving the new OH on the more substituted carbon
epoxides.why: Hydride is a strong nucleophile that reacts via an SN2-like pathway, so like other strong nucleophiles it attacks the less sterically hindered carbon, which ends up bonded to the delivered hydrogen while the OH remains on the more substituted carbon.

epoxides.q: Treating an unsymmetrical epoxide with a Grignard reagent (RMgX) opens the ring with the carbon nucleophile attacking:
options: The less hindered carbon, consistent with an SN2-like strong-nucleophile mechanism
The more substituted carbon, as in acid-catalyzed opening
Whichever carbon is closer to the oxygen's lone pairs, which is both equally
Neither carbon; Grignards do not react with epoxides
epoxides.why: Grignard reagents are strong, basic carbon nucleophiles that react with epoxides under essentially basic-type conditions, favoring backside SN2 attack at the more accessible, less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: Treating a simple epoxide with HBr produces, as the initial product:
epoxides.why: Under acidic conditions the protonated epoxide is opened by bromide acting as the nucleophile at one carbon, while the oxygen (now an OH after losing its proton) remains on the adjacent carbon, giving a halohydrin.

epoxides.q: In the acid-catalyzed ring-opening of 2-methyl-2,3-epoxybutane with methanol, the methanol oxygen attacks mainly at:
options: The less substituted carbon, exactly as it would under basic conditions
Neither carbon; methanol is too weak a nucleophile to react
epoxides.why: Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the C-O bonds partial cationic character, concentrated at the carbon that would form the more stable carbocation; even a weak nucleophile like methanol is then directed to that more substituted carbon.

epoxides.q: In the basic ring-opening of 2-methyl-2,3-epoxybutane with sodium methoxide, methoxide attacks mainly at:
options: The more substituted carbon, exactly as under acidic conditions
Whichever carbon bears the oxygen lone pairs
The reaction does not proceed under basic conditions
epoxides.why: Under basic or neutral conditions the epoxide is not protonated, so the strong methoxide nucleophile simply performs a straightforward SN2 attack at the more sterically accessible, less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: The oxirane (epoxide) ring consists of one oxygen atom and two carbon atoms joined in a three-membered ring.
epoxides.why: An epoxide, or oxirane, is defined by this specific three-membered ring of two carbons and one oxygen, which is what gives it its characteristic angle strain and heightened reactivity.

epoxides.q: Compared to a typical acyclic dialkyl ether, an epoxide reacts with nucleophiles much faster mainly because of:
options: Relief of significant ring strain upon opening the three-membered ring
Epoxides having a much more electronegative oxygen atom
Epoxides containing an extra oxygen atom
epoxides.why: The epoxide's three-membered ring has bond angles far smaller than the ideal tetrahedral angle, storing substantial strain energy; breaking a C-O bond releases that strain, which strongly drives the ring-opening reaction forward.

epoxides.q: Why does switching from basic to acidic conditions change where a nucleophile attacks an unsymmetrical epoxide, even though the same general C-O bond region is ultimately broken?
options: Acid always breaks the bond on the side nearer the larger substituent for purely steric reasons
Protonation makes the more substituted carbon cation-like; under base, sterics decide
Base-catalyzed openings never actually break a C-O bond
The identity of the solvent, not the catalyst, controls the regiochemistry
epoxides.why: Under acid, protonation weakens the C-O bonds and shifts positive character toward whichever carbon can better stabilize it (the more substituted one), directing even weak nucleophiles there; under base, the unprotonated, still-strained ring is simply attacked wherever the strong nucleophile can approach most easily, favoring the less hindered carbon.

epoxides.q: Under acidic conditions, even weak nucleophiles such as water or alcohols can open an epoxide, whereas under neutral or basic conditions only strong nucleophiles react efficiently.
epoxides.why: Protonating the epoxide oxygen makes the ring vastly more electrophilic, so weak nucleophiles that would otherwise be unreactive can now attack; without that activation, only strong, good nucleophiles can open the strained but un-activated ring at a useful rate.

epoxides.q: An epoxide reacting with an amine nucleophile under neutral or basic-type conditions opens to give:
options: A beta-amino alcohol, with the amine attacking the more hindered carbon
An imine with loss of the oxygen entirely
A beta-amino alcohol, with the amine attacking the less hindered carbon
No reaction; amines do not open epoxides
epoxides.why: Amines are good, strongly basic nucleophiles, so like other strong nucleophiles they attack the less sterically hindered carbon of the epoxide via an SN2-like pathway, generating a beta-amino alcohol.

epoxides.q: Opening a meso epoxide with an achiral nucleophile under SN2-like (basic) conditions produces:
options: A mixture of diastereomers, not enantiomers
A racemic (1:1) mixture of two enantiomeric products
epoxides.why: A meso epoxide has two carbons that are enantiotopic to each other; an achiral nucleophile has no way to distinguish between them, so it attacks each one with equal probability, producing equal amounts of both resulting enantiomers.

epoxides.q: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of 2,2-dimethyloxirane (isobutylene oxide) directs the incoming water molecule mainly to:
options: The more substituted carbon (bearing the two methyls)
The unsubstituted CH2 carbon, exactly as it would under basic conditions
Either carbon with statistically equal likelihood
Neither carbon; tertiary epoxide carbons do not react with water
epoxides.why: Protonation of the epoxide oxygen gives the more substituted carbon significant carbocation-like character in the transition state, so water (even though it is a weak nucleophile) is directed there preferentially, just as with other acid-catalyzed epoxide openings.

epoxides.q: The fundamental driving force behind epoxide ring-opening reactions, under both acidic and basic conditions, is:
options: Formation of a new pi bond
Relief of angle strain stored in the three-membered ring
Loss of a proton from the nucleophile
epoxides.why: The highly strained bond angles of the oxirane ring store considerable potential energy; opening the ring to form a less strained, acyclic product is thermodynamically favorable and is the underlying reason epoxides react so readily compared to ordinary ethers.

epoxides.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the behavior of an epoxide versus an ordinary dialkyl ether toward aqueous NaOH at room temperature?
options: Both react at similar, moderate rates
The ordinary ether reacts faster because it has more accessible carbons
The epoxide ring-opens readily while the ether stays inert
Neither reacts with aqueous NaOH under any conditions
epoxides.why: An unstrained ether's C-O bond is simply too strong and the oxygen too poor a leaving group for hydroxide to displace at room temperature, but the epoxide's ring strain dramatically lowers the barrier for the same kind of backside nucleophilic attack.

epoxides.q: Acid-catalyzed ring-opening of an epoxide proceeds through a fully formed, free carbocation intermediate, exactly as in a classic SN1 substitution on an alkyl halide.
epoxides.why: The reaction is usually described as borderline or concerted, with the nucleophile beginning to attack as the C-O bond breaks rather than waiting for a fully independent, freely rotating carbocation to form first; this is why some stereochemical and regiochemical control is retained even under acidic conditions.

epoxides.q: Protonation of an epoxide's oxygen by a strong acid makes subsequent ring-opening much easier mainly because it:
options: Permanently removes the ring strain before any bond breaks
Converts the epoxide into an ether with no further reactivity
Reduces the electrophilicity of the ring carbons
Improves the leaving group and raises electrophilicity
epoxides.why: A neutral ether oxygen is a poor leaving group, but once protonated it becomes a much better one (similar to protonating an alcohol); this protonation also pulls electron density away from the ring carbons, making them more attractive targets for even weak nucleophiles.

epoxides.q: Which property makes epoxides so much more reactive toward ring-opening than larger cyclic ethers such as tetrahydropyran?
options: Severe angle strain from ~60 degree angles
The presence of an extra oxygen atom
Aromatic character in the three-membered ring
epoxides.why: The three-membered epoxide ring forces C-O-C and C-C-O bond angles down to roughly 60 degrees, well below the ideal ~109.5 degrees for sp3 atoms, storing substantial strain energy that is released upon ring-opening; six-membered cyclic ethers have nearly ideal bond angles and little such strain.

epoxides.q: An epoxide treated with a thiolate nucleophile (RS-) under basic conditions opens to give:
options: A beta-hydroxy thioether, with sulfur attacking the more substituted carbon
A beta-hydroxy thioether, with sulfur attacking the less hindered carbon
A disulfide with loss of the oxygen
No reaction; thiolates do not open epoxides
epoxides.why: Thiolate is a strong, highly polarizable nucleophile, so it follows the same basic-conditions pattern as other strong nucleophiles, attacking the less sterically hindered carbon via an SN2-like pathway to give a beta-hydroxy sulfide.

epoxides.q: Epoxidation of an alkene with mCPBA is described as a concerted, stereospecific reaction mainly because:
options: The reaction proceeds through a long-lived, freely rotating diradical intermediate
mCPBA first forms a carbocation that then captures an oxygen atom
Concerted syn delivery of oxygen from one face in one transition state
The alkene's geometry is scrambled during the reaction and then reset afterward
epoxides.why: Because both new C-O bonds form in a single step without any intermediate that could allow rotation about the former double bond, the spatial relationship of the substituents on the alkene is carried over faithfully into the epoxide product.

epoxides.q: Epoxides can be opened by intramolecular nucleophiles, such as a hydroxyl group elsewhere in the same molecule, to form cyclic ether products; this is a common strategy in some natural product and polyether syntheses.
epoxides.why: If a nucleophilic group like an alcohol is positioned correctly within the same molecule, it can attack the strained epoxide ring intramolecularly, closing a new ring and forming a cyclic ether, a key step used to build many natural polyether frameworks.

epoxides.q: Compared to the C-O bonds of a non-strained ether, the C-O bonds of an epoxide are:
options: Stronger and less reactive because of the smaller ring size
Weaker and far more easily broken by nucleophiles
epoxides.why: The severe angle strain in the three-membered ring distorts the hybridization and bonding at the ring carbons, making the C-O bonds considerably easier to cleave by nucleophilic attack than the analogous bonds in an unstrained, open-chain ether.

aldehydes-ketones.q: The carbonyl carbon in aldehydes and ketones is hybridized as:
aldehydes-ketones.why: The carbonyl carbon has 3 regions of electron density (trigonal planar) — sp², just like an alkene carbon.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Ketones are generally less reactive toward nucleophilic addition than aldehydes because:
aldehydes-ketones.why: Extra alkyl groups add steric bulk (hindering attack) and donate electron density (reducing the carbonyl’s electrophilicity) compared to aldehydes.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which is more electrophilic at its carbonyl carbon: an aldehyde or a ketone?
aldehydes-ketones.why: An aldehyde has only one electron-donating alkyl group (vs. two for a ketone) and less steric bulk, leaving its carbonyl carbon more electron-poor and more reactive toward nucleophiles.

aldehydes-ketones.q: What functional group suffix is used in IUPAC nomenclature for a ketone?
aldehydes-ketones.why: Ketones take the suffix -one (e.g., propan-2-one, acetone), while aldehydes use -al. The position of the carbonyl is indicated by a locant for ketones but not needed for aldehydes since the carbonyl must be terminal.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Formaldehyde (methanal) has the structure H2C=O, making it the only aldehyde with two hydrogens on the carbonyl carbon.
aldehydes-ketones.why: Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde, with two hydrogens bonded to the carbonyl carbon instead of one H and one R group. This makes it especially small and electrophilic.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which common name refers to propan-2-one?
aldehydes-ketones.why: Acetone is the everyday name for propan-2-one, the simplest ketone, commonly used as a solvent and nail polish remover.

aldehydes-ketones.q: The carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone bears a partial positive charge (δ+).
aldehydes-ketones.why: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls electron density from the C=O bond toward itself, leaving the carbonyl carbon electron-poor and susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Tollens' test (silver mirror test) is used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones because:
options: Ketones reduce Ag+ to metallic silver but aldehydes do not
Aldehydes are oxidized by Ag(NH3)2+, ketones are not
Both aldehydes and ketones give a positive result
The test detects the presence of an alpha hydrogen
aldehydes-ketones.why: Aldehydes have a C-H bond on the carbonyl carbon that allows them to be oxidized to a carboxylic acid, reducing the diamine silver complex to metallic Ag(0). Ketones lack that hydrogen and resist oxidation.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which of these carbonyl compounds would be expected to have the lowest boiling point relative to its molecular weight, compared to an alcohol of similar size?
options: An alcohol, because it has an O-H group
A ketone, because of extensive hydrogen bonding
An aldehyde, because it cannot hydrogen-bond to itself
They all boil at identical temperatures
aldehydes-ketones.why: Aldehydes and ketones lack an O-H (or N-H) group, so they cannot hydrogen-bond with themselves, giving them lower boiling points than comparably sized alcohols, even though the polar C=O allows dipole-dipole attraction.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which carbonyl compound is generally the LEAST reactive toward nucleophilic addition?
aldehydes-ketones.why: Benzophenone has two bulky, electron-donating aryl groups that sterically block approach of a nucleophile and electronically stabilize the carbonyl carbon through resonance, making it one of the least electrophilic common carbonyls.

aldehydes-ketones.q: An aromatic aldehyde such as benzaldehyde is typically more reactive toward nucleophilic addition than an aliphatic aldehyde like acetaldehyde.
aldehydes-ketones.why: The aromatic ring can donate electron density into the carbonyl through resonance, partially stabilizing the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and making aromatic aldehydes somewhat less electrophilic than simple aliphatic aldehydes.

aldehydes-ketones.q: In an infrared (IR) spectrum, the C=O stretch of a simple aliphatic aldehyde or ketone typically appears around:
aldehydes-ketones.why: The carbonyl C=O stretch is a strong, diagnostic IR absorption typically found between about 1700 and 1750 cm-1 for non-conjugated aldehydes and ketones; conjugation with a ring or double bond shifts it to slightly lower wavenumber.

aldehydes-ketones.q: In 1H NMR, the aldehyde proton (the H directly on the carbonyl carbon) typically appears in which chemical shift range?
aldehydes-ketones.why: The aldehyde C-H is strongly deshielded by the adjacent electron-withdrawing carbonyl, pushing its signal far downfield to roughly 9-10 ppm, a distinctive marker used to confirm the presence of an aldehyde.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Rank these three carbonyl compounds from MOST to LEAST electrophilic at the carbonyl carbon: acetone, acetaldehyde, formaldehyde.
aldehydes-ketones.why: Electrophilicity decreases as more alkyl groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon, since alkyl groups are electron-donating (inductively) and bulkier. Formaldehyde (two H's) is most electrophilic, acetone (two methyls) is least.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Why do ketones resist further oxidation under conditions that readily oxidize aldehydes to carboxylic acids?
options: Ketones have a weaker C=O bond
Ketones are more sterically hindered, blocking the oxidizing agent entirely
Ketones are already in their most oxidized form regardless of structure
Ketones have no hydrogen directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon, so there is no C-H bond to break during oxidation
aldehydes-ketones.why: Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid requires removing the hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon. Ketones have two carbon substituents on that carbon instead of a hydrogen, so this oxidation pathway is unavailable to them.

aldehydes-ketones.q: An aldehyde or ketone dissolved in water exists in equilibrium with a small amount of its geminal diol (hydrate) form.
aldehydes-ketones.why: Water can add reversibly across the carbonyl to form a geminal diol (two OH groups on one carbon). For most ketones and aldehydes this equilibrium favors the carbonyl form, but for very electrophilic carbonyls like formaldehyde, the hydrate can dominate.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Formaldehyde in aqueous solution ('formalin') exists predominantly as its geminal diol rather than as free H2C=O. This is best explained by:
options: Formaldehyde is small and highly electrophilic
Formaldehyde cannot form a carbonyl at all in water
Water is too weak a nucleophile to react with any aldehyde
The geminal diol is aromatic and therefore highly stable
aldehydes-ketones.why: Formaldehyde's minimal steric hindrance and strongly electrophilic carbonyl carbon allow water to add efficiently, shifting the hydration equilibrium far toward the diol, unlike bulkier or less electrophilic carbonyls where the free carbonyl dominates.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which alpha-hydrogen-related property is shared by most aldehydes and ketones but absent in a carbonyl like formaldehyde?
options: The ability to absorb IR radiation
The ability to form an enol tautomer via an alpha hydrogen
aldehydes-ketones.why: Keto-enol tautomerism requires an alpha carbon bearing at least one hydrogen adjacent to the carbonyl. Formaldehyde has no carbon atom alpha to the carbonyl (only hydrogens on the carbonyl carbon itself), so it cannot tautomerize to an enol.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which reagent would selectively reduce an aldehyde or ketone's C=O to a C-OH without reducing other common functional groups like esters under mild conditions?
options: H2/Pd catalyst, which reduces C=C bonds preferentially
NaBH4, which does not reduce esters
aldehydes-ketones.why: Sodium borohydride (NaBH4) is a milder, more selective hydride donor than lithium aluminum hydride, commonly used to reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols while leaving less reactive carbonyls such as esters largely untouched.

aldehydes-ketones.q: The carbonyl carbon in both aldehydes and ketones is sp2 hybridized with a bond angle close to:
aldehydes-ketones.why: sp2 hybridization gives a trigonal planar geometry around the carbonyl carbon, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees between the three attached groups.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Acetone is fully miscible with water.
aldehydes-ketones.why: Although acetone cannot hydrogen-bond with itself as a pure liquid, its carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from water, and its small size allows it to mix completely with water in all proportions.

aldehydes-ketones.q: What is the simplest possible ketone?
aldehydes-ketones.why: Acetone (propan-2-one) is the simplest ketone because a ketone's carbonyl carbon must be bonded to two other carbons; a three-carbon chain is the minimum needed to place the carbonyl in the middle position.

aldehydes-ketones.q: In naming a compound, the prefix 'oxo-' is used to indicate a ketone carbonyl group when it is not the principal characteristic group (for example, when a carboxylic acid is present elsewhere in the molecule).
aldehydes-ketones.why: When another group outranks the ketone in IUPAC priority (such as a carboxylic acid), the ketone oxygen is named as a substituent using 'oxo-' with a locant, rather than using the -one suffix.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which statement about dipole moments of aldehydes/ketones versus alkanes of similar molar mass is correct?
options: Aldehydes and ketones have essentially zero dipole moment, identical to alkanes
The C=O bond gives aldehydes and ketones a significant permanent dipole moment, higher than comparable alkanes
Only aromatic ketones have a measurable dipole moment
Dipole moment is irrelevant to boiling point
aldehydes-ketones.why: The polarized C=O bond creates a substantial molecular dipole in aldehydes and ketones, leading to stronger dipole-dipole intermolecular forces and higher boiling points than nonpolar alkanes of similar size.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Cyclohexanone is an example of a cyclic ketone in which the carbonyl carbon is part of a six-membered ring.
aldehydes-ketones.why: Cyclohexanone has a six-membered carbon ring with one ring carbon replaced by a carbonyl (C=O), making it a common cyclic ketone used in industry and as a synthetic intermediate.

aldehydes-ketones.q: A chemist wants to use a color/precipitate test to tell whether an unknown liquid is an aldehyde or a ketone. Which classic reagent combination would give a positive (color change/precipitate) result specifically with the aldehyde?
aldehydes-ketones.why: Tollens' reagent selectively oxidizes aldehydes (which have an oxidizable C-H on the carbonyl carbon), depositing metallic silver, while ketones generally give no reaction, making it useful for distinguishing the two.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Which of the following best explains why steric bulk around the carbonyl carbon reduces reactivity toward nucleophilic addition in ketones compared to aldehydes?
options: Bulkier groups increase the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
Bulkier groups make the carbonyl oxygen more basic, which has no effect on sterics
Steric bulk has no measurable effect on reaction rate
Bulky groups hinder the nucleophile's approach, raising the barrier
aldehydes-ketones.why: As the incoming nucleophile approaches the planar sp2 carbonyl carbon to form a tetrahedral intermediate, larger substituents (two alkyl/aryl groups in ketones vs. one in aldehydes) crowd that approach and raise the energy of the transition state, slowing the reaction.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Benzaldehyde's carbonyl carbon is less electrophilic than that of a comparable aliphatic aldehyde mainly because of:
options: Resonance donation from the ring into the carbonyl
Steric hindrance from the phenyl ring blocking nucleophiles
The phenyl ring's inductive electron withdrawal, which increases electrophilicity
Hydrogen bonding between the ring and the carbonyl oxygen
aldehydes-ketones.why: The aromatic pi system can conjugate with the carbonyl, delocalizing electron density toward the carbonyl carbon through resonance and reducing (though not eliminating) its electrophilicity relative to a simple alkyl aldehyde.

aldehydes-ketones.q: A molecule containing both an aldehyde group and a ketone group in the same chain would be named using which suffix for the principal characteristic group?
options: Both suffixes are used together as '-alone'
Neither; it must be renamed as a diketone
aldehydes-ketones.why: In the standard IUPAC seniority order of functional groups, aldehydes rank higher than ketones, so when both are present the molecule is named as an '-al' with the ketone indicated by an 'oxo-' substituent prefix and locant.

aldehydes-ketones.q: Glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone are both three-carbon sugars that differ specifically in that one is an aldehyde and the other is a ketone.
aldehydes-ketones.why: Glyceraldehyde is an aldotriose (aldehyde at C1) while dihydroxyacetone is a ketotriose (ketone at C2); both share the same molecular formula but differ in the position and type of the carbonyl group.

nucleophilic-addition.q: In nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, the nucleophile attacks:
nucleophilic-addition.why: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ due to oxygen’s electronegativity, making it the site of nucleophilic attack.

nucleophilic-addition.q: What happens to the C=O pi bond during nucleophilic addition?
options: It breaks, pushing electrons onto the oxygen as an alkoxide
It becomes a new sigma bond to the nucleophile without changing oxygen
nucleophilic-addition.why: The nucleophile forms a new bond to carbon while the C=O pi electrons shift entirely onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.

nucleophilic-addition.q: After a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl, what intermediate typically forms before a final proton transfer?
nucleophilic-addition.why: The carbonyl carbon becomes sp³ and tetrahedral, bearing the new nucleophile bond and a negatively charged oxygen (alkoxide), which is then typically protonated.

nucleophilic-addition.q: In the mechanism of base-catalyzed nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, what is generally the rate-determining step?
options: Attack of the nucleophile on the carbonyl carbon
nucleophilic-addition.why: For simple nucleophilic addition (not substitution), the nucleophile's attack on the electrophilic, sp2 carbonyl carbon to form the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is typically the slow, rate-determining step; the final proton transfer is usually fast.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Under acid catalysis, the carbonyl oxygen is typically protonated before the nucleophile attacks.
nucleophilic-addition.why: Protonating the carbonyl oxygen makes the molecule an oxocarbenium-like species, pulling even more electron density away from the carbonyl carbon and making it a much stronger electrophile, which speeds up nucleophile attack, especially useful for weak nucleophiles like alcohols.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which trajectory angle (relative to the carbonyl plane) does a nucleophile typically follow when approaching a carbonyl carbon, known as the Bürgi-Dunitz angle?
options: Approximately 90 degrees, directly perpendicular to the C=O bond
Approximately 180 degrees, directly in line with the C=O bond
Approximately 0 degrees, in the same plane as the carbonyl
nucleophilic-addition.why: The nucleophile approaches at roughly 107 degrees relative to the C=O axis (the Bürgi-Dunitz angle) to minimize repulsion with the forming oxygen lone pair, trajectory that leads smoothly to the tetrahedral geometry of the product.

nucleophilic-addition.q: When cyanide ion (CN-) adds to an aldehyde, the product formed (before any workup) is called a:
nucleophilic-addition.why: Cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon, and after protonation of the resulting alkoxide, the product is a cyanohydrin, which has both a hydroxyl group and a nitrile group on the same carbon.

nucleophilic-addition.q: When a primary amine adds to a ketone and the reaction proceeds to completion with loss of water, the final product is typically a(n):
nucleophilic-addition.why: A primary amine first adds to give a hemiaminal (carbinolamine), which then loses water to form a C=N double bond, known as an imine or Schiff base.

nucleophilic-addition.q: A secondary amine reacting with a ketone that has an alpha hydrogen ultimately forms an enamine rather than an imine, because:
options: Secondary amines cannot form a hemiaminal intermediate at all
Enamines are less stable than imines and therefore always form first
Secondary amines are stronger nucleophiles than primary amines
The nitrogen has no H left to lose, so an alpha C-H is lost
nucleophilic-addition.why: A secondary amine's nitrogen, after addition, only has one hydrogen. When water leaves, the nitrogen cannot also lose its one remaining hydrogen to form a neutral C=N (that would leave nitrogen positively charged/unstable), so instead a proton is removed from the alpha carbon, forming a conjugated carbon-carbon/nitrogen double bond system: the enamine.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Grignard reagents (RMgX) add to aldehydes and ketones via nucleophilic addition, and the resulting alkoxide must be protonated in a separate aqueous acid workup step to give the final alcohol.
nucleophilic-addition.why: Grignard reagents are strongly basic/nucleophilic and react irreversibly with carbonyls to form a magnesium alkoxide salt. This intermediate is stable until an aqueous acid workup protonates it, releasing the neutral alcohol product.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Why is addition of a Grignard reagent to a carbonyl considered essentially irreversible, unlike addition of water or an alcohol?
options: Because both the alkoxide and the carbanion are poor leaving groups
Because the carbon-carbon bond formed is extremely weak and can easily break
Because Grignard reagents do not actually bond to the carbonyl carbon
Because the reaction only occurs in the gas phase
nucleophilic-addition.why: Reversibility in carbonyl addition depends on whether the newly added group can leave again. An alkoxide (from an organometallic addition) is a strong base and terrible leaving group, so once the strongly nucleophilic carbanion adds, it essentially never leaves, making the reaction irreversible under normal conditions.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Addition of water to an aldehyde or ketone to form a geminal diol (hydrate) is generally reversible, with the equilibrium position depending on the electrophilicity of the starting carbonyl.
nucleophilic-addition.why: Hydration of carbonyls is a classic reversible nucleophilic addition. Highly electrophilic, unhindered carbonyls (like formaldehyde or chloral) favor the hydrate, while typical ketones favor the free carbonyl form at equilibrium.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Compared to hydroxide ion, water is a much weaker nucleophile toward carbonyls mainly because:
options: Water has no lone pairs on oxygen
Hydroxide's charge makes its lone pairs more available
Water is a larger molecule than hydroxide
Water cannot approach the carbonyl carbon at the correct angle
nucleophilic-addition.why: A negatively charged nucleophile like hydroxide has more electron density available to donate than a neutral nucleophile like water, making it significantly more reactive in attacking an electrophilic carbonyl carbon.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which factor would be expected to INCREASE the electrophilicity of a carbonyl carbon, making it more reactive toward nucleophilic addition?
options: Placing an electron-donating alkyl group directly on the carbonyl carbon
Increasing steric bulk around the carbonyl carbon
Placing an electron-withdrawing group (such as a halogen) near the carbonyl carbon
Conjugating the carbonyl with an aromatic ring
nucleophilic-addition.why: An electron-withdrawing group nearby pulls electron density away from the carbonyl carbon inductively, intensifying its partial positive charge and making it a better target for a nucleophile.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral) is significantly MORE reactive toward nucleophilic addition than acetaldehyde. The best explanation is:
options: The three chlorine atoms sterically shield the carbonyl, slowing addition
Chlorine atoms donate electrons into the carbonyl through resonance
Chlorine has no electronic effect on nearby carbons
The three chlorines withdraw electron density inductively
nucleophilic-addition.why: The three strongly electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms on the adjacent carbon pull electron density away inductively, greatly increasing the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and favoring nucleophilic addition (chloral hydrate forms readily as a stable solid, unlike most simple hydrates).

nucleophilic-addition.q: In nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, what structural change happens to the carbonyl carbon's hybridization and geometry?
options: It stays sp2 and trigonal planar throughout
It changes from sp3 to sp2
It becomes sp hybridized and linear
nucleophilic-addition.why: The carbonyl carbon starts as sp2 and planar (bonded to three groups). After the nucleophile adds and the pi bond breaks, that carbon becomes sp3 with four substituents arranged tetrahedrally.

nucleophilic-addition.q: During nucleophilic addition, the two pi electrons of the C=O bond end up localized as a lone pair on the oxygen atom.
nucleophilic-addition.why: As the nucleophile forms a new sigma bond to carbon, the C=O pi bond breaks and its electron pair moves entirely onto the oxygen, generating a negatively charged alkoxide intermediate.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which of the following nucleophiles, when added to a ketone, would give a product best described as a hemiketal (a type of hemiacetal)?
nucleophilic-addition.why: When one equivalent of alcohol adds to a ketone's carbonyl carbon, the product bears both an -OH and an -OR group on the same carbon, which is defined as a hemiacetal (specifically a hemiketal when derived from a ketone).

nucleophilic-addition.q: If a nucleophile adds to one face of a planar carbonyl carbon and creates a new stereocenter, with no other chiral influence present, the product forms as:
nucleophilic-addition.why: A planar sp2 carbonyl carbon is equally accessible to the nucleophile from either face (top or bottom) in the absence of a chiral catalyst or existing stereocenter nearby, so both possible stereochemical outcomes form in equal amounts, giving a racemic mixture.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Ketones generally undergo nucleophilic addition more slowly than aldehydes for what combination of reasons?
options: Only steric effects matter; electronics are identical
Only electronic effects matter; sterics are identical
Ketones simply lack a carbonyl carbon
More steric hindrance and less electrophilicity
nucleophilic-addition.why: Having two carbon substituents instead of one both physically blocks nucleophile approach (sterics) and donates more electron density into the carbonyl carbon (electronics), both factors working together to slow nucleophilic addition in ketones relative to aldehydes.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Nucleophilic ADDITION to an aldehyde/ketone and nucleophilic ACYL SUBSTITUTION at a carboxylic acid derivative (like an ester) both proceed through a tetrahedral intermediate, but they differ because:
options: Only acyl substitution expels a leaving group
Addition has no tetrahedral intermediate at all
Acyl substitution never involves a nucleophile
Aldehydes and ketones always have a leaving group attached
nucleophilic-addition.why: Esters, acid chlorides, and amides have an additional electronegative group (OR, Cl, NR2) on the carbonyl carbon that can leave after the tetrahedral intermediate forms, regenerating the C=O and substituting the nucleophile for the leaving group. Aldehydes and ketones have only H or alkyl/aryl groups (poor leaving groups), so the tetrahedral intermediate persists as the final addition product.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Sodium borohydride (NaBH4) delivering a hydride ion to a ketone's carbonyl carbon is an example of nucleophilic addition in which hydride acts as the nucleophile.
nucleophilic-addition.why: Hydride (H-) attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon just like other nucleophiles, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate that is then protonated (often during an aqueous workup) to give the alcohol product.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which of the following is the best order of relative nucleophile strength toward a carbonyl carbon, from STRONGEST to WEAKEST, for this set: hydride (from LiAlH4), an amine, and water?
options: All three are equally nucleophilic toward carbonyls
nucleophilic-addition.why: Hydride delivered from a reactive metal hydride is an extremely strong, essentially irreversible nucleophile toward carbonyls, a neutral amine is a good but more moderate nucleophile that forms reversible addition products first, and neutral water is comparatively weak, needing acid or base assistance to react efficiently.

nucleophilic-addition.q: A strong, weakly basic nucleophile such as iodide ion (I-) reacts poorly with aldehydes and ketones in simple nucleophilic addition reactions. Why?
options: Iodide has no lone pairs available
Iodide's negative charge repels the carbonyl oxygen, preventing any approach
Iodide is weakly basic and an excellent leaving group
Carbonyls never react with halide ions for any reason
nucleophilic-addition.why: While iodide is a great leaving group and decent nucleophile in substitution chemistry, its addition to a carbonyl is not thermodynamically favorable here; there's little driving force, and any adduct would readily revert, so iodide addition to simple carbonyls is not a standard useful reaction.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes how an acid catalyst versus a base catalyst helps nucleophilic addition of an alcohol to a ketone proceed?
options: Acid and base catalysis work by an identical mechanism with no meaningful difference
Base protonates the carbonyl oxygen; acid deprotonates the alcohol
Neither acid nor base has any effect on this reaction
Acid protonates the carbonyl; base deprotonates the alcohol
nucleophilic-addition.why: Because alcohols are weak, neutral nucleophiles, catalysis helps either by activating the electrophile (acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen) or by activating the nucleophile (base removes the alcohol's proton to generate a more reactive alkoxide).

nucleophilic-addition.q: In the reaction of an aldehyde with excess hydrazine (H2N-NH2) followed by strong base and heat (the Wolff-Kishner-type sequence), the initial step is still a nucleophilic addition of the amine nitrogen to the carbonyl carbon.
nucleophilic-addition.why: Regardless of the final multistep outcome, the first mechanistic event when any amine reacts with a carbonyl is nucleophilic addition of the nitrogen lone pair to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate (hemiaminal) before any subsequent dehydration or reduction steps.

nucleophilic-addition.q: Which best describes why an alkoxide intermediate formed during nucleophilic addition is typically quenched with water or dilute acid at the end of a reaction?
options: To protonate the alkoxide to the neutral alcohol
To oxidize the alkoxide into a carboxylic acid
To reverse the addition and regenerate starting carbonyl
nucleophilic-addition.why: The alkoxide intermediate carries a negative charge on oxygen and is a strong base; an aqueous or mildly acidic workup simply transfers a proton onto that oxygen to give the stable, neutral alcohol final product.

nucleophilic-addition.q: When comparing nucleophilic addition rates, an aldehyde reacting with a bulky nucleophile (such as a branched Grignard reagent) will generally react slower than with a small nucleophile (such as methylmagnesium bromide), due to:
options: Electronic effects dominating entirely, with no steric component
Steric hindrance in the tetrahedral transition state
Bulky nucleophiles always being poor nucleophiles electronically
No difference; nucleophile size never matters
nucleophilic-addition.why: As any nucleophile approaches the carbonyl carbon to form the crowded tetrahedral intermediate, a bulkier nucleophile experiences greater steric strain with the existing substituents on that carbon, slowing the reaction relative to a smaller nucleophile.

nucleophilic-addition.q: During acid-catalyzed addition of an alcohol to a ketone, protonating the carbonyl oxygen converts the neutral ketone into a resonance-stabilized cation often described as an oxocarbenium-like species before nucleophilic attack occurs.
nucleophilic-addition.why: Protonation places a full positive charge on oxygen, which is stabilized by resonance delocalization onto the adjacent carbon, greatly enhancing that carbon's electrophilicity and priming it for nucleophilic attack by the alcohol.

nucleophilic-addition.q: If two different carbonyl compounds are placed in a flask along with a limited amount of a moderately strong nucleophile, which one would you expect to react fastest: an unhindered aliphatic aldehyde, or a sterically hindered diaryl ketone?
options: The diaryl ketone, because aromatic stabilization speeds up addition
They would react at identical rates
The aldehyde, less hindered and more electrophilic
Neither would react under any circumstances
nucleophilic-addition.why: Unhindered aldehydes combine low steric bulk with high electrophilicity, both of which favor fast nucleophilic addition, whereas bulky diaryl ketones are both sterically hindered and electronically stabilized by resonance, making them poor substrates for addition.

acetals.q: An acetal forms from a carbonyl reacting with how many equivalents of alcohol (under acid catalysis)?
options: Two, giving a full acetal (two ether-like oxygens)
acetals.why: The first alcohol gives a hemiacetal; a second equivalent (after loss of water) gives the full acetal with two OR groups on the former carbonyl carbon.

acetals.q: Acetals are stable under basic conditions but revert back to the carbonyl under:
acetals.why: Acetal formation/hydrolysis is acid-catalyzed and reversible — acetals are stable to base, making them useful as protecting groups, but hydrolyze back to the carbonyl in aqueous acid.

acetals.q: Why are acetals useful as protecting groups for aldehydes/ketones during multi-step synthesis?
options: They make the carbonyl more reactive, not less
They resist base yet hydrolyze in acid
They only work on carboxylic acids
acetals.why: Converting a reactive carbonyl into a stable acetal lets other parts of a molecule be modified under basic/non-acidic conditions without the carbonyl interfering, then mild aqueous acid hydrolyzes the acetal back.

acetals.q: An acetal is formed when a carbonyl compound reacts, under acid catalysis, with how many equivalents of an alcohol?
acetals.why: Acetal formation requires two separate additions of alcohol: the first gives a hemiacetal, and the second, after loss of water, replaces the hemiacetal's OH group with a second OR group to give the full acetal.

acetals.q: A hemiacetal carbon bears both an -OH group and an -OR group attached to the same carbon, along with an H and/or R group from the original carbonyl.
acetals.why: A hemiacetal is the product of adding just one equivalent of alcohol to an aldehyde or ketone; that carbon now carries one OH (from the original carbonyl oxygen, now protonated) and one OR (from the added alcohol).

acetals.q: Acetals are stable under basic or neutral aqueous conditions but hydrolyze back to the parent carbonyl compound under:
options: High temperature alone with no other reagent
acetals.why: Acetal hydrolysis requires protonation of one of the alkoxy oxygens to kick off the reverse mechanism (loss of alcohol, formation of an oxocarbenium ion, then addition of water); this only proceeds efficiently under acidic aqueous conditions.

acetals.q: Why are acetals commonly used as protecting groups for aldehydes and ketones during multi-step organic synthesis?
options: Because acetals are more reactive than the original carbonyl, allowing faster synthesis
They are stable to base, nucleophiles, and oxidants, but removed by aqueous acid
Because acetals permanently replace the carbonyl group with no way back
Because acetals only form in the presence of strong base
acetals.why: Masking a reactive carbonyl as an acetal lets chemists run reactions elsewhere in the molecule (such as Grignard additions or reductions) that would otherwise also attack the carbonyl; afterward, brief treatment with dilute aqueous acid cleanly regenerates the original aldehyde or ketone.

acetals.q: Which term specifically describes an acetal made from a ketone (as opposed to an aldehyde)?
acetals.why: Although modern IUPAC usage often groups both under 'acetal,' the traditional and still widely used term 'ketal' specifically refers to the double-alkoxy product derived from a ketone rather than an aldehyde.

acetals.q: In the acid-catalyzed mechanism of acetal formation, after the first alcohol adds to give the protonated hemiacetal, what key intermediate forms upon loss of water?
options: An oxocarbenium ion (resonance-stabilized carbocation with an adjacent oxygen)
acetals.why: Protonation of the hemiacetal's hydroxyl allows water to leave, generating a cation on the carbon that is stabilized by resonance donation from the remaining oxygen's lone pair, forming the key oxocarbenium intermediate that the second alcohol then attacks.

acetals.q: When a carbonyl compound reacts with a diol such as ethylene glycol under acid catalysis, the two hydroxyl groups can both attack the same carbonyl carbon, typically forming a:
options: A polymer with no defined ring size
acetals.why: Ethylene glycol's two OH groups are positioned to both add intramolecularly to the same carbonyl carbon, closing a five-membered ring containing two oxygens (a 1,3-dioxolane), a very common cyclic acetal protecting group.

acetals.q: Acetal formation from a carbonyl compound and an alcohol is an equilibrium reaction, and using a large excess of alcohol (or removing water as it forms, e.g., with a Dean-Stark trap) helps drive the equilibrium toward the acetal product.
acetals.why: Because acetal formation is reversible, Le Chatelier's principle applies: increasing alcohol concentration or physically removing the water byproduct shifts the equilibrium in favor of acetal formation rather than staying as the hemiacetal or reverting to the carbonyl.

acetals.q: Glucose in aqueous solution exists predominantly as a cyclic structure formed by an intramolecular reaction between its aldehyde carbon and one of its own hydroxyl groups. This cyclic form is best classified as a:
options: Ether with no other functional character
acetals.why: Only one hydroxyl group from within the glucose chain adds to the aldehyde carbon, giving a ring carbon with one OH and one OR (the ring oxygen) attached, the classic structure of a cyclic hemiacetal, not a full acetal.

acetals.q: The anomeric carbon in a cyclic sugar hemiacetal is the carbon that was originally the carbonyl carbon before ring closure.
acetals.why: When the open-chain aldose or ketose cyclizes, the original carbonyl carbon becomes a new stereocenter bearing both an OH and a ring oxygen; this carbon is specifically called the anomeric carbon, and its two possible configurations are the alpha and beta anomers.

acetals.q: Mutarotation, the slow change in optical rotation observed when crystalline glucose is dissolved in water, occurs because:
options: Glucose decomposes into smaller sugars over time
Water oxidizes glucose to gluconic acid
The anomers interconvert via the open form
Glucose forms a full acetal with water
acetals.why: Because the cyclic hemiacetal is in equilibrium with the open-chain carbonyl form, the ring can open and re-close repeatedly, randomizing which face the new hydroxyl ends up on and gradually establishing an equilibrium mixture of alpha and beta anomers, changing the observed optical rotation over time.

acetals.q: Compared to ketones, aldehydes generally form acetals more readily under the same acid-catalyzed conditions. This is mainly due to:
options: Aldehydes having a more basic carbonyl oxygen
Ketones lacking a carbonyl group entirely
Acetal formation being impossible for ketones
acetals.why: The same structural features that make aldehydes generally more reactive toward nucleophilic addition overall (less steric hindrance, greater electrophilicity) also apply to acetal formation, so aldehydes convert to acetals more readily and under milder conditions than most ketones.

acetals.q: A chemist performs a Grignard addition on a molecule containing both a ketone and an ester, wanting the Grignard reagent to react only with the ester. What is a reasonable strategy using acetal chemistry to achieve this selectivity?
options: Protect the ketone as a cyclic acetal, run the Grignard, then hydrolyze
There is no way to control this selectivity
Protect the ester as an acetal instead, since esters and acetals are chemically identical
Add excess water to deactivate the Grignard reagent near the ketone only
acetals.why: Because Grignard reagents react readily with ketones but an acetal is essentially inert to strongly basic/nucleophilic organometallic reagents, temporarily converting the ketone into an acetal shields it during the Grignard step; mild aqueous acid afterward cleanly unmasks the ketone again.

acetals.q: Thioacetals, formed from a carbonyl compound and two equivalents of a thiol (RSH) instead of an alcohol, are generally LESS easily hydrolyzed back to the carbonyl under aqueous acid than ordinary oxygen acetals.
acetals.why: Sulfur is a weaker base than oxygen and less able to stabilize a positive charge through resonance in the way needed for the acid-catalyzed hydrolysis mechanism, so thioacetals (such as dithianes) are notably more robust toward aqueous acid than their oxygen analogs and require special reagents (like Hg2+ salts) to remove.

acetals.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical catalyst used to promote acetal formation from a ketone and an alcohol?
acetals.why: Acetal formation (and its reverse, hydrolysis) proceeds through cationic intermediates that require acid catalysis; a strong base like NaOH does not activate the carbonyl for this pathway and acetals are, in fact, stable to basic conditions rather than promoted by them.
