c-nmr.why: The linear, cylindrically symmetric pi system of a triple bond interacts with the applied field differently than a planar double bond's pi system, producing an anisotropic effect that shields sp alkyne carbons relative to sp2 alkene or aromatic carbons.

c-nmr.q: Because of its molecular symmetry, how many distinct ¹³C NMR signals would toluene (methylbenzene) show, given that the ring carbons pair up by symmetry?
c-nmr.why: Toluene has a mirror plane that makes the two carbons ortho to the methyl group equivalent to each other, and the two meta carbons equivalent to each other, giving five unique carbons total: the methyl carbon, the ipso carbon, the equivalent ortho pair, the equivalent meta pair, and the para carbon.

c-nmr.q: In a DEPT experiment, quaternary carbons (carbons with no attached hydrogens) are distinguished from CH, CH2, and CH3 carbons because:
options: Quaternary carbons vanish; DEPT needs attached hydrogens
Quaternary carbons always appear as the tallest peaks in DEPT
DEPT can only detect quaternary carbons and nothing else
Quaternary carbons are shown in a completely different color on the spectrum
c-nmr.why: DEPT transfers polarization from attached protons to the carbon nucleus, so a carbon with no attached hydrogens has nothing to receive that transfer from and simply does not show up in the DEPT spectrum.

c-nmr.q: Quaternary carbons typically show weaker peak intensities in a standard proton-decoupled ¹³C NMR spectrum compared to protonated carbons of similar abundance.
c-nmr.why: Quaternary carbons lack the nuclear Overhauser enhancement from directly attached protons and often relax more slowly, both of which tend to make their signals weaker relative to protonated carbons, even at equal molar amounts.

c-nmr.q: Between a simple aldehyde's carbonyl carbon and a simple ketone's carbonyl carbon, which is generally found further downfield in ¹³C NMR?
options: The aldehyde carbonyl carbon is always further downfield
The ketone carbonyl carbon is further downfield
They are always identical in shift
Aldehydes have no carbonyl carbon at all
c-nmr.why: Ketone carbonyl carbons typically fall around 205-220 ppm, while aldehyde carbonyl carbons are usually a bit more shielded, around 190-205 ppm, due to differences in the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon.

c-nmr.q: An sp3 carbon directly attached to a hydroxyl oxygen (as in an alcohol) typically appears around 50-90 ppm in ¹³C NMR, well downfield of a typical alkane carbon (0-40 ppm). This shift is mainly due to:
options: Alcohols having no carbon atoms bonded to oxygen
Oxygen always shielding nearby carbons rather than deshielding them
The electronegative oxygen withdrawing electron density from the attached carbon, deshielding it
This shift only happens in aromatic alcohols
c-nmr.why: Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density away from the carbon it is bonded to, deshielding that carbon and shifting its signal downfield relative to an ordinary alkane carbon.

c-nmr.q: Two carbons related by an internal mirror plane of symmetry in an achiral molecule will typically give the same ¹³C NMR chemical shift.
c-nmr.why: Just as with ¹H NMR, carbons related by a genuine symmetry operation of the molecule occupy chemically equivalent environments and therefore resonate at the same shift.

c-nmr.q: A carboxylic acid's carbonyl carbon (roughly 170-185 ppm) and an ester's carbonyl carbon (roughly 165-175 ppm) can sometimes be distinguished mainly by:
options: Carboxylic acids never show a carbonyl carbon signal
Esters always appear further downfield than carboxylic acids
There is no possible way to distinguish the two by any NMR method
Their overlapping shift ranges plus the O-H signature
c-nmr.why: The shift ranges for these two carbonyl types overlap somewhat, so chemists often combine the ¹³C shift with other evidence, such as the presence of a broad O-H absorption in IR or an O-H proton in ¹H NMR, to tell them apart confidently.

c-nmr.q: A nitrile carbon (C of a C≡N group) typically appears around 115-120 ppm in ¹³C NMR, a range that is useful diagnostically mainly because:
options: It falls in an open region, away from aromatic carbons
Nitrile carbons are never detectable by ¹³C NMR
This range is identical to a typical aldehyde carbonyl carbon
Nitrile carbons always overlap exactly with TMS
c-nmr.why: Although close to the aromatic/alkene region, a nitrile carbon's shift around 115-120 ppm, especially combined with a sharp triple-bond stretch in IR, helps distinguish it from other unsaturated carbons.

c-nmr.q: A para-disubstituted benzene ring with two different substituents, which breaks the ring's six-fold symmetry down to a single mirror plane, would be expected to show how many distinct aromatic ¹³C signals?
c-nmr.why: The mirror plane running through the two substituted carbons makes the two carbons next to one substituent equivalent to each other, and the two carbons next to the other substituent equivalent to each other, giving four unique aromatic carbons: the two substituted carbons plus the two equivalent pairs.

c-nmr.q: Why do we not typically observe carbon-carbon (¹³C-¹³C) spin coupling in a routine ¹³C NMR spectrum, even though carbons are directly bonded to each other throughout the molecule?
options: Carbon-carbon bonds are incapable of transmitting any spin coupling
All carbon-carbon coupling constants are zero by definition
Two bonded carbons are almost never both ¹³C
The decoupler used for proton decoupling also removes all carbon-carbon coupling
c-nmr.why: Since roughly 99 percent of carbon atoms are the spin-inactive ¹²C isotope, the probability that a given ¹³C nucleus happens to be bonded to another ¹³C nucleus is small, so carbon-carbon coupling is rarely visible above the noise in a normal spectrum.

c-nmr.q: A molecule can sometimes show a different total number of distinct ¹H NMR signals than distinct ¹³C NMR signals for the same structure. What is one reasonable explanation for this?
options: The two techniques must always give exactly the same number of signals for any molecule
¹³C NMR always shows more signals than ¹H NMR for every molecule
¹H NMR cannot show more than one signal per molecule
Coincidental overlap, or symmetry that equates protons but not carbons
c-nmr.why: Because chemical shift differences and coincidental overlaps differ between ¹H and ¹³C environments, and because symmetry can relate protons without necessarily relating the carbons carrying them (or vice versa), the number of resolved signals does not have to match between the two spectra.

c-nmr.q: In a DEPT-135 experiment, CH and CH3 carbons appear as positive peaks, CH2 carbons appear as negative (inverted) peaks, and quaternary carbons are absent altogether. This pattern is useful mainly because it allows chemists to:
options: Tell how many hydrogens each carbon bears
Directly count the total number of hydrogens in the molecule
Measure the exact bond angles in the molecule
c-nmr.why: Because DEPT signal phase and intensity depend on the number of attached protons, comparing a DEPT-135 spectrum to the standard ¹³C spectrum lets chemists sort carbons into CH3/CH, CH2, and quaternary categories, something ordinary ¹³C peak height cannot reliably do.

c-nmr.q: ¹³C NMR chemical shifts generally follow the same electronegativity-based deshielding trends seen in ¹H NMR, where attaching a more electronegative atom shifts the signal downfield, though the magnitude of the shift differs between the two techniques.
c-nmr.why: Both techniques respond to the same underlying electron-withdrawing inductive and resonance effects, so electronegative substituents deshield nearby carbons in ¹³C NMR in a way that parallels ¹H NMR trends, even though the absolute ppm shifts differ in scale.

c-nmr.q: Neopentane, (CH3)4C, has five carbon atoms but shows only two signals in ¹³C NMR. This is best explained by:
options: Neopentane actually contains only two carbon atoms
Symmetry makes the four methyl carbons equivalent
¹³C NMR cannot detect quaternary carbons under any circumstances
The four methyl groups are not actually bonded to the central carbon
c-nmr.why: The four methyl groups are related by the molecule's high symmetry (effectively a tetrahedral arrangement around the central carbon), making them all chemically equivalent and giving just one methyl signal plus one signal for the unique central quaternary carbon.

c-nmr.q: Obtaining a good ¹³C NMR spectrum often requires longer acquisition times or more scans rather than simply increasing sample concentration, partly because:
options: ¹³C nuclei are immune to any relaxation effects
Increasing concentration always fully compensates for ¹³C's low natural abundance with no need for extra scans
Long relaxation times, especially for quaternary carbons, require signal averaging over many scans
Longer scans have no effect on signal-to-noise ratio
c-nmr.why: Slow relaxation, particularly for quaternary carbons lacking nearby protons to help them relax, limits how quickly a ¹³C signal can be repeatedly sampled, so extending the number of scans (not just raising concentration) is often needed to achieve a usable spectrum.

c-nmr.q: Rank the following carbonyl-containing carbons from LOWEST to HIGHEST typical ¹³C chemical shift: amide carbonyl, ester carbonyl, ketone carbonyl.
c-nmr.why: The amide nitrogen donates electron density into the carbonyl most effectively by resonance, shielding its carbon the most, followed by the ester oxygen's somewhat weaker donation, while the ketone, lacking this extra heteroatom donation, appears furthest downfield.

c-nmr.q: In ¹³C NMR, a carbon's chemical shift is strongly affected by nearby electronegative atoms even two or three bonds away, similar to the pattern seen in ¹H NMR, though the size of the effect attenuates with distance in both techniques.
c-nmr.why: Inductive electron withdrawal from an electronegative atom propagates through several bonds in both ¹H and ¹³C NMR, deshielding nearby nuclei, with the effect weakening as the number of intervening bonds increases.

mass-spec.q: In mass spectrometry, the molecular ion peak (M+) corresponds to:
mass-spec.why: The molecular ion forms when the neutral molecule loses an electron in the ionization source, giving a radical cation at the molecule’s full mass.

mass-spec.q: A mass spec fragmentation pattern showing loss of 15 mass units from the molecular ion is most consistent with loss of:
mass-spec.why: A mass loss of 15 corresponds to CH₃ (methyl, 12+3=15), a very common fragmentation for molecules with a methyl group attached to a stabilizing center.

mass-spec.q: In mass spectrometry, the "base peak" refers to:
options: The peak at the lowest mass
mass-spec.why: The base peak is defined as the most intense peak in the spectrum (100% relative abundance) — it is often, but not always, the same as the molecular ion peak.

mass-spec.q: In mass spectrometry, the term m/z refers to:
options: The total mass of the neutral, un-ionized sample
The melting point of the sample
The number of fragments produced per second
The mass-to-charge ratio of an ion detected by the instrument
mass-spec.why: Mass spectrometers separate and detect ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio, m/z, which for most singly charged ions in an intro course is essentially equal to the ion's mass.

mass-spec.q: In electron ionization (EI) mass spectrometry, the molecular ion is typically formed by:
options: Removing one electron from the molecule
Adding a proton to the neutral molecule
Removing an entire atom from the molecule
Adding an electron to the neutral molecule
mass-spec.why: A high-energy electron beam knocks one electron out of the neutral molecule, leaving behind an odd-electron, positively charged species called the molecular ion or radical cation.

mass-spec.q: The molecular ion peak (M+) always corresponds to the most intense peak in the entire mass spectrum.
mass-spec.why: The most intense peak is called the base peak, and it is very often a fragment ion rather than the molecular ion, especially for molecules that fragment easily; M+ itself can be weak or even absent for some compounds.

mass-spec.q: The relative height of the M+1 isotope peak compared to M+ in a mass spectrum is mainly useful for estimating:
options: The number of nitrogen atoms in the molecule
The approximate number of carbon atoms
The boiling point of the compound
The number of oxygen atoms in the molecule
mass-spec.why: Since about 1.1 percent of carbon atoms are naturally ¹³C, the M+1 peak's relative intensity grows roughly in proportion to the number of carbons present, giving a rough estimate of carbon count.

mass-spec.q: A compound containing a single chlorine atom typically shows an M+2 peak with what approximate relative intensity compared to M+?
options: About 10 times the intensity of M+
mass-spec.why: Chlorine's two natural isotopes, 35Cl and 37Cl, occur in roughly a 3:1 ratio, so a single-chlorine compound's M+2 peak (containing 37Cl) appears at roughly one-third the height of the M+ peak (containing 35Cl).

mass-spec.q: A compound containing a single bromine atom typically shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly what relative intensity to each other?
options: M+2 is about ten times more intense than M+
Roughly equal intensity, close to a 1:1 ratio
mass-spec.why: Bromine's two natural isotopes, 79Br and 81Br, occur in nearly equal abundance, so a single-bromine compound shows M+ and M+2 peaks of roughly similar height, a distinctive pattern compared to chlorine.

mass-spec.q: Loss of a methyl radical, corresponding to a mass loss of 15 units, from the molecular ion is a common fragmentation for branched alkyl compounds.
mass-spec.why: Cleaving off a methyl group is a frequent and often favorable fragmentation pathway, especially when it generates a more stable remaining cation, which is common in branched structures.

mass-spec.q: A mass spectral fragment showing a loss of 18 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly indicates loss of:
mass-spec.why: Loss of 18 mass units corresponds to H2O, a very common fragmentation pathway for alcohols (and some other oxygen-containing compounds) under electron ionization conditions.

mass-spec.q: The nitrogen rule states that, for typical organic compounds containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, and similar common elements, the molecular weight will be odd if the molecule contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms.
mass-spec.why: Because nitrogen has an odd valence (typically three bonds) while carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen follow patterns that keep the overall mass even in their absence, each nitrogen atom added in a stable structure shifts the molecular weight's parity, making an odd number of nitrogens correspond to an odd molecular weight.

mass-spec.q: A loss of 28 mass units from a molecular ion is ambiguous on its own because it could correspond to either:
options: Loss of water or loss of ammonia
Loss of carbon monoxide (CO) or loss of ethylene (C2H4)
Loss of chlorine or loss of bromine
Loss of a proton or loss of a methyl group
mass-spec.why: Both CO (common from ketones, aldehydes, and aromatic ethers) and C2H4 (common from retro-type eliminations) have a mass of 28, so this loss alone does not uniquely identify the fragmentation pathway without additional supporting evidence.

mass-spec.q: Alpha cleavage, the preferential breaking of a bond adjacent to a heteroatom such as nitrogen or oxygen, is a favorable fragmentation pathway mainly because:
options: Alpha cleavage never actually occurs in real spectra
Breaking bonds near heteroatoms requires less energy than breaking any other bond in the molecule under all circumstances
The resulting cation can be stabilized by resonance donation from the heteroatom's lone pair
Heteroatoms always prevent any fragmentation nearby
mass-spec.why: When the bond next to an oxygen or nitrogen breaks, the heteroatom's lone pair can donate into the resulting cation through resonance, stabilizing it and making that fragmentation pathway especially favorable.

mass-spec.q: A McLafferty rearrangement in a carbonyl-containing compound requires the presence of what structural feature, and produces what kind of products?
options: Any aromatic ring, producing two radical fragments
A triple bond anywhere in the molecule, producing a gas
A halogen atom, producing an odd-electron radical cation only
A gamma-hydrogen, producing an ion and a neutral alkene
mass-spec.why: The McLafferty rearrangement requires a gamma-hydrogen relative to the carbonyl so that a six-membered transition state can form, transferring that hydrogen and cleaving a bond to release a neutral alkene while leaving behind a stable, even-electron cation.

mass-spec.q: The characteristic tropylium cation at m/z 91 is commonly observed in the mass spectra of which class of compounds?
options: Primary amines with no ring present
mass-spec.why: Benzylic cleavage of an alkylbenzene's side chain generates a benzylic cation that readily rearranges into the highly stable, resonance-delocalized seven-membered tropylium cation, observed at m/z 91.

mass-spec.q: More highly branched alkanes generally show a weaker molecular ion peak than their straight-chain isomers, because branching provides additional, more easily accessible fragmentation pathways that generate more stable carbocations.
mass-spec.why: Branch points allow formation of more stable secondary or tertiary carbocations upon fragmentation, making it energetically easier for the branched molecular ion to fall apart rather than survive intact, weakening the M+ peak relative to a straight-chain isomer.

mass-spec.q: A loss of 43 mass units from a molecular ion commonly corresponds to loss of which fragment(s)?
mass-spec.why: Both the isopropyl radical (C3H7, mass 43) and the acetyl cation-forming group (CH3CO, also mass 43) are common fragments lost from molecular ions, so a loss of 43 alone is often ambiguous without further context.

mass-spec.q: In the mass spectrum of a simple aldehyde, a loss of 29 mass units from the molecular ion most commonly corresponds to loss of:
mass-spec.why: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the aldehyde carbonyl commonly ejects the formyl radical, CHO, which has a mass of 29, leaving behind a stabilized carbon-centered cation.

mass-spec.q: Aromatic compounds often show a strong, easily recognized molecular ion peak relative to many aliphatic compounds mainly because:
options: Aromatic compounds never undergo any fragmentation at all
Aromatic rings always weigh less than aliphatic chains
Aromatic compounds cannot be ionized by electron ionization
Ring delocalization stabilizes the radical cation
mass-spec.why: The aromatic ring can delocalize the positive charge and radical character of the molecular ion over the ring system, stabilizing it and making the intact M+ more likely to survive and be detected as a prominent peak.

mass-spec.q: In a standard mass spectrum plot, the x-axis (m/z) represents a peak's relative abundance, while the y-axis (intensity) represents its mass-to-charge ratio.
mass-spec.why: It is actually the reverse: the x-axis shows the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of each ion, while the y-axis shows that ion's relative intensity, or abundance, compared to the base peak.

mass-spec.q: When an alkane's molecular ion fragments by breaking a carbon-carbon bond, the fragmentation pathway that generates the most stable resulting carbocation (tertiary over secondary over primary) is generally favored. This principle is analogous to:
options: The general stability order of carbocations
A rule that applies only in mass spectrometry and nowhere else in organic chemistry
The idea that all carbocations are equally stable regardless of substitution
A rule that favors primary carbocations above all others
mass-spec.why: Fragmentation in the gas phase favors pathways that produce the most stable cation, following the same substitution-based stability trend (tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary) used to rationalize carbocation stability throughout organic chemistry.

mass-spec.q: An unknown compound's mass spectrum shows significant fragment peaks corresponding to loss of 15 (a methyl group) and loss of 29 (an ethyl-related fragment) from the molecular ion, both consistent with alpha cleavage next to a carbonyl. This pattern is most consistent with a ketone structure in which:
options: The molecule contains no carbonyl group at all
The carbonyl is flanked by a methyl and an ethyl group, as in 2-butanone
The molecule must be a symmetrical ketone with identical groups on both sides of the carbonyl
The molecule is necessarily an aromatic compound
mass-spec.why: Alpha cleavage on either side of an asymmetric ketone's carbonyl generates two different acylium-type cations, explaining why both a methyl loss (15) and a loss consistent with the other alkyl substituent pattern can appear together in the spectrum of a compound like methyl ethyl ketone.

mass-spec.q: Loss of a single hydrogen atom, a mass loss of just 1 unit, from the molecular ion is relatively uncommon as a dominant fragmentation pathway compared to loss of larger groups. Why?
options: Hydrogen atoms cannot be removed from a molecule under any circumstances
Molecular ions never lose hydrogen atoms in any real spectrum
Losing a lone hydrogen radical is less favorable than losing a larger one
Losing a hydrogen atom always produces the most intense peak in every spectrum
mass-spec.why: Because forming larger, more stable radicals (or undergoing favorable rearrangements like McLafferty) is usually more thermodynamically favorable than simply ejecting a lone hydrogen atom, simple H-loss is typically a minor pathway rather than the dominant one.

mass-spec.q: A high-resolution mass spectrometer can distinguish between two different molecular formulas that share the same nominal (whole-number) mass, such as C2H4O and CO2, both of which equal 44 to the nearest whole number. This is possible because:
options: All atoms have exactly the same mass, so this distinction is actually impossible
High-resolution instruments simply guess the formula from the compound's color
Nominal mass and exact mass are always identical for every molecule
Different atom combinations have slightly different exact masses
mass-spec.why: Individual isotopes have exact masses that are not perfectly whole numbers (for example, carbon-12 is defined as exactly 12, but hydrogen and oxygen have slightly different fractional exact masses), so formulas with the same nominal mass usually have distinguishably different exact masses when measured with sufficient precision.

mass-spec.q: The relative intensity of a peak in a mass spectrum reflects the relative abundance of that particular gas-phase ion reaching the detector, which is governed by the kinetics and thermodynamics of fragmentation in the gas phase, not by the compound's stability or solubility in a liquid solution.
mass-spec.why: Mass spectral peak intensities depend on how readily a given ion forms and survives under gas-phase ionization and fragmentation conditions, a distinct context from solution-phase stability, solubility, or reactivity, which are not what mass spectrometry intensities measure.

mass-spec.q: A cyclic secondary alcohol's mass spectrum can show both a loss of 18 (water) and a loss of 28 (often consistent with ethylene or CO) from the molecular ion. A reasonable explanation for seeing multiple distinct losses like this is:
options: The molecular ion can fragment by more than one competing pathway
A molecule can only ever show exactly one fragmentation pathway in its entire spectrum
Loss of water and loss of ethylene must always occur together as a single simultaneous event
Cyclic alcohols never lose water under any circumstances
mass-spec.why: Molecular ions are not limited to a single fragmentation route; different bonds can break under the conditions of electron ionization, so a cyclic alcohol can plausibly show both a straightforward water loss and a separate ring-related elimination pathway in the same spectrum.

mass-spec.q: For a simple carboxylic acid, a loss of 45 mass units from the molecular ion typically corresponds to loss of:
mass-spec.why: Alpha cleavage adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing carbon of a carboxylic acid commonly ejects the COOH group, which has a combined mass of 45, leaving behind the remaining alkyl cation.

mass-spec.q: Why does electron ionization (EI) typically produce a radical cation (an odd-electron species) as the molecular ion, rather than an even-electron cation?
options: EI always adds an extra electron to the molecule instead of removing one
Even-electron cations are impossible to form under any ionization method
EI removes one electron, leaving one unpaired electron
EI removes two electrons at once from every molecule
mass-spec.why: Since a neutral organic molecule normally has all its electrons paired, knocking out just one electron during EI necessarily leaves an odd, unpaired electron along with the resulting positive charge, producing a radical cation.

mass-spec.q: Combining the nitrogen rule with an observed odd molecular ion mass for a compound containing only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, what can be concluded about its nitrogen content?
options: The compound must contain an even number of nitrogen atoms
The compound cannot contain any nitrogen at all
No conclusion about nitrogen content can be drawn from the molecular ion mass
The compound must contain an odd number of nitrogen atoms
mass-spec.why: According to the nitrogen rule, an odd molecular weight for a typical CHNO compound implies an odd number of nitrogen atoms, since each nitrogen (with its odd valence pattern) shifts the overall parity of the molecular mass.

retrosynthesis.q: What does the open double-lined arrow mean in retrosynthesis?
retrosynthesis.why: It points the other way in time from an ordinary reaction arrow, which is why it is drawn differently.

retrosynthesis.q: What is a disconnection?
options: A bond broken on paper, backwards
A bond physically broken in the flask
retrosynthesis.why: Nothing physically breaks. You are asking which two pieces, joined by a reaction you know, would give that bond.

retrosynthesis.q: What makes a disconnection legitimate?
options: It splits the molecule into two equal halves
You can name the forward reaction that makes that bond
retrosynthesis.why: If you cannot say what reagents would rejoin the pieces, you have drawn a picture rather than planned a synthesis.

retrosynthesis.q: What is a synthon?
options: A real reagent you can buy off the shelf
retrosynthesis.why: The synthon is the idea; the synthetic equivalent is what you actually order.

retrosynthesis.q: What is the synthetic equivalent of the synthon R-?
options: An alkyl halide such as RBr
retrosynthesis.why: A carbanion is not a bottle on a shelf; RMgBr behaves like one.

retrosynthesis.q: What is the synthetic equivalent of the synthon R+?
retrosynthesis.why: Or an alcohol with acid, which generates the cation in situ.

retrosynthesis.q: What is the synthetic equivalent of an acylium synthon RCO+?
options: An aldehyde with a Lewis acid
retrosynthesis.why: Which is what makes Friedel-Crafts acylation the forward reaction for that disconnection.

retrosynthesis.q: What is a retron?
options: A reaction run in the reverse direction
retrosynthesis.why: Learning to see retrons is most of what makes an experienced chemist fast at this.

retrosynthesis.q: A beta-hydroxy ketone is the retron for which reaction?
retrosynthesis.why: Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the carbinol carbon: the fragments are an enolate and a carbonyl.

retrosynthesis.q: A 1,3-dicarbonyl is the retron for which reaction?
retrosynthesis.why: Disconnect between the alpha carbon and the second carbonyl, giving an ester enolate and an ester.

retrosynthesis.q: A cyclohexene is the retron for which reaction?
retrosynthesis.why: One disconnection undoing two bonds, which is why it is the highest-value move in the list.

retrosynthesis.q: A tertiary alcohol is the retron for which reaction?
retrosynthesis.why: Any C-C bond to the carbinol carbon can be disconnected into a carbanion and a ketone.

retrosynthesis.q: Which is generally the best place to disconnect?
options: The middle of a long chain
retrosynthesis.why: Functional groups are where reactivity lives, so those bonds are the ones you have reactions for.

retrosynthesis.q: Why is a branch point a good disconnection site?
options: It is where the molecule was assembled
Branches are the most reactive positions
retrosynthesis.why: Cutting a branch usually splits the target into two comparably simple pieces.

retrosynthesis.q: When do you stop disconnecting?
options: When all the fragments are neutral
When every piece is something you can buy
retrosynthesis.why: A question usually names the permitted starting materials, and that constraint is the real definition of done.

retrosynthesis.q: Ten steps at 80% yield each gives roughly what overall yield?
retrosynthesis.why: Yields multiply, which is why each extra step is genuinely expensive.

retrosynthesis.q: Disconnecting 2-phenylbutan-2-ol at the ethyl group gives which pair?
retrosynthesis.why: The synthons are the carbanion and the ketone; their equivalents are the Grignard and acetophenone.

retrosynthesis.q: A tertiary alcohol has three possible Grignard disconnections. What does that mean?
options: It cannot be made by a Grignard route
retrosynthesis.why: Several valid answers is the normal state of a synthesis problem.

retrosynthesis.q: Every polar bond-forming disconnection produces what?
retrosynthesis.why: Which is what a polar bond-forming reaction is.

retrosynthesis.q: What is the synthetic equivalent of an enolate synthon?
options: An alkyl halide plus a base
retrosynthesis.why: Deprotonating the alpha carbon generates the nucleophile in situ.

retrosynthesis.q: What is the synthetic equivalent of the -CN synthon?
retrosynthesis.why: Sodium cyanide performs an SN2 on an alkyl halide.

retrosynthesis.q: Why write the forward route out at the end?
options: Order errors hide in the tree
It is the required notation for an exam
retrosynthesis.why: The forward list is a claim: every step has reagents, a product, and a check that it survives the next step.

retrosynthesis.q: Retrosynthesis differs from forward planning in what way?
options: It uses an entirely different set of reactions
It is exploratory, and dead ends are expected
retrosynthesis.why: The forward route is the claim; the backward analysis is the search.

retrosynthesis.q: Which disconnection undoes two bonds at once?
retrosynthesis.why: Cutting across a six-membered ring containing an alkene gives a diene and a dienophile.

retrosynthesis.q: What does a symmetric target suggest?
retrosynthesis.why: Which halves the problem immediately.

retrosynthesis.q: The synthon RC-C- corresponds to which reagent?
retrosynthesis.why: Deprotonating a terminal alkyne gives the acetylide, which does SN2 on an alkyl halide.

retrosynthesis.q: Why is a shorter route usually preferred?
options: Each step loses material and can fail
retrosynthesis.why: Though the arithmetic is worth doing: a longer route of good steps can beat a shorter one of poor steps.

retrosynthesis.q: What should you do before disconnecting anything?
retrosynthesis.why: The difference tells you how many C-C bonds must form and what size pieces you need.

retrosynthesis.q: Which statement about synthons is correct?
retrosynthesis.why: R- is a useful idea and not something you can order.

retrosynthesis.q: What is the relationship between a retron and a disconnection?
retrosynthesis.why: Spotting the pattern is what makes the disconnection obvious.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Roughly how many ways are there to make a C-C bond in an introductory course?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Which is what makes synthesis learnable: the skeleton can only be built in a few places.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does a Grignard plus a ketone give?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: The carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon, and workup protonates the alkoxide.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does a Grignard plus CO2 give?
options: An alcohol of the same length
A carboxylic acid one carbon longer
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: One of the three standard one-carbon extensions.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does a Grignard plus formaldehyde give?
options: A primary alcohol one carbon longer
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Formaldehyde has no other substituent, so the product is primary.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does an acetylide plus an alkyl halide give?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: An SN2 reaction, so it works best with primary halides.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does cyanide plus an alkyl halide give?
options: An amine of the same length
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Which can then be hydrolyzed to an acid or reduced to a primary amine.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which route gives a primary amine one carbon longer than RX?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: The cyanide adds the carbon and the reduction converts the nitrile to CH2NH2.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which route gives a carboxylic acid one carbon longer than RX?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Nitrile hydrolysis. RMgBr + CO2 is the other standard answer.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does an aldol reaction produce?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: An enolate attacking a carbonyl.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does a Claisen condensation produce?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: An ester enolate attacking another ester.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does a Michael addition produce?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Conjugate addition of an enolate to an enone.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What does a Wittig reaction produce?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: An ylide plus a carbonyl, giving a C=C where the C=O was.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: How many C-C bonds does a Diels-Alder form?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Which is why it is the highest-value single disconnection available.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which reaction attaches a carbon chain to a benzene ring?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Alkylation or acylation, though acylation is usually preferred.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: An enolate is nucleophilic at which carbon?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Which is how you build a bond NEXT to a carbonyl rather than at it.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Conjugate addition builds a bond at which carbon?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Two positions away from the carbonyl, which is the third attachment point a carbonyl offers.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: A Grignard builds a bond at which carbon?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Direct attack on the electrophilic carbon of the C=O.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Target and starting material have the same carbon count. What does that mean?
options: No C-C bond formation is needed
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: The whole problem is functional group interconversion, which is much easier.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: A target has six more carbons and contains a benzene ring. What does that suggest?
options: Six separate C-C bonds must form
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Counting tells you the ring came in whole rather than being built.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which two reactions build rings?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Ring formation is otherwise hard, which is why both are worth spotting early.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What is the retron for an intramolecular aldol?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Which closes a five- or six-membered ring respectively.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What is a Dieckmann condensation?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: The same Claisen chemistry with both esters in one molecule.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Why is counting carbons the fastest diagnostic?
options: It tells you how many C-C bonds must form
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: And roughly what size pieces you need, which narrows ten reactions to two or three.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which reaction gives an alkene from a carbonyl?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: An ylide replaces the carbonyl oxygen with a carbon fragment.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which enolate reactions are essentially one idea?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: An enolate attacking something electrophilic, differing in what the electrophile is.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: What limits an acetylide alkylation?
options: It is SN2, so it works best on primary halides
It requires a ring in the substrate
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: A tertiary halide would eliminate instead.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which is NOT a C-C bond-forming reaction?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Hydroboration adds B and H across a C=C; no carbon-carbon bond is formed.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: A carbonyl offers how many distinct attachment points for a new carbon?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: The carbonyl carbon, the alpha carbon via an enolate, and the beta carbon via conjugate addition.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Why do carbonyls dominate synthesis?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Three attachment points from one functional group is unusual.

carbon-carbon-bonds.q: Which disconnection should you try first on a target containing a cyclohexene?
carbon-carbon-bonds.why: Two bonds undone in one step, with the stereochemistry already defined.

functional-group-interconversion.q: A move up or down the oxidation ladder needs what kind of reagent?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Sideways moves within one level are substitutions and need no redox reagent at all.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Alcohol to alkyl halide is which kind of move?
functional-group-interconversion.why: One bond to an electronegative atom traded for another, with the hydrogen count unchanged.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Primary alcohol to aldehyde is which kind of move?
functional-group-interconversion.why: A C-H on the carbinol carbon is replaced by a second bond to oxygen.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Ketone to secondary alcohol is which kind of move?
functional-group-interconversion.why: A bond to oxygen becomes a bond to hydrogen.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Ester to amide is which kind of move?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Both carbons sit at +3, so it is nucleophilic acyl substitution.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent converts an alcohol to an alkyl bromide?
functional-group-interconversion.why: SOCl2 does the chloride equivalent, and HX also works.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent gives a Markovnikov alcohol from an alkene?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Hydroboration is the anti-Markovnikov partner of this pair.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent gives an anti-Markovnikov alcohol from an alkene?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Boron adds to the less hindered carbon, and the OH replaces it with retention.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which conditions give a cis alkene from an alkyne?
functional-group-interconversion.why: A poisoned catalyst stops at the alkene, and the surface delivery is syn.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which conditions give a trans alkene from an alkyne?
functional-group-interconversion.why: A dissolving-metal reduction through radical anions, which adopt the less hindered arrangement.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent converts a nitrile to a carboxylic acid?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Reducing the same nitrile with LiAlH4 gives a primary amine instead.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent converts a nitrile to a primary amine?
functional-group-interconversion.why: The other half of the nitrile pair.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent converts a carboxylic acid to an acyl chloride?
functional-group-interconversion.why: From which esters and amides follow directly.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent reduces an ester to a primary alcohol?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Two hydrides are delivered, and you cannot normally stop at the aldehyde.

functional-group-interconversion.q: How do you make an aldehyde from an ester using only standard reagents?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Down two rungs and back up one, because the reduction cannot be stopped halfway.

functional-group-interconversion.q: How do you convert propan-2-ol to propan-1-ol?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Eliminate to the alkene, then add back with the opposite regiochemistry.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Why does PBr3 then NaOH fail to move an OH along a chain?
functional-group-interconversion.why: You end up with the OH back where it started.

functional-group-interconversion.q: How do you get an anti-Markovnikov alkyl halide from an alkene?
functional-group-interconversion.why: No direct acid does it, so you go via the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which oxidant takes a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid?
functional-group-interconversion.why: The aqueous conditions let the aldehyde hydrate and be oxidized again.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which oxidant stops at the aldehyde?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Along with the Swern and DMP, all of which are anhydrous.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent gives a syn diol from an alkene?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Both oxygens are delivered to the same face through a cyclic osmate ester.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which sequence gives an anti diol from an alkene?
functional-group-interconversion.why: The epoxide is opened by backside attack, putting the oxygens on opposite faces.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reagent converts a ketone to an alkene?
functional-group-interconversion.why: The carbonyl oxygen is replaced by a carbon fragment.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which reactions convert a ketone all the way to CH2?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Down two rungs, and the pair exists because they tolerate opposite conditions.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Fischer esterification converts an acid to an ester using what?
functional-group-interconversion.why: An equilibrium, usually driven by removing water or using excess alcohol.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Which is the commonest planning error this map prevents?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Or the reverse: trying to convert an ester to an amide with a reducing agent.

functional-group-interconversion.q: An alkene plus H2 over Pd/C gives what?
functional-group-interconversion.why: Syn addition of two hydrogens across the double bond.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Why are reagent PAIRS the important thing in this table?
options: They are cheaper when bought together
functional-group-interconversion.why: Markovnikov against anti-Markovnikov, cis against trans, aldehyde against acid, syn against anti.

functional-group-interconversion.q: Alcohol to alkene by concentrated H2SO4 gives which product?
functional-group-interconversion.why: It goes through a carbocation, so rearrangement is also possible.

functional-group-interconversion.q: How do you control where an alkene forms from an alcohol?
options: Make a halide, pick the base
functional-group-interconversion.why: Acid-catalyzed dehydration gives Zaitsev and can rearrange; E2 on a halide lets you choose.

protecting-groups.q: Why is a Grignard destroyed by an alcohol?
protecting-groups.why: The Grignard becomes an alkane before it can reach any carbonyl.

protecting-groups.q: What is the approximate pKa of an alcohol O-H?
protecting-groups.why: More than acidic enough to destroy a carbanion instantly.

protecting-groups.q: Which groups also destroy a Grignard?
options: N-H, S-H and a carboxylic acid O-H
protecting-groups.why: Any acidic proton, which is also why the reaction is run in scrupulously dry ether.

protecting-groups.q: What protects an alcohol from a Grignard?
protecting-groups.why: TBSCl with imidazole replaces the O-H with an O-Si bond, leaving no acidic proton.

protecting-groups.q: How is a silyl ether removed?
protecting-groups.why: The Si-F bond is exceptionally strong, so the deprotection needs nothing harsh.

protecting-groups.q: What protects a ketone from a hydride or Grignard?
protecting-groups.why: The acetal has no C=O and no electrophilic carbon, so there is nothing to attack.

protecting-groups.q: How is an acetal formed?
protecting-groups.why: Ethylene glycol is standard, and the equilibrium is driven by removing water.

protecting-groups.q: How is an acetal removed?
protecting-groups.why: The same equilibrium run backwards, which is why it is so reliable.

protecting-groups.q: What does orthogonal mean for two protecting groups?
protecting-groups.why: Which lets a molecule carry both and have them unmasked in a chosen order.

protecting-groups.q: Why can an acetal not be used if a later step needs aqueous acid?
options: Aqueous acid is exactly what removes it
protecting-groups.why: Choosing a protecting group means checking it against every remaining step.

protecting-groups.q: A molecule has a ketone and an ester, and you want to reduce only the ketone. Protect?
protecting-groups.why: Using a protecting group here would be three steps where one works.

protecting-groups.q: A molecule has an alkene and a ketone, and you want to hydrogenate only the alkene. Protect?
protecting-groups.why: Not every functional group present is a threat.

protecting-groups.q: A molecule has a ketone and a free alcohol, treated with CH3MgBr. Protect?
options: No, the ketone is more reactive
protecting-groups.why: There is no reagent trick that makes a Grignard tolerate a free alcohol.

protecting-groups.q: A molecule has an aldehyde and an ester, and you want to reduce only the ester. Protect?
options: Yes, protect the aldehyde as an acetal
protecting-groups.why: The aldehyde is the MORE reactive of the two, so there is no way to reach the ester selectively.

protecting-groups.q: How many steps does using a protecting group add?
protecting-groups.why: Protection and deprotection, which is why it is a last resort.

protecting-groups.q: What should you check before using a protecting group?
options: Whether a selective reagent or a reordering already solves it
protecting-groups.why: Installing the interfering group later is always cheaper than protecting it.

protecting-groups.q: Adding two equivalents of Grignard to a molecule with a free OH does what?
options: It works; one equivalent is left over
protecting-groups.why: The first equivalent is destroyed and the substrate is no longer clean.

protecting-groups.q: What reagent pair installs a silyl ether?
protecting-groups.why: The base mops up the HCl produced.

protecting-groups.q: Why is the silyl deprotection unusually gentle?
protecting-groups.why: Which is what makes it usable on a molecule carrying almost anything else.

protecting-groups.q: What does an acetal do to the carbonyl carbon?
protecting-groups.why: No C=O means nothing for a hydride or Grignard to attack.

protecting-groups.q: Which diol is standard for acetal protection?
protecting-groups.why: It gives a five-membered cyclic acetal.

protecting-groups.q: Why is protection a last resort rather than a first move?
protecting-groups.why: Worth it when the alternative is no product at all, not merely a lower yield.

protecting-groups.q: Which is the archetype of a problem needing protection?
options: A Grignard and a free alcohol
protecting-groups.why: Because no reagent choice can solve it.

protecting-groups.q: What happens to a Grignard in wet solvent?
options: It is protonated to an alkane
protecting-groups.why: Water does exactly what an alcohol O-H does, which is why dry ether is essential.

protecting-groups.q: A silyl ether and an acetal in one molecule can be removed in which order?
protecting-groups.why: One needs fluoride and one needs aqueous acid, and neither touches the other.

protecting-groups.q: What is the product of treating an alcohol with TBSCl and imidazole?
protecting-groups.why: The O-H becomes an O-Si bond with no acidic proton left.

protecting-groups.q: Which is NOT a reason to skip protection?
options: The group is not reactive here
protecting-groups.why: Size is irrelevant; the other three are the real questions to ask.

protecting-groups.q: Protecting a ketone and then trying to add a Grignard to it does what?
protecting-groups.why: A common trap: protect the interfering group, not the target.

protecting-groups.q: What makes the acetal deprotection reliable?
options: It is catalyzed by added base
protecting-groups.why: Formation is driven by removing water; removal is driven by adding it back.

protecting-groups.q: Why is an ester not usually a threat during catalytic hydrogenation?
protecting-groups.why: Which is one of the cases where no protection is needed at all.

multistep-synthesis.q: What should you do after finishing a retrosynthetic analysis?
multistep-synthesis.why: Errors of order are invisible in a retrosynthetic tree and obvious in a forward list.

multistep-synthesis.q: Which question finds missing protecting groups?
options: How long does the step take?
multistep-synthesis.why: Look at every functional group present, not just the one you are aiming at.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why should sensitive groups be installed late?
multistep-synthesis.why: Reordering is always cheaper than protecting.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why acylate rather than alkylate when attaching a chain to a ring?
multistep-synthesis.why: The acylium ion is resonance-stabilized and does not shift.

multistep-synthesis.q: After a Friedel-Crafts acylation, how do you remove the carbonyl?
multistep-synthesis.why: Which leaves the unrearranged straight chain on the ring.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why does Friedel-Crafts fail on a nitrobenzene?
multistep-synthesis.why: Friedel-Crafts does not work on a strongly deactivated ring.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why is a nitro group reduced at the end of a synthesis?
multistep-synthesis.why: An amine is a strong activator and its nitrogen complexes the Lewis acid.

multistep-synthesis.q: On a benzene ring, what decides where the second substituent lands?
multistep-synthesis.why: Which is why the order of substitution is often the whole question.

multistep-synthesis.q: What is wrong with a route giving a single enantiomer from achiral inputs?
multistep-synthesis.why: Getting one enantiomer needs a chiral reagent, catalyst, starting material, or a resolution.

multistep-synthesis.q: What is the commonest error in student syntheses?
options: A Grignard with a free O-H
multistep-synthesis.why: Any acidic proton destroys the reagent before it reaches the carbonyl.

multistep-synthesis.q: What final check catches an extra carbon in your route?
multistep-synthesis.why: Cyanide, CO2 and formaldehyde routes all add exactly one carbon, so mixing them up is easy.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why prefer a route with no carbocation when the skeleton matters?
multistep-synthesis.why: Which is also why hydroboration and the Diels-Alder are trusted.

multistep-synthesis.q: What does the question 'does this product survive the next step' catch?
options: A step that undoes the last
multistep-synthesis.why: Making an aldehyde and then running a reaction in aqueous base will not leave you with an aldehyde.

multistep-synthesis.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation with 1-bromopropane gives what group on the ring?
multistep-synthesis.why: The primary cation rearranges to the secondary one before it reaches the ring.

multistep-synthesis.q: In making 1-bromo-4-propylbenzene, why acylate before brominating?
options: Bromine would block the para position
multistep-synthesis.why: Acylating the more reactive ring first is the better order on rate grounds.

multistep-synthesis.q: An alkyl group on a benzene ring directs an incoming group where?
multistep-synthesis.why: Which is why an alkyl group and a bromine end up para to each other.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why does the para product dominate over ortho with a propyl group present?
multistep-synthesis.why: Sterics, rather than electronics, breaks the tie between the two.

multistep-synthesis.q: Which is a legitimate reason to skip a protecting group?
multistep-synthesis.why: Reordering removes the problem entirely.

multistep-synthesis.q: What should you ask about stereochemistry in a route?
multistep-synthesis.why: If the target has defined stereochemistry, some step has to set it, and you should be able to name it.

multistep-synthesis.q: A route uses aqueous CrO3 where an aldehyde was wanted. What went wrong?
options: The reagent used was too weak
multistep-synthesis.why: Water lets the aldehyde hydrate and be oxidized a second time.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why write the four questions out for every step?
multistep-synthesis.why: Reagent scope, survival, regiochemistry, stereochemistry.

multistep-synthesis.q: Retrosynthesis is best described as what?
options: A required format for an exam
multistep-synthesis.why: The forward route is the claim; the backward analysis is the search.

multistep-synthesis.q: What is the effect of an amine on a Lewis acid catalyst?
options: It has no effect on it at all
multistep-synthesis.why: Which is the second reason Friedel-Crafts fails on an aniline.

multistep-synthesis.q: Which two ordering rules are really the same idea?
multistep-synthesis.why: A carbocation rearranges if a better one is available.

multistep-synthesis.q: If a target looks like the starting material with a group on the wrong carbon, what is the move?
multistep-synthesis.why: Almost always the intended answer to that shape of question.

multistep-synthesis.q: What does a Clemmensen reduction require?
multistep-synthesis.why: Strongly acidic, and the Wolff-Kishner is its basic partner.

multistep-synthesis.q: What does a Wolff-Kishner reduction require?
multistep-synthesis.why: For molecules that cannot survive acid.

multistep-synthesis.q: Why do Clemmensen and Wolff-Kishner exist as a pair?
multistep-synthesis.why: Whichever your substrate tolerates, the other is available.

multistep-synthesis.q: What does counting carbons at the END of a route check?
multistep-synthesis.why: It is the cheapest final check available.

multistep-synthesis.q: Which is the best summary of synthesis planning?
options: Always reach for a protecting group
multistep-synthesis.why: If a problem stalls, the useful move is rarely a new reagent.

carbohydrates.q: What is a carbohydrate, in functional-group terms?
carbohydrates.why: Every property of a sugar follows from a carbonyl surrounded by alcohols on the same chain.

carbohydrates.q: A sugar whose carbonyl is at the end of the chain is called what?
carbohydrates.why: Aldehyde at C1. A carbonyl inside the chain, usually C2, makes it a ketose instead.

carbohydrates.q: Fructose has its carbonyl at C2. What does that make it?
carbohydrates.why: Six carbons and an internal carbonyl: keto- for the position, -hexose for the count.

carbohydrates.q: How many stereocenters does an aldohexose have?
carbohydrates.why: C2 through C5 each carry an H and an OH; C1 is the carbonyl and C6 is a CH2OH.

carbohydrates.q: How many stereoisomeric aldohexoses are there?
carbohydrates.why: Two to the power of four stereocenters.

carbohydrates.q: In a Fischer projection, which carbon decides whether a sugar is D or L?
carbohydrates.why: One carbon carries the whole label, and it is the one at the bottom of the drawing.

carbohydrates.q: A Fischer projection shows the OH on the right at the bottom stereocenter. Which is it?
options: Neither, until the rotation is measured
carbohydrates.why: Right means D. The label is read off the drawing, not off a polarimeter.

carbohydrates.q: Does calling a sugar D tell you which way it rotates polarized light?
options: No — the two are unrelated labels
carbohydrates.why: D fixes one stereocenter's drawn position; the observed rotation is a measured property of the whole molecule.

carbohydrates.q: What forms when the C5 OH of glucose adds to its own C1 carbonyl?
carbohydrates.why: One alcohol plus one carbonyl gives a hemiacetal; it takes a second alcohol to reach an acetal.

carbohydrates.q: A six-membered sugar ring is called what?
carbohydrates.why: Named after pyran. The five-membered ring is a furanose, after furan.

carbohydrates.q: Which carbon of the ring form is the anomeric carbon?
options: The ring oxygen's other neighbor only
carbohydrates.why: It was the carbonyl carbon, so after cyclization it holds the ring oxygen and an OH.

carbohydrates.q: What are anomers?
carbohydrates.why: They differ at the anomeric carbon only, which is the one stereocenter the ring can open and reset.

carbohydrates.q: In a Haworth drawing of a D-pyranose, where does the alpha anomeric OH point?
carbohydrates.why: Alpha is down and beta is up for the D series.

carbohydrates.q: Why does a solution of pure alpha-D-glucopyranose change its optical rotation over time?
options: The D configuration inverts to L
carbohydrates.why: Mutarotation. Only the anomeric center can change, because only it opens.

carbohydrates.q: What is the name for that change in rotation?
carbohydrates.why: A specific term for the anomeric equilibration of a sugar in solution.

carbohydrates.q: Which anomer of D-glucopyranose dominates at equilibrium?
carbohydrates.why: Beta puts the anomeric OH equatorial, and glucose is the sugar that can get every substituent equatorial.

carbohydrates.q: What makes a sugar a reducing sugar?
carbohydrates.why: The test oxidizes the open-chain aldehyde, so the ring has to be able to open to supply it.

carbohydrates.q: Capping the anomeric OH with a second alcohol gives what?
carbohydrates.why: Two OR groups on the anomeric carbon is a full acetal, and the sugar-specific name for it is glycoside.

carbohydrates.q: Is a methyl glycoside a reducing sugar?
options: Yes, acetals open freely in base
carbohydrates.why: An acetal is stable to base, so no open-chain aldehyde is ever available.

carbohydrates.q: Sucrose is glucose joined to fructose. Why is it non-reducing?
carbohydrates.why: The bond runs anomeric carbon to anomeric carbon, so neither ring can open.

carbohydrates.q: Maltose is two glucoses joined alpha-1,4. Is it reducing?
options: No, both anomeric centers are tied up
No, the link blocks ring opening
carbohydrates.why: A 1,4 link commits one anomeric carbon, leaving the other end free to open.

carbohydrates.q: What kind of bond joins two sugar units in a disaccharide?
carbohydrates.why: One anomeric carbon, two OR groups, made by an alcohol displacing the anomeric OH under acid.

carbohydrates.q: What does alpha-1,4 describe in a polysaccharide?
options: The configuration and the carbons joined
carbohydrates.why: Alpha names the anomeric configuration; 1,4 names which carbon bonds to which.

carbohydrates.q: Cellulose and amylose are both 1,4 chains of D-glucose. What differs?
options: D in one, L in the other
Ester links in one, ether in the other
carbohydrates.why: One stereocenter on one carbon, and the two materials could hardly behave less alike.

carbohydrates.q: Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
options: Cellulose is not made of glucose
carbohydrates.why: The enzyme reads the configuration at the anomeric carbon, and it only fits alpha.

carbohydrates.q: Why do cellulose chains form rigid sheets?
options: Beta links let them lie flat
carbohydrates.why: Alpha-1,4 chains coil into helices instead, which is why starch is soft.

carbohydrates.q: Fructose is a ketose, yet it gives a positive Tollens' test. Why?
options: It contains glucose as an impurity
Its furanose ring is oxidized intact
Base isomerizes it to an aldose
carbohydrates.why: The test medium is basic, and an alpha deprotonation gives an enediol that can collapse to the aldose.

carbohydrates.q: Which reagent distinguishes an aldehyde from an acetal at the anomeric carbon?
carbohydrates.why: Tollens' oxidizes the free aldehyde a hemiacetal supplies, and an acetal supplies none.

carbohydrates.q: Why is beta-D-glucopyranose the most stable common hexose ring?
carbohydrates.why: No 1,3-diaxial strain anywhere in the chair, which is a conformational argument, not a new one.

carbohydrates.q: Epimers are stereoisomers differing at how many stereocenters?
carbohydrates.why: A single center. Differing at the anomeric one specifically makes them anomers.

amino-acids.q: Which four groups sit on the alpha carbon of an amino acid?
options: NH2, COOH, H, and a side chain
Two NH2 groups and two COOH groups
OH, COOH, H, and a side chain
NH2, CHO, H, and a side chain
amino-acids.why: The alpha carbon is defined as the one next to the carboxyl, and it carries the amine.

amino-acids.q: Which standard amino acid is achiral?
amino-acids.why: Its side chain is H, so the alpha carbon has two identical substituents.

amino-acids.q: Which stereochemical series do the amino acids of proteins belong to?
amino-acids.why: Read from a Fischer projection with COOH at the top and NH2 on the left.

amino-acids.q: Which L-amino acid has the R configuration?
amino-acids.why: Sulfur outranks the carboxyl carbon in CIP priority, so the ranking around the alpha carbon reshuffles.

amino-acids.q: What is the dominant form of an amino acid near neutral pH?
options: The neutral COOH and NH2 form
amino-acids.why: A pKa 2 acid and a pKa 9 base in one molecule transfer the proton to each other.

amino-acids.q: Roughly what is the pKa of an amino acid's carboxyl group?
amino-acids.why: Lower than acetic acid's 4.8, because the nearby ammonium withdraws inductively.

amino-acids.q: Roughly what is the pKa of an amino acid's alpha-ammonium group?
amino-acids.why: Typical for an alkylammonium ion, pulled down slightly by the adjacent carboxylate.

amino-acids.q: Why are amino acids high-melting solids insoluble in ether?
amino-acids.why: A zwitterion is ionic, and ionic solids behave like this.

amino-acids.q: What is the isoelectric point?
options: The pH of zero net charge
The pH at which the acid is half ionized
The pH of a pure water solution
amino-acids.why: Plus and minus cancel exactly, which is a property of the pH rather than of the molecule alone.

amino-acids.q: For a side chain that does not ionize, how is pI calculated?
options: Subtract the smaller from the larger
amino-acids.why: The two values bracketing the neutral form, which for a simple side chain are the only two.

amino-acids.q: Glycine has pKa values 2.34 and 9.60. What is its pI?
amino-acids.why: Half of the sum. Note it is below 7, so an isoelectric solution is mildly acidic.

amino-acids.q: Alanine has pKa values 2.34 and 9.69. What is its pI?
amino-acids.why: The same average, and the result is close to glycine's because the side chain is inert in both.

amino-acids.q: An amino acid is at a pH above its pI. What is its net charge?
options: It depends on the side chain only
amino-acids.why: More base than the isoelectric condition means more protons removed.

amino-acids.q: At a pH below its pI, which electrode does an amino acid move toward?
amino-acids.why: Below the pI it is a cation, and cations are drawn to the negative electrode.

amino-acids.q: Aspartic acid has a pI of 2.77. Why so low?
amino-acids.why: Two acidic groups have to be neutralized before the molecule is uncharged, so the balance point drops.

amino-acids.q: Lysine has a pI near 9.7. What does that tell you?
amino-acids.why: A second amine has to stay protonated, so you must go to high pH before the charge cancels.

amino-acids.q: At pH 7, what is the charge on a lysine side chain?
amino-acids.why: The side-chain ammonium has a pKa near 10.5, so at pH 7 it is overwhelmingly protonated.

amino-acids.q: At pH 7, what is the charge on a glutamic acid side chain?
amino-acids.why: The side-chain carboxyl has a pKa near 4.3, so at pH 7 it is deprotonated.

amino-acids.q: Which class does phenylalanine's side chain belong to?
amino-acids.why: A benzyl group with no heteroatom, so water pushes it into the protein's interior.

amino-acids.q: Which class does serine's side chain belong to?
amino-acids.why: A CH2OH hydrogen bonds well and carries no charge at any ordinary pH.

amino-acids.q: What is unusual about proline?
options: Its side chain reaches the nitrogen
amino-acids.why: The ring stiffens the backbone, which is why proline interrupts helices.

amino-acids.q: Which amino acid can form a covalent cross-link in a protein?
amino-acids.why: Two SH groups oxidize to a disulfide, the only covalent link outside the backbone.

amino-acids.q: What does oxidizing two cysteine residues produce?
amino-acids.why: R-S-S-R, and reducing it undoes the cross-link.

amino-acids.q: Where do nonpolar side chains end up in a folded, water-soluble protein?
amino-acids.why: The hydrophobic effect: burying them frees the water that would otherwise be ordered around them.

amino-acids.q: Histidine is the only side chain with a pKa near 6. Why does that matter?
options: It can act as acid or base
amino-acids.why: A pKa near the working pH means the residue can act as either an acid or a base in a mechanism.

amino-acids.q: How would you separate two amino acids with pI values of 3.2 and 9.7?
amino-acids.why: A pH between the two pI values forces them to opposite signs, so they migrate in opposite directions.

amino-acids.q: Why is an amino acid least soluble in water at its pI?
amino-acids.why: Without a net charge there is no electrostatic repulsion keeping the molecules apart.

amino-acids.q: How many ionizable groups does aspartic acid have?
amino-acids.why: Two carboxyls and one ammonium, so three pKa values and a pI set by the lowest two.

amino-acids.q: Why is the carboxyl pKa of an amino acid lower than that of acetic acid?
options: The nitrogen donates a lone pair
amino-acids.why: An inductive effect stabilizing the carboxylate, on the neighboring carbon.

amino-acids.q: Which single reagent class distinguishes cysteine from serine chemically?
amino-acids.why: Thiols dimerize to disulfides under mild oxidation; alcohols do not.

peptides-proteins.q: What functional group is a peptide bond?
peptides-proteins.why: A carboxyl joined to an amine with loss of water gives an amide, and nothing about proteins changes that.

peptides-proteins.q: Which end of a written peptide sequence comes first?
peptides-proteins.why: Sequences run N to C, so the direction is part of the information.

peptides-proteins.q: Which terminus keeps a free carboxyl group?
peptides-proteins.why: That carboxyl was never consumed by an amide bond.

peptides-proteins.q: Are Gly-Ala and Ala-Gly the same compound?
peptides-proteins.why: Same atoms and formula, opposite order, and the chain has a direction.

peptides-proteins.q: How many different tripeptides can be made from the 20 standard amino acids?
peptides-proteins.why: Twenty choices at each of three positions, and repeats are allowed.

peptides-proteins.q: What does amide resonance do to the C-N bond?
peptides-proteins.why: The nitrogen lone pair pushes into the carbonyl, so the real bond is between single and double.

peptides-proteins.q: Roughly how long is the peptide C-N bond?
peptides-proteins.why: Between a single bond at 1.47 and a double bond, exactly as the resonance picture predicts.

peptides-proteins.q: How many atoms of the amide unit lie in one plane?
peptides-proteins.why: The two alpha carbons plus C, O, N and H, held flat by the partial pi bond.

peptides-proteins.q: Why is rotation about the peptide C-N bond restricted?
options: Steric bulk of the side chains
peptides-proteins.why: Rotating would break the overlap that the second resonance structure depends on.

peptides-proteins.q: Is the peptide nitrogen basic?
options: Yes, about the same as an alkylamine
No — its lone pair is delocalized
peptides-proteins.why: A lone pair already spent on the neighboring carbonyl cannot also grab a proton.

peptides-proteins.q: Where is an amide protonated in strong acid?
options: It is not protonated at all
peptides-proteins.why: Protonating oxygen keeps the resonance stabilization; protonating nitrogen would destroy it.

peptides-proteins.q: How does an amide rank among acyl derivatives for reactivity?
peptides-proteins.why: The strongest lone-pair donation gives the greatest stabilization and the lowest reactivity.

peptides-proteins.q: What conditions hydrolyze a peptide bond in the laboratory?
peptides-proteins.why: An amide is the least reactive acyl derivative, so it takes force or an enzyme.

peptides-proteins.q: What is primary structure?
peptides-proteins.why: The only level whose structure is its covalent bonds, and the one from which the others follow.

peptides-proteins.q: What is secondary structure?
options: The full shape of one chain
peptides-proteins.why: Defined as involving the backbone only, which is why any sequence can form it.

peptides-proteins.q: What holds an alpha helix together?
peptides-proteins.why: Every residue supplies an N-H and a C=O regardless of its side chain.

peptides-proteins.q: What is tertiary structure?
peptides-proteins.why: Set mostly by side-chain interactions rather than by the backbone.

peptides-proteins.q: What is quaternary structure?
peptides-proteins.why: Hemoglobin's four subunits are the standard example, and a single-chain protein has none.

peptides-proteins.q: What contributes most to tertiary structure?
peptides-proteins.why: Burying nonpolar side chains releases the ordered water around them, which is the large term.

peptides-proteins.q: Which interaction in a folded protein is covalent?
peptides-proteins.why: Everything else holding a fold together is noncovalent, which is why folding is reversible.

peptides-proteins.q: What is a salt bridge in a protein?
options: An ion pair of side chains
peptides-proteins.why: For example a lysine ammonium paired with a glutamate carboxylate.

peptides-proteins.q: What does denaturing a protein destroy?
peptides-proteins.why: Heat overwhelms weak noncovalent forces long before it touches an amide.

peptides-proteins.q: Why does boiling not hydrolyze a protein to amino acids?
peptides-proteins.why: An amide is the least reactive acyl derivative, and 100 C water is nowhere near enough.

peptides-proteins.q: What reagent cleaves disulfide bonds without touching the backbone?
peptides-proteins.why: A disulfide is the oxidized form, so reduction takes it back to two thiols.

peptides-proteins.q: Why does proline disrupt an alpha helix?
peptides-proteins.why: No N-H means no hydrogen bond donor at that position, and the ring restricts the geometry.

peptides-proteins.q: Which level of structure does a single point mutation change directly?
peptides-proteins.why: It changes one residue in the sequence, and the other levels change only as a consequence.

peptides-proteins.q: Why is the peptide backbone described as rigid plates hinged at the alpha carbons?
peptides-proteins.why: That restriction is what makes a finite, predictable set of folds possible.

peptides-proteins.q: What does hydrolyzing a protein completely give?
peptides-proteins.why: Every amide is cut, and each residue is released with its own carboxyl and amine restored.

peptides-proteins.q: Why can any sequence form a beta sheet in principle?
peptides-proteins.why: Secondary structure is a backbone property, so the side chains only tip the preference.

peptides-proteins.q: What makes a protein water soluble?
peptides-proteins.why: The fold puts the polar residues outside and the nonpolar ones in, which is the hydrophobic effect stated the other way round.

lipids.q: How is the lipid class defined?
lipids.why: It collects the cell components that dissolve in nonpolar solvents, which is why it holds fats and steroids together.

lipids.q: What is a fatty acid?
lipids.why: The acid group is the only functional group on an otherwise plain hydrocarbon.

lipids.q: Why do most natural fatty acids have an even number of carbons?
lipids.why: Biosynthesis adds acetate units, so the count comes out even.

lipids.q: What is a triglyceride?
lipids.why: Glycerol has three OH groups, and all three are esterified.

lipids.q: What distinguishes a fat from an oil?
options: Fats have esters and oils do not
lipids.why: They are the same compound class in two physical states.

lipids.q: Which fatty acid has the higher melting point at equal chain length?
options: The one with two cis double bonds
lipids.why: A straight chain stacks against its neighbors along its full length.

lipids.q: Why does a cis double bond lower a fatty acid's melting point?
lipids.why: Melting separates molecules, and a bent chain makes much less contact with the next one.

lipids.q: Stearic acid melts near 69 C and oleic acid near 13 C. Both are C18. Why?
lipids.why: Chain length is held constant, so only the geometry can be responsible.

lipids.q: Elaidic acid is C18 with one trans double bond and melts near 44 C. What does that show?
lipids.why: It is unsaturated and still nearly as high-melting as the saturated acid, because it is still straight.

lipids.q: Which has the lowest melting point?
options: A C18 acid with one cis double bond
A C18 acid with one trans double bond
A C18 acid with two cis double bonds
lipids.why: More kinks means worse packing, and the melting point falls with each one.

lipids.q: What intermolecular force holds fatty acid chains together?
lipids.why: Hydrocarbon chains are nonpolar, so contact area is what matters.

lipids.q: What does heating a triglyceride with aqueous NaOH give?
lipids.why: Base-promoted ester hydrolysis three times over, and the excess base deprotonates each acid.

lipids.q: What is that reaction called?
lipids.why: Literally soap-making, which is exactly what it produces.

lipids.q: Why is saponification irreversible?
options: The ester is destroyed by heat
lipids.why: A carboxylate is a poor electrophile, so nothing runs backwards.

lipids.q: What makes a molecule amphipathic?
lipids.why: A soap is the standard case: an ionic head on a long hydrocarbon tail.

lipids.q: What is a micelle?
lipids.why: It resolves the solubility conflict by hiding the tails from water.

lipids.q: How does soap remove grease?
options: It reacts with the grease chemically
It lowers the grease's melting point
lipids.why: The nonpolar core is a pocket of nonpolar solvent that water can carry away.

lipids.q: What is a phospholipid?
lipids.why: Two fatty acid tails and one charged phosphate group in place of the third.

lipids.q: Why do phospholipids form bilayers rather than micelles?
lipids.why: A one-tailed molecule tapers into a sphere; a two-tailed one is a cylinder and tiles into a sheet.

lipids.q: What is the lipid bilayer?
lipids.why: Tails inward and heads facing the water on both sides, which is every cell membrane.

lipids.q: Which lipid class has no ester group at all?
lipids.why: Four fused rings and nothing else, grouped as lipids purely by solubility.

lipids.q: How many fused rings does a steroid have?
lipids.why: Three six-membered and one five-membered, fused in a fixed arrangement.

lipids.q: What does cholesterol do in a membrane?
lipids.why: A rigid ring system inserted among flexible chains changes how easily they move.

lipids.q: What structural feature distinguishes estradiol from testosterone?
lipids.why: Aromatizing the A ring also converts the ketone there to a phenol.

lipids.q: What is partial hydrogenation used for industrially?
lipids.why: Removing double bonds straightens chains, so the material packs better and melts higher.

lipids.q: Why does partial hydrogenation create trans fats?
lipids.why: An alkene that picks up one hydrogen and loses it again does not remember its original geometry.

lipids.q: Why does a trans fat behave like a saturated fat physically?
lipids.why: The property that sets the melting point is shape, and trans barely bends the chain.

lipids.q: What is a wax, chemically?
options: An ester of two long chains
lipids.why: One ester joining two long chains, which is why waxes are hard and very water-repellent.

lipids.q: Why are lipids a compact energy store compared with carbohydrates?
lipids.why: A more reduced carbon has further to fall on oxidation, so more energy is released per gram.

lipids.q: What are terpenes built from?
lipids.why: Counting in fives is the quickest way to recognize one.

nucleic-acids.q: What three parts make up a nucleotide?
options: An amino acid and a sugar
nucleic-acids.why: Assembling them in that order makes the vocabulary fall out on its own.

nucleic-acids.q: What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?
nucleic-acids.why: Sugar plus base is a nucleoside; adding the phosphate ester makes it a nucleotide.

nucleic-acids.q: Which sugar does DNA use?
nucleic-acids.why: Deoxy names the missing OH, and the missing OH is at C2 prime.

nucleic-acids.q: What is the only structural difference between ribose and 2-deoxyribose?
nucleic-acids.why: One hydroxyl group, and it decides which molecule lasts and which does not.

nucleic-acids.q: Why are the sugar carbons numbered with primes?
nucleic-acids.why: Both rings have numbered atoms, so the sugar's get primes.

nucleic-acids.q: Which bases are purines?
nucleic-acids.why: Two fused rings. The single-ring bases are the pyrimidines.

nucleic-acids.q: Which base does RNA use in place of thymine?
nucleic-acids.why: Uracil is thymine without the methyl group.

nucleic-acids.q: What kind of bond joins a base to its sugar?
nucleic-acids.why: A nitrogen displaces the anomeric OH, which is acetal formation with N in place of O.

nucleic-acids.q: Which carbon of the sugar bonds to the base?
nucleic-acids.why: The anomeric carbon is the electrophilic one, exactly as in ordinary glycoside formation.

nucleic-acids.q: Which OH of the sugar carries the phosphate that a polymerase adds to a growing chain?
nucleic-acids.why: Polymerases use 5 prime triphosphates, and the 3 prime OH of the chain is the nucleophile that attacks one. A 3 prime monophosphate is a perfectly good nucleotide too, but it is not what gets added.

nucleic-acids.q: What links one nucleotide to the next?
nucleic-acids.why: One phosphorus esterified to two different sugars, 3 prime of one and 5 prime of the next.

nucleic-acids.q: In which direction are nucleic acid sequences written?
nucleic-acids.why: The chain has distinguishable ends, so direction is part of the information.

nucleic-acids.q: Why are nucleic acids called acids?
options: They release protons from the 2 prime OH
nucleic-acids.why: A row of negative charges on the outside, which is also why they dissolve in water.

nucleic-acids.q: How many hydrogen bonds join an A-T pair?
nucleic-acids.why: G-C uses three, which is why G-C rich DNA melts higher.

nucleic-acids.q: How many hydrogen bonds join a G-C pair?
nucleic-acids.why: One more than A-T, and that difference shows up directly in melting temperature.

nucleic-acids.q: What holds the two strands of DNA together?
nucleic-acids.why: Weak bonds on purpose, because anything read must first be opened without being destroyed.

nucleic-acids.q: A purine always pairs with what?
nucleic-acids.why: One large plus one small keeps every rung of the ladder the same width.

nucleic-acids.q: How do the two strands of a double helix run relative to each other?
nucleic-acids.why: One runs 5 prime to 3 prime while its partner runs the other way.

nucleic-acids.q: What is on the outside of the double helix?
nucleic-acids.why: Charges face the water and the flat nonpolar bases stack away from it.

nucleic-acids.q: If a DNA sample is 30% adenine, how much thymine does it contain?
nucleic-acids.why: A pairs only with T, so their amounts are equal in double-stranded DNA.

nucleic-acids.q: Why does G-C rich DNA melt at a higher temperature?
nucleic-acids.why: Melting separates the strands, so it measures what joins them.

nucleic-acids.q: What does denaturing DNA do?
