nucleic-acids.why: Only the hydrogen bonds between bases are undone, which is why the strands can re-anneal.

nucleic-acids.q: Why does RNA hydrolyze much faster than DNA in base?
options: Its backbone is an ester and DNA's is an ether
Its 2 prime OH attacks the phosphorus
nucleic-acids.why: An intramolecular attack through a five-membered ring is enormously faster than one from solution.

nucleic-acids.q: What product does base-promoted RNA cleavage form at the cut?
nucleic-acids.why: The five-membered ring the intramolecular attack closes.

nucleic-acids.q: Why is DNA rather than RNA used for long-term storage?
nucleic-acids.why: Removing one hydroxyl removes the internal nucleophile, and with it the built-in self-destruct.

nucleic-acids.q: What conditions cleave the base from the sugar?
nucleic-acids.why: It is an N,O-acetal, and acetals are cut by aqueous acid and stable to base. The rate is very uneven: purines depurinate far more readily than pyrimidines.

nucleic-acids.q: What is the 3 prime end of a strand?
options: The end with a free OH
The end with a free phosphate
nucleic-acids.why: The other end keeps the free 5 prime phosphate.

nucleic-acids.q: What does a nucleoside triphosphate such as ATP provide?
nucleic-acids.why: Diphosphate leaves well because the charge is spread over many oxygens.

nucleic-acids.q: Which part of a nucleotide carries the genetic information?
nucleic-acids.why: Sugar and phosphate repeat identically along the chain, so only the bases can vary.

nucleic-acids.q: What does complementary mean for two DNA strands?
options: They run in the same direction
nucleic-acids.why: That is what makes each strand a template for rebuilding the other.

organometallic-bonding.q: Why is the carbon of a Grignard reagent nucleophilic?
options: Magnesium donates a lone pair to it
The C-Mg bond is fully ionic
Magnesium withdraws electron density from it
organometallic-bonding.why: Carbon at 2.55 against magnesium at 1.31, so the bonding electrons sit on carbon.

organometallic-bonding.q: What is umpolung?
options: Reversing the direction of a reaction
organometallic-bonding.why: An alkyl halide's carbon is an electrophile; the Grignard made from it is a nucleophile at the same carbon.

organometallic-bonding.q: Where is carbon's Pauling electronegativity?
organometallic-bonding.why: Magnesium is 1.31, lithium 0.98 and oxygen 3.44, which is why the first two invert the polarity and the third does not.

organometallic-bonding.q: In C-Cl, which atom carries the partial negative charge?
organometallic-bonding.why: Chlorine at 3.16 beats carbon at 2.55, so the carbon is the electrophile.

organometallic-bonding.q: In C-Li, which atom carries the partial negative charge?
organometallic-bonding.why: Lithium at 0.98 is far below carbon, so the electrons stay on carbon.

organometallic-bonding.q: Is the C-Mg bond ionic?
organometallic-bonding.why: A Grignard is not a free carbanion, though it behaves like one and the arrow starts at the C-metal bond.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which organometallic is the most reactive?
organometallic-bonding.why: The widest electronegativity gap gives the most carbanion character and the least selectivity.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which organometallic is the most selective?
organometallic-bonding.why: Copper sits close to carbon, so the bond is barely polar and the reagent can be pointed at one site.

organometallic-bonding.q: What does high reactivity cost an organometallic reagent?
organometallic-bonding.why: The two trade against each other more visibly here than anywhere else in the course.

organometallic-bonding.q: Approximately what is the pKa of an alkane C-H?
organometallic-bonding.why: That makes R- one of the strongest bases in organic chemistry.

organometallic-bonding.q: What happens when a Grignard reagent meets water?
organometallic-bonding.why: Water at pKa 15.7 against an alkane at 50 is not a close call.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which group destroys a Grignard reagent?
options: An alkyl halide on a different molecule
organometallic-bonding.why: Any O-H, N-H or S-H does it, and a terminal alkyne C-H as well.

organometallic-bonding.q: Why must Grignard reactions be run in dry glassware?
organometallic-bonding.why: The symptom is usually not a mess but nothing happening at all.

organometallic-bonding.q: Why are Grignard reagents made in ether?
options: Ether is a nucleophile for the reaction
Ether is acidic enough to help
Ether oxygen coordinates to the magnesium
organometallic-bonding.why: That coordination is what keeps the reagent in solution and usable.

organometallic-bonding.q: What does quenching a Grignard with D2O accomplish?
organometallic-bonding.why: The same destructive protonation, used deliberately to label one position.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which nucleophiles has this course mostly used before organometallics?
organometallic-bonding.why: Hydroxide, alkoxides, amines, halides, cyanide — and a heteroatom nucleophile can only attach a heteroatom.

organometallic-bonding.q: Why is a carbon nucleophile needed to build a skeleton?
options: The nucleophile supplies the new bond
Carbon skeletons form by radical routes
organometallic-bonding.why: Whatever attacks is what gets attached, so attaching carbon means attacking with carbon.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which two carbon nucleophiles appeared before this chapter?
organometallic-bonding.why: Both are narrow: cyanide brings one carbon with a nitrile attached, and an acetylide must come from a terminal alkyne.

organometallic-bonding.q: How is a Grignard reagent made?
options: A halide with a magnesium salt
organometallic-bonding.why: The metal inserts into the carbon-halogen bond; nothing is added and nothing leaves.

organometallic-bonding.q: How many equivalents of lithium does R-Br need?
organometallic-bonding.why: Each lithium carries one electron, and one of them departs as LiBr.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which halide will not form a Grignard reagent?
options: One bearing a free OH group
organometallic-bonding.why: The reagent would destroy itself on its own acidic proton as fast as it formed.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which reaction gives a magnesium alkoxide WITHOUT forming a new C-C bond?
options: A Grignard adding to a ketone
organometallic-bonding.why: Deprotonating an alcohol gives the same magnesium alkoxide that a Grignard addition does, but the reagent has been spent on a proton and no carbon was joined to anything.

organometallic-bonding.q: Why is an aryl Grignard useful even though aryl halides resist substitution?
organometallic-bonding.why: The metal inserts into the C-X bond rather than displacing the halide from behind.

organometallic-bonding.q: What does a larger electronegativity gap between C and the metal produce?
organometallic-bonding.why: More charge on carbon means a more reactive and less discriminating reagent.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which of these will a Grignard reagent tolerate in the same molecule?
organometallic-bonding.why: An ether has no acidic hydrogen, which is also why it can be the solvent.

organometallic-bonding.q: Why does a terminal alkyne quench an organometallic?
options: It adds across the C-metal bond
Its C-H has a pKa near 25
organometallic-bonding.why: The sp carbanion is stabilized, so that hydrogen is acidic enough to be taken.

organometallic-bonding.q: If a substrate has an OH and a ketone, which does a Grignard reach first?
organometallic-bonding.why: Proton transfer is the fastest reaction available, so the reagent is spent before it can add.

organometallic-bonding.q: What is the cheapest fix for an acidic proton in a Grignard substrate?
organometallic-bonding.why: Reordering costs nothing; protection costs two steps and therefore two yields.

organometallic-bonding.q: Which reagent needs a palladium catalyst to be useful?
organometallic-bonding.why: Boron sits close to carbon, so the reagent is barely nucleophilic on its own.

organometallic-bonding.q: What is the practical signal that a Grignard preparation has failed?
organometallic-bonding.why: Wet glassware quenches the reagent as fast as it forms, so the metal never gets used up.

grignard-reagents.q: A Grignard reagent plus formaldehyde gives what after workup?
grignard-reagents.why: Formaldehyde has two hydrogens on its carbonyl carbon, so after one R group is added that carbon still carries two.

grignard-reagents.q: A Grignard plus an aldehyde other than formaldehyde gives what?
grignard-reagents.why: One hydrogen and one R group were already there; the Grignard adds the second R.

grignard-reagents.q: A Grignard plus a ketone gives what?
grignard-reagents.why: The ketone brings two carbon groups and the Grignard adds a third.

grignard-reagents.q: A Grignard plus CO2, then acid, gives what?
grignard-reagents.why: One carbon longer, and it arrives already at the carboxylic acid oxidation level.

grignard-reagents.q: A Grignard plus an epoxide gives what?
grignard-reagents.why: The attack is an SN2 at the less hindered carbon, and the alkoxide is protonated on workup.

grignard-reagents.q: Where does a Grignard attack an epoxide?
grignard-reagents.why: There is no acid present, so no carbocation character develops and sterics decide.

grignard-reagents.q: A Grignard plus a nitrile, then hydrolysis, gives what?
grignard-reagents.why: The imine anion that forms is hydrolyzed on workup.

grignard-reagents.q: How many equivalents of Grignard does an ester consume?
grignard-reagents.why: The ketone formed after the first addition is more electrophilic than the ester was.

grignard-reagents.q: What is the product of an ester plus excess Grignard?
grignard-reagents.why: Two identical R groups from the reagent end up on the carbinol carbon.

grignard-reagents.q: Why can an ester not be stopped at the ketone with one equivalent?
grignard-reagents.why: The OR group donates into the carbonyl and makes the ester the sluggish one of the pair.

grignard-reagents.q: Which two R groups appear on the product of an ester plus Grignard?
options: One of each, plus a hydroxyl
Two identical ones from the reagent
One from the reagent, one from the ester
grignard-reagents.why: Both additions come from the same reagent, so they cannot differ.

grignard-reagents.q: Which reagent gives a ketone from an acyl chloride?
grignard-reagents.why: A cuprate is too mild to attack the ketone it just made; a Grignard is not.

grignard-reagents.q: What is a Weinreb amide used for?
options: Stopping an acyl addition at the ketone
grignard-reagents.why: Its chelated intermediate survives until workup, so no second addition can occur.

grignard-reagents.q: Which three electrophiles extend a chain by exactly one carbon?
options: CO2, an epoxide and a ketone
An epoxide, a nitrile and an aldehyde
grignard-reagents.why: Each lands somewhere different: an alcohol, an acid and a ketone.

grignard-reagents.q: How many carbons does ethylene oxide add to a chain?
grignard-reagents.why: Which is why it is the standard two-carbon extension. A substituted epoxide adds more, and the attack still goes at the less hindered carbon.

grignard-reagents.q: CH3MgBr is added to a molecule containing both a ketone and a carboxylic acid. What happens first?
grignard-reagents.why: A carboxylic acid at pKa 5 is the most acidic thing present by a wide margin.

grignard-reagents.q: What leaves the flask when a Grignard meets an O-H?
grignard-reagents.why: The carbanion takes the proton and departs as the alkane.

grignard-reagents.q: What is the workup step in every Grignard reaction?
grignard-reagents.why: The alkoxide or carboxylate intermediate has to be protonated.

grignard-reagents.q: Which target is 1-bromopropane plus Mg plus CO2 plus acid?
grignard-reagents.why: Three carbons in, one carbon added, and it arrives as the carboxyl.

grignard-reagents.q: Which target is 1-bromopropane plus Mg plus formaldehyde plus acid?
grignard-reagents.why: One carbon added, ending as a primary alcohol.

grignard-reagents.q: Which target is 1-bromopropane plus Mg plus propanone plus acid?
grignard-reagents.why: A ketone plus a Grignard gives a tertiary alcohol, here with methyl, methyl and propyl.

grignard-reagents.q: Why does a Grignard fail on a substrate bearing a terminal alkyne?
options: The alkyne adds to the metal
grignard-reagents.why: pKa 25 against an effective 50 for the reagent.

grignard-reagents.q: Which is the last resort for an acidic proton in a Grignard substrate?
grignard-reagents.why: Two extra steps means two extra yields lost, so it is worth it only when the alternatives fail.

grignard-reagents.q: What functional group does a Grignard plus an aldehyde always produce?
grignard-reagents.why: The alkoxide formed is protonated on workup, whatever the substituents are.

grignard-reagents.q: Why does acetaldehyde sometimes give poor yields with a Grignard?
options: It is enolized by the reagent
grignard-reagents.why: A very strong base and an alpha hydrogen in the same flask is an acid-base reaction waiting to happen.

grignard-reagents.q: What is the correct order of operations for a Grignard reaction?
options: Add the electrophile to the magnesium
grignard-reagents.why: Having the electrophile present while the reagent forms invites enolization and self-condensation.

grignard-reagents.q: Which functional group survives a Grignard reaction untouched?
grignard-reagents.why: Esters, nitriles and ketones are all electrophiles the reagent attacks.

grignard-reagents.q: What does a vinyl Grignard let you attach?
grignard-reagents.why: The metal insertion does not touch the double bond.

grignard-reagents.q: What class of alcohol comes from a Grignard plus an acyl chloride in excess?
grignard-reagents.why: Two additions again, but not for the ester's reason: an acyl chloride is the most electrophilic acyl derivative, and the ketone it gives is simply still reactive enough to be attacked as fast as it forms.

grignard-reagents.q: Which is the correct disconnection for a tertiary alcohol?
options: The bond furthest from the OH
A C-C bond at the carbinol
grignard-reagents.why: Each cut gives a carbanion and a ketone, and there are three legitimate choices.

organolithium-reagents.q: How is an organolithium made from R-Br?
organolithium-reagents.why: Each lithium supplies one electron, and one departs as LiBr.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why is RLi more reactive than RMgX?
options: RLi is ionic and RMgX is not
organolithium-reagents.why: A wider gap puts more negative charge on carbon.

organolithium-reagents.q: Which reagent adds to a hindered ketone that a Grignard only enolizes?
organolithium-reagents.why: Smaller and more reactive, so addition outruns deprotonation.

organolithium-reagents.q: What does RLi plus a carboxylic acid give after workup?
organolithium-reagents.why: Two equivalents: one takes the acidic proton and one adds to the carboxylate.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why does RLi plus a carboxylic acid stop at the ketone?
options: The dianion cannot collapse until workup
RLi adds only once by design
organolithium-reagents.why: The ketone does not exist in the flask, so there is nothing for a second equivalent to attack.

organolithium-reagents.q: How many equivalents of RLi does a carboxylic acid need?
organolithium-reagents.why: One for the O-H and one for the addition.

organolithium-reagents.q: What is LDA made from?
organolithium-reagents.why: An organolithium used as a base rather than as a nucleophile.

organolithium-reagents.q: What makes LDA useful?
options: Both weakly basic and weakly nucleophilic
Strongly basic but too hindered to add
organolithium-reagents.why: That pairing is what allows complete enolate formation without attack on the carbonyl.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why is LDA a weaker base than n-BuLi?
options: It is the conjugate base of an amine, not an alkane
It is stabilized by the ring
organolithium-reagents.why: An amine pKa near 36 against an alkane near 50, and it is still far more than enough.

organolithium-reagents.q: What is n-BuLi most often used for besides addition?
organolithium-reagents.why: Half its value is what it removes a proton from rather than what it attacks.

organolithium-reagents.q: What distinguishes t-BuLi from n-BuLi in practice?
options: It is far more basic and pyrophoric
It is a much weaker base
It is not hindered at all
organolithium-reagents.why: Bulk does slow its approach to a hindered carbonyl, but t-BuLi is still a fine nucleophile and the standard reagent for lithium-halogen exchange. LDA is the reagent for which basic-but-not-nucleophilic actually holds.

organolithium-reagents.q: What is the approximate pKa of a terminal alkyne C-H?
organolithium-reagents.why: An alkene is 44 and an alkane 50, so the alkyne is by far the most acidic of the three.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why is a terminal alkyne so much more acidic than an alkane?
options: The carbanion sits in an sp orbital
organolithium-reagents.why: Half s character holds the lone pair close to the nucleus.

organolithium-reagents.q: Which bases deprotonate a terminal alkyne?
organolithium-reagents.why: You need a base whose conjugate acid has a pKa well above 25.

organolithium-reagents.q: What kind of halide will an acetylide alkylate cleanly?
organolithium-reagents.why: With anything more substituted the acetylide acts as a base and E2 wins.

organolithium-reagents.q: What does sodium acetylide plus 2-bromopropane give?
organolithium-reagents.why: A secondary halide plus a strong base means elimination, not substitution.

organolithium-reagents.q: What does an acetylide plus an aldehyde give?
organolithium-reagents.why: Ordinary nucleophilic addition, with the alkyne left intact.

organolithium-reagents.q: What does Lindlar hydrogenation of an internal alkyne give?
organolithium-reagents.why: Both hydrogens are delivered to one face on the catalyst surface.

organolithium-reagents.q: What does Na in liquid NH3 give from an internal alkyne?
organolithium-reagents.why: A dissolving-metal reduction through a vinyl radical anion, which settles trans.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why is acetylide alkylation followed by reduction a useful pair?
organolithium-reagents.why: One substrate, two conditions, two geometries.

organolithium-reagents.q: Which is the odd one out among n-BuLi, t-BuLi and LDA?
options: LDA, which is an amide base
organolithium-reagents.why: The other two are carbanions; LDA is a nitrogen base made from one.

organolithium-reagents.q: Can an organolithium do everything a Grignard does?
options: Yes, and more, with less selectivity
organolithium-reagents.why: The extra reactivity is mostly something to manage rather than something to use.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why can an alkyne not be alkylated twice in the same step?
organolithium-reagents.why: Alkylating a terminal alkyne makes it internal, and an internal alkyne has no acidic C-H.

organolithium-reagents.q: Which reagent turns a terminal alkyne into a nucleophile?
organolithium-reagents.why: Deprotonation, not addition, is what makes it nucleophilic.

organolithium-reagents.q: What is the product of an acetylide plus a ketone after workup?
options: A ketone with a longer chain
organolithium-reagents.why: Addition to the carbonyl, protonated on workup.

organolithium-reagents.q: What is a propargylic position?
organolithium-reagents.why: By analogy with allylic, which is next to a double bond.

organolithium-reagents.q: Why is RLi used rather than RMgX for a very hindered ketone?
organolithium-reagents.why: The Grignard stalls and acts as a base; the smaller, hotter reagent gets in.

organolithium-reagents.q: What is the intermediate in the RLi plus carboxylic acid reaction?
organolithium-reagents.why: Two negative charges on one carbon's oxygens. It cannot collapse, because that would mean expelling O2- and adding a third charge, so it survives until workup.

organolithium-reagents.q: Which reagent would you choose to form a ketone enolate completely?
organolithium-reagents.why: Hydroxide gives an equilibrium, n-BuLi attacks the carbonyl, and pyridine is far too weak.

organolithium-reagents.q: What does the s character of an orbital do to a lone pair in it?
organolithium-reagents.why: Which is why acidity rises sp3 to sp2 to sp.

gilman-reagents.q: How is a Gilman reagent made?
options: Two RLi plus a copper(I) salt
gilman-reagents.why: R2CuLi, with one lithium iodide left over.

gilman-reagents.q: Where does a Gilman reagent add to an enone?
gilman-reagents.why: Soft nucleophile, orbital control, largest coefficient at beta.

gilman-reagents.q: Where does a Grignard add to an enone?
gilman-reagents.why: Hard nucleophile, charge control, and the carbonyl carbon carries the most positive charge.

gilman-reagents.q: What is the product of an enone plus a Grignard?
gilman-reagents.why: 1,2 addition to the carbonyl, protonated on workup.

gilman-reagents.q: What is the product of an enone plus a cuprate?
gilman-reagents.why: 1,4 addition gives an enolate, which protonates and tautomerizes back to the ketone.

gilman-reagents.q: What decides 1,2 against 1,4 addition?
gilman-reagents.why: Same substrate and same R group; only the metal changes the answer.

gilman-reagents.q: Why is a cuprate less reactive than a Grignard?
gilman-reagents.why: A less polar C-metal bond means less carbanion character.

gilman-reagents.q: What intermediate forms immediately after 1,4 addition?
gilman-reagents.why: It picks up a proton on workup, which is how the carbonyl reappears.

gilman-reagents.q: How many of a cuprate's two R groups are transferred?
gilman-reagents.why: The reagent runs at half efficiency, which nobody minds.

gilman-reagents.q: Which halides couple with a Gilman reagent?
gilman-reagents.why: The vinyl and aryl cases are the point, since neither does SN2 at all.

gilman-reagents.q: Why can a cuprate couple with a vinyl halide?
options: The pi bond activates the carbon
It does not need an SN2 trajectory
Vinyl halides have better leaving groups
gilman-reagents.why: A vinyl carbon is sp2 and its backside is shielded, so substitution is unavailable.

gilman-reagents.q: What happens to double-bond geometry in a cuprate coupling?
gilman-reagents.why: Which is a large part of why the reaction is worth running.

gilman-reagents.q: What does a cuprate plus an acyl chloride give?
gilman-reagents.why: The reagent is too mild to attack the ketone it just made.

gilman-reagents.q: What do a cuprate's three abilities have in common?
options: They follow from copper's d orbitals
They follow from its low reactivity
gilman-reagents.why: The mildness is the property being used, not a limitation being worked around.

gilman-reagents.q: Which functional groups does a cuprate tolerate?
gilman-reagents.why: Which is what makes it usable on a real substrate rather than a model one.

gilman-reagents.q: What does hard mean for a nucleophile?
gilman-reagents.why: Hard nucleophiles are charge-controlled, so they go where the charge is.

gilman-reagents.q: What does soft mean for a nucleophile?
gilman-reagents.why: Soft nucleophiles are orbital-controlled, so they go where the coefficient is.

gilman-reagents.q: Which carbon of an enone carries the greater positive charge?
gilman-reagents.why: Which is exactly why the hard Grignard picks it.

gilman-reagents.q: What is 1,4 addition also called?
gilman-reagents.why: And 1,2 addition is the direct one.

gilman-reagents.q: Why does an enone have two electrophilic carbons?
gilman-reagents.why: Resonance puts positive character on the beta carbon as well as the carbonyl carbon.

gilman-reagents.q: Which reagent gives 3-methylcyclohexanone from cyclohex-2-enone?
gilman-reagents.why: Only the cuprate delivers the methyl to the beta carbon.

gilman-reagents.q: What does CH3MgBr plus cyclohex-2-enone give?
gilman-reagents.why: 1,2 addition to the carbonyl gives a tertiary allylic alcohol.

gilman-reagents.q: Why can PCC not fix a tertiary alcohol into a ketone?
gilman-reagents.why: An oxidation at that carbon needs a C-H to remove, and a tertiary alcohol has none.

gilman-reagents.q: Which organometallic is mild enough to be made with an ester present?
gilman-reagents.why: That tolerance is why zinc reagents appear in palladium chemistry.

gilman-reagents.q: Does temperature switch a cuprate from 1,4 to 1,2?
gilman-reagents.why: Choosing the reagent is how you choose the product here.

gilman-reagents.q: What would a Grignard do to a substrate containing both an enone and an ester?
gilman-reagents.why: Low selectivity is the cost of high reactivity; a cuprate would leave the ester alone.

gilman-reagents.q: What is the general fix when a reagent attacks too many sites?
gilman-reagents.why: Cleverer conditions rarely solve a selectivity problem that the reagent causes.

gilman-reagents.q: Which product comes from 1,4 addition followed by workup?
gilman-reagents.why: The enolate tautomerizes once it is protonated.

gilman-reagents.q: Why is a cuprate used at half efficiency?
gilman-reagents.why: The second R group stays on the copper.

gilman-reagents.q: What kind of control does a soft nucleophile follow?
gilman-reagents.why: Which points it at the largest LUMO coefficient rather than the largest partial charge.

cross-coupling.q: Which metal catalyzes the standard cross-coupling reactions?
cross-coupling.why: Copper appears as a cocatalyst in the Sonogashira, but palladium runs the cycle.

cross-coupling.q: What are the three steps of the cross-coupling cycle?
cross-coupling.why: The first and last names describe what happens to the palladium's oxidation state.

cross-coupling.q: What happens in oxidative addition?
options: The two groups join and leave
Pd inserts into the Ar-X bond
The R group moves to Pd
cross-coupling.why: Pd(0) becomes Pd(II), holding both pieces.

cross-coupling.q: What happens to palladium during oxidative addition?
cross-coupling.why: Oxidized by two, which is where the step name comes from.

cross-coupling.q: What happens in transmetalation?
options: The R group moves to Pd
cross-coupling.why: The palladium oxidation state does not change in this step.

cross-coupling.q: What happens in reductive elimination?
cross-coupling.why: Pd(II) becomes Pd(0) and the catalyst is back where it started.

cross-coupling.q: Why is palladium a catalyst rather than a reagent?
options: It is regenerated by the base
It ends each cycle as it began
It is not consumed by the solvent
cross-coupling.why: Reductive elimination hands back the Pd(0) the cycle started with, so a few mole percent turns over thousands of times.

cross-coupling.q: Which coupling uses a boronic acid?
cross-coupling.why: And it needs a base, which the Stille does not.

cross-coupling.q: Which coupling uses an organostannane?
cross-coupling.why: Chemically excellent, but organotin reagents are seriously toxic.

cross-coupling.q: Which coupling uses an organozinc reagent?
cross-coupling.why: Zinc is mild enough that esters survive the cycle.

cross-coupling.q: Which coupling joins an aryl halide to a terminal alkyne?
cross-coupling.why: A copper cocatalyst forms the acetylide that transmetalates.

cross-coupling.q: Which coupling uses no organometallic partner at all?
cross-coupling.why: An alkene inserts into the Ar-Pd bond instead, so there is no transmetalation step.

cross-coupling.q: Why does a Suzuki coupling need a base?
cross-coupling.why: A neutral boronic acid transfers its R group poorly; the four-coordinate borate does it well.

cross-coupling.q: Why did the Suzuki coupling displace the Stille industrially?
cross-coupling.why: The chemistry of the Stille is at least as good; the toxicity of organotin is what settled it.

cross-coupling.q: Which step is unique to the Heck reaction?
cross-coupling.why: It replaces transmetalation, which the Heck has nothing to perform.

cross-coupling.q: What geometry does the Heck reaction usually give?
cross-coupling.why: And the new bond forms at the less substituted carbon.

cross-coupling.q: Why can an aryl halide not undergo SN2?
options: The halide is a poor leaving group
cross-coupling.why: And SN1 is no better, since an aryl cation is badly unstable.

cross-coupling.q: How does palladium make an aryl halide reactive?
cross-coupling.why: Nothing has to attack that carbon, which is the whole point.

cross-coupling.q: What does convergent mean for a synthesis?
cross-coupling.why: Since yields multiply, joining two short branches beats one long chain.

cross-coupling.q: Why does a convergent route return more material?
options: Each branch is shorter in time
cross-coupling.why: Ten linear steps at 85% gives about 20%; two five-step branches joined gives about 37%.

cross-coupling.q: Which functional groups survive a Suzuki coupling?
cross-coupling.why: The reactive carbon is bound to a metal throughout and never exists as a free carbanion.

cross-coupling.q: Which bond should signal a cross-coupling disconnection?
options: A C-C bond next to a carbonyl
cross-coupling.why: Neither ring is nucleophilic or electrophilic enough for anything from earlier chapters.

cross-coupling.q: What prize recognized cross-coupling?
cross-coupling.why: Shared by Heck, Negishi and Suzuki.

cross-coupling.q: Why would a Grignard fail on a substrate carrying a free phenol?
cross-coupling.why: A phenol pKa near 10 is easily acidic enough to consume the reagent.

cross-coupling.q: Can an aryl Grignard be made from an aryl bromide?
options: No, aryl halides are inert to magnesium
cross-coupling.why: Bromides and iodides go readily. Aryl chlorides are sluggish and need heat or activation, and aryl fluorides do not go at all. The trouble with the reagent is what it does afterward, not whether it forms.

cross-coupling.q: What is the oxidation state of palladium during transmetalation?
cross-coupling.why: Only the two elimination and addition steps move it.

cross-coupling.q: What is a mole percent loading typical of a palladium catalyst?
cross-coupling.why: Because the cycle regenerates the active species every turn.

cross-coupling.q: Which partner is oxidatively added in a Suzuki coupling?
cross-coupling.why: The organometallic partner arrives later, at transmetalation.

cross-coupling.q: Why is cross-coupling suited to making many analogs?
cross-coupling.why: Fifty analogs cost fifty final steps rather than fifty syntheses.

cross-coupling.q: Which is not a step in the standard catalytic cycle?
cross-coupling.why: The aryl halide is activated by the metal, not by attacking the ring.

wittig-reaction.q: What does a Wittig reaction convert a C=O into?
wittig-reaction.why: The new double bond lands exactly where the carbonyl oxygen was.

wittig-reaction.q: What reagent class performs a Wittig?
wittig-reaction.why: A negative carbon bonded directly to a positive phosphorus, neutral overall.

wittig-reaction.q: What is an ylide?
options: Adjacent opposite charges in a neutral molecule
wittig-reaction.why: Both charges are real and next to each other, which is why the thing is reactive.

wittig-reaction.q: How is a phosphonium salt made?
wittig-reaction.why: Triphenylphosphine is a large, polarizable, soft nucleophile.

wittig-reaction.q: Which halides can be used to make a Wittig ylide?
wittig-reaction.why: The first step is an SN2, and that is the whole limitation on the reaction.

wittig-reaction.q: Why will a tertiary halide not give an ylide?
options: It eliminates on contact with PPh3
Its backside is blocked to SN2
wittig-reaction.why: No phosphonium salt forms, so the route dies at step one.

wittig-reaction.q: Why can bromobenzene not be used to make an ylide?
options: An aryl halide will not do SN2
Aryl halides are too stable to handle
wittig-reaction.why: Aryl groups reach a Wittig product from the carbonyl side instead.

wittig-reaction.q: What base deprotonates a phosphonium salt?
wittig-reaction.why: The hydrogen next to P+ is acidic, but not that acidic.

wittig-reaction.q: Why is the hydrogen next to P+ acidic?
options: It sits beside a plus charge
The C-H bond is unusually long
wittig-reaction.why: Adjacent opposite charge is the stabilization, and it is why the ylide exists.

wittig-reaction.q: What by-product does a Wittig give?
wittig-reaction.why: And forming it is the reaction's driving force.

wittig-reaction.q: What drives the Wittig forward?
wittig-reaction.why: A P=O double bond at around 130-140 kcal/mol, one of the strongest in organic chemistry, formed in the last step.

wittig-reaction.q: What is the four-membered intermediate called?
wittig-reaction.why: It falls apart in the one way it can, giving the alkene and the phosphine oxide.

wittig-reaction.q: How does a Wittig differ from an elimination?
wittig-reaction.why: An elimination forms the C=C between two carbons already bonded, so Zaitsev chooses where.

wittig-reaction.q: What decides where the double bond goes in an elimination?
wittig-reaction.why: Which is the problem a Wittig avoids entirely.

wittig-reaction.q: Where does the Wittig double bond end up?
wittig-reaction.why: There is only one position available, so there is no competition to lose.

wittig-reaction.q: What does cyclohexanone plus Ph3P=CH2 give?
wittig-reaction.why: An exocyclic alkene, and the less stable of the two isomers, which is exactly the point.

wittig-reaction.q: What does an unstabilized ylide give?
wittig-reaction.why: It adds fast and irreversibly, so the geometry of the transition state is locked in.

wittig-reaction.q: What does a stabilized ylide give?
wittig-reaction.why: It adds reversibly, so the equilibrium finds the more stable arrangement.

wittig-reaction.q: What makes an ylide stabilized?
options: Being made from a primary halide
Conjugation to an ester or ketone
wittig-reaction.why: Delocalizing the carbanion makes it less reactive and the addition reversible.

wittig-reaction.q: Which gives the less stable alkene geometry?
wittig-reaction.why: A fast irreversible step has no time to equilibrate, which inverts the usual intuition.

wittig-reaction.q: What kind of control gives the cis alkene here?
wittig-reaction.why: The product that forms fastest, rather than the one that is most stable.

wittig-reaction.q: Which ylide would you use for PhCH=CH-CO2Et?
wittig-reaction.why: The aldehyde supplies the phenyl half, so the ester has to come from the ylide.

wittig-reaction.q: What does a Wittig disconnection look like?
options: Cut next to the double bond
wittig-reaction.why: Both assignments are usually drawable, and you pick by which halide is easier.

wittig-reaction.q: When two Wittig disconnections exist, how do you choose?
wittig-reaction.why: The halide has to survive an SN2, and that is what eliminates one of the two.

wittig-reaction.q: Why is phosphorus used stoichiometrically here?
wittig-reaction.why: Expensive, and the main practical objection to the reaction.

wittig-reaction.q: Which carbon of the ylide ends up in the alkene?
wittig-reaction.why: It bonds to the old carbonyl carbon, which is the new double bond.

wittig-reaction.q: Does a Wittig rearrange?
wittig-reaction.why: No carbocation is ever formed, so there is nothing to shift.

wittig-reaction.q: Which alkene is hard to reach by elimination but easy by Wittig?
wittig-reaction.why: Zaitsev pushes an elimination toward the more substituted isomer.

wittig-reaction.q: What happens if you try a Wittig with a secondary halide?
wittig-reaction.why: SN2 on a secondary center is sluggish, so yields fall.

wittig-reaction.q: Which part of the target does the carbonyl compound supply?
options: One half of the new C=C
wittig-reaction.why: The ylide supplies the other half, and the two are joined at that bond.

imines-enamines.q: What does a primary amine plus a ketone give?
imines-enamines.why: One hydrogen is left on nitrogen after the addition, so the C=N+ cation loses it.

imines-enamines.q: What does a secondary amine plus a ketone give?
imines-enamines.why: No N-H is left, so the proton comes from the alpha carbon instead.

imines-enamines.q: What does a tertiary amine plus a ketone give?
imines-enamines.why: With no N-H at all there is no way forward, which is why tertiary amines serve as bases here.

imines-enamines.q: What is the first intermediate in imine formation?
imines-enamines.why: A tetrahedral carbon carrying both an OH and an NR2.

imines-enamines.q: What decides imine against enamine?
options: How many H remain on nitrogen
imines-enamines.why: One left gives an imine, none gives an enamine.

imines-enamines.q: Where is the double bond in an imine?
imines-enamines.why: C=N-R, with the R from the amine.

imines-enamines.q: Where is the double bond in an enamine?
imines-enamines.why: C=C-NR2, because the proton had to come from the alpha carbon.

imines-enamines.q: Roughly what pH does imine formation need?
imines-enamines.why: Enough acid to protonate the OH, not enough to protonate the amine.

imines-enamines.q: Why is acid required?
imines-enamines.why: A hydroxide is a terrible leaving group; water is a fine one.

imines-enamines.q: Why does strong acid stop the reaction?
imines-enamines.why: An ammonium ion is not a nucleophile, so nothing attacks in the first place.

imines-enamines.q: How is the equilibrium pulled forward?
imines-enamines.why: A Dean-Stark trap or molecular sieves; every step of the sequence is reversible.

imines-enamines.q: What reverses imine formation?
imines-enamines.why: Adding the water back runs the whole sequence in reverse.

imines-enamines.q: What is reductive amination?
options: Forming an imine and reducing it
imines-enamines.why: NaBH3CN reduces the imine as it forms, avoiding the over-alkylation of direct SN2.

imines-enamines.q: Why is reductive amination better than alkylating ammonia?
options: It works only on tertiary amines
imines-enamines.why: Direct SN2 on ammonia keeps going, giving a mixture of amine classes.

imines-enamines.q: What reagent selectively reduces an imine?
imines-enamines.why: Mild enough to leave the ketone alone while reducing the more electrophilic iminium.

imines-enamines.q: What does hydroxylamine plus a ketone give?
imines-enamines.why: A crystalline derivative, which is how carbonyl compounds were once identified.

imines-enamines.q: Which carbon of an enamine is nucleophilic?
imines-enamines.why: Pushing the lone pair into the C=C puts the negative charge at the far carbon.

imines-enamines.q: What is an enamine comparable to?
imines-enamines.why: Same job, reached without a strong base, and neutral rather than anionic.

imines-enamines.q: How does an enamine differ from an enolate?
imines-enamines.why: Which is why it usually stops after one alkylation.

imines-enamines.q: What is the Stork enamine synthesis?
imines-enamines.why: Net result is an alpha-substituted ketone, by a gentler route than an enolate.

imines-enamines.q: What does hydrolyzing an enamine give back?
imines-enamines.why: Which is how the sequence releases its product at the end.

imines-enamines.q: Why does an enamine alkylate only once?
options: It is consumed by the halide
It is not basic enough to form again
imines-enamines.why: An enolate route deprotonates its own product and goes again.

imines-enamines.q: What is an enamine good at besides alkylation?
imines-enamines.why: A mild Michael donor, where a full enolate would compete with 1,2-addition.

imines-enamines.q: Which amine is most used for making enamines?
imines-enamines.why: A cyclic secondary amine, so two carbons on nitrogen and one hydrogen.

imines-enamines.q: What class of amine is pyrrolidine?
imines-enamines.why: Being in a ring changes nothing about the count.

imines-enamines.q: Which step of imine formation is rate-determining near pH 4.5?
imines-enamines.why: Which is why acid helps up to the point where it switches off the nucleophile.

imines-enamines.q: What is the product of cyclohexanone and pyrrolidine?
imines-enamines.why: Two carbons already on nitrogen means no N-H survives the addition.

imines-enamines.q: Which reaction makes a secondary amine cleanly?
imines-enamines.why: It stops where you want it to, because the imine forms once.

imines-enamines.q: Why is a tertiary amine used as a base in these reactions?
options: It is a stronger base than others
imines-enamines.why: No N-H means no route to a stable condensation product.

imines-enamines.q: What kind of curve does the rate of imine formation follow with pH?
imines-enamines.why: Acid helps one step and kills another, so the best rate is between the two.

michael-robinson.q: What is a Michael addition?
options: Conjugate addition of an enolate to an enone
michael-robinson.why: 1,4 rather than 1,2, with an enolate as the nucleophile.

michael-robinson.q: What is the Michael donor?
michael-robinson.why: Almost always a compound with an alpha hydrogen between two carbonyls.

michael-robinson.q: What is the Michael acceptor?
michael-robinson.why: An alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl, with the beta carbon as the electrophilic site.

michael-robinson.q: What spacing does a Michael addition leave?
michael-robinson.why: Joining the donor alpha carbon to the acceptor beta carbon puts them five apart.

michael-robinson.q: What spacing does an aldol leave?
michael-robinson.why: The nucleophile hit a carbonyl carbon and the oxygen stayed as an alcohol.

michael-robinson.q: What spacing does a Claisen leave?
michael-robinson.why: The nucleophile hit an ester and the alkoxide left.

michael-robinson.q: What is the Michael retron?
michael-robinson.why: See one and disconnect the bond beta to a carbonyl.

michael-robinson.q: Roughly what pKa does a typical Michael donor have?
michael-robinson.why: Low enough that a catalytic alkoxide deprotonates it completely.

michael-robinson.q: Why must the donor be doubly stabilized?
michael-robinson.why: Spreading the charge over two carbonyls is what makes the enolate soft rather than hard.

michael-robinson.q: What would a simple ketone enolate do to an enone?
michael-robinson.why: A hard, charge-dense nucleophile goes for the carbonyl carbon.

michael-robinson.q: Why is a catalytic alkoxide enough?
options: Alkoxides are regenerated by the enone
The donor is far more acidic
The reaction is catalytic in donor
michael-robinson.why: So no strong base ever sits in the flask next to the acceptor.

michael-robinson.q: Which of these is a common Michael donor?
michael-robinson.why: An alpha hydrogen between two ester carbonyls, pKa near 13.

michael-robinson.q: What is methyl vinyl ketone used as?
michael-robinson.why: Cheap, and the ring its Robinson product gives is the one steroid chemistry needed.

michael-robinson.q: What is a Robinson annulation?
options: A Michael then an intramolecular aldol
michael-robinson.why: And it builds a ring in the process.

michael-robinson.q: What ring size does a Robinson annulation give?
michael-robinson.why: A 1,5-dicarbonyl has its ends exactly far enough apart to meet without strain.

michael-robinson.q: What functional group does a Robinson annulation leave?
michael-robinson.why: The final dehydration conjugates the new C=C with the carbonyl.

michael-robinson.q: Which step makes a Robinson annulation irreversible?
michael-robinson.why: Conjugating the alkene with the carbonyl is the stabilization it cannot climb back out of.

michael-robinson.q: Why is the ring six-membered rather than some other size?
michael-robinson.why: The reaction is not choosing a ring size; the chain length already chose it.

michael-robinson.q: How do you undo a Robinson annulation on paper?
options: Open the ring at the carbonyl
michael-robinson.why: Reverse order: put the water back, break the aldol bond, then cut beta to a carbonyl.

michael-robinson.q: Where does the Michael bond form?
michael-robinson.why: Which is exactly what puts the two carbonyls five apart.

michael-robinson.q: What does diethyl malonate plus NaOEt plus MVK give?
michael-robinson.why: A soft enolate adding 1,4, with the Michael fingerprint in the product.

michael-robinson.q: What is an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl also called?
michael-robinson.why: And as a substrate for conjugate addition, a Michael acceptor.

michael-robinson.q: Why does a soft nucleophile add 1,4?
michael-robinson.why: Orbital control rather than charge control, and the beta carbon has the larger coefficient.

michael-robinson.q: Which carbon of an enone carries more positive charge?
michael-robinson.why: Which is why a hard nucleophile picks it, and a soft one does not.

michael-robinson.q: What does an intramolecular aldol need to close a ring?
options: An enolate and a carbonyl that can reach
michael-robinson.why: Five- and six-membered closures happen far faster than anything larger.

michael-robinson.q: Which reaction sequence builds a cyclohexenone from two acyclic pieces?
michael-robinson.why: A Diels-Alder builds a ring too, but it gives a cyclohexene rather than a cyclohexenone.

michael-robinson.q: What should a cyclohexenone in an exam question make you check?
michael-robinson.why: If it does, a Robinson annulation made it and the two pieces fall out.

michael-robinson.q: What is a 1,3-diketone's approximate alpha pKa?
michael-robinson.why: Two carbonyls flanking one carbon, so the carbanion is delocalized onto both.

michael-robinson.q: Which product spacing tells you a Claisen happened?
michael-robinson.why: One carbon between the two carbonyls.

michael-robinson.q: Why is reading product spacing useful?
michael-robinson.why: It works forwards to predict a product and backwards to disconnect one.

ester-syntheses.q: What does a malonic ester synthesis give?
ester-syntheses.why: Malonate has two esters: one carboxyl is lost as CO2 and the other stays as the acid.

ester-syntheses.q: What does an acetoacetic ester synthesis give?
ester-syntheses.why: One ester and one ketone: the ester's carboxyl goes, the ketone survives.

ester-syntheses.q: What are the three steps of both syntheses?
ester-syntheses.why: Identical for both; only the starting material differs.

ester-syntheses.q: What is the approximate alpha pKa of diethyl malonate?
ester-syntheses.why: Delocalizing the carbanion onto two ester oxygens is worth twelve orders of magnitude.

ester-syntheses.q: What is the approximate alpha pKa of an ordinary ester?
ester-syntheses.why: Too high for a convenient base, and a strong base would attack the ester instead.

ester-syntheses.q: What base deprotonates diethyl malonate?
ester-syntheses.why: At pKa 13 the alkoxide that matches your solvent is enough.

ester-syntheses.q: Why is the second carbonyl there?
options: To act as a leaving group
ester-syntheses.why: It is thrown away once the alkylation is done, which is what an activating group is.

ester-syntheses.q: What is an activating group?
options: One that speeds up a catalyst
ester-syntheses.why: This is the clearest example of one in the course.

ester-syntheses.q: What type of reaction is the alkylation step?
ester-syntheses.why: Which is why the halide must be methyl, primary, allylic or benzylic.

ester-syntheses.q: Which halide will not work in either synthesis?
ester-syntheses.why: The enolate is a base as well as a nucleophile, so E2 takes over.

ester-syntheses.q: What happens with a secondary halide?
ester-syntheses.why: The backside is crowded, so the enolate reaches for a beta hydrogen instead.

ester-syntheses.q: Why does the intermediate decarboxylate on heating?
options: A second carbonyl sits beta to it
ester-syntheses.why: A six-membered cyclic transition state reaches from the carboxyl O-H to that second carbonyl. It is a ketone in the acetoacetic route and the other carboxyl in the malonic one, and either works.

ester-syntheses.q: What is lost in the decarboxylation?
ester-syntheses.why: And an enol forms, which tautomerizes to the product.

ester-syntheses.q: Would an alpha-keto acid decarboxylate on warming?
options: Yes, faster than a beta one
ester-syntheses.why: The geometry needs the second carbonyl exactly beta, whether that carbonyl is a ketone or another carboxyl.

ester-syntheses.q: How many times can malonate be alkylated?
ester-syntheses.why: Its CH2 has two acidic hydrogens, so both can be replaced in turn.

ester-syntheses.q: What is diethyl malonate's structure?
ester-syntheses.why: One CH2 between two ester carbonyls.

ester-syntheses.q: What is ethyl acetoacetate's structure?
ester-syntheses.why: One ketone and one ester flanking the acidic CH2.

ester-syntheses.q: Why does the ketone survive in the acetoacetic route?
options: It has no carboxyl to lose
ester-syntheses.why: Only a carboxyl can decarboxylate, and the ketone is not one.

ester-syntheses.q: What product would ethyl acetoacetate plus benzyl bromide give?
ester-syntheses.why: A methyl ketone carrying the benzyl group, after hydrolysis and decarboxylation.

ester-syntheses.q: What product would diethyl malonate plus bromoethane give?
ester-syntheses.why: The ethyl group ends up on the carbon alpha to the surviving carboxyl.

ester-syntheses.q: Which halides would make 2-methylpentanoic acid from malonate?
ester-syntheses.why: The alpha carbon of the target carries a methyl and a propyl, installed in two rounds.

ester-syntheses.q: Which target is out of reach for an acetoacetic ester synthesis?
ester-syntheses.why: All four are methyl ketones, so the product class does not decide it; the halide does.

ester-syntheses.q: What should an alpha-substituted carboxylic acid make you look for?
ester-syntheses.why: That is the retrosynthetic use of the malonic ester synthesis.

ester-syntheses.q: Which reagent performs the hydrolysis and decarboxylation?
ester-syntheses.why: One step does both, because the beta-keto acid does not survive the temperature.

ester-syntheses.q: Why can a plain ester not be alkylated this way?
ester-syntheses.why: pKa 25 against 13 is the whole reason the second carbonyl is installed.

ester-syntheses.q: What does the alkoxide base need to match?
ester-syntheses.why: Using ethoxide with an ethyl ester avoids scrambling the ester by transesterification.

ester-syntheses.q: Which carbon of malonate is alkylated?
ester-syntheses.why: That is the only acidic position, and it is acidic because of the flanking carbonyls.

ester-syntheses.q: How many carboxyls does malonate have after hydrolysis?
ester-syntheses.why: One of them is beta to the other, which is why exactly one is lost on heating.

ester-syntheses.q: What survives from acetoacetate into the product?
ester-syntheses.why: Which is what makes every product of that route a methyl ketone.

ester-syntheses.q: Which constraint should you check first on either route?
options: The order of the two carbonyls
Whether the halide survives an SN2
ester-syntheses.why: The target never tells you whether the route works; the halide does.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does a Baeyer-Villiger oxidation do to a ketone?
options: Inserts an oxygen into a C-C bond
Adds an oxygen to the alpha carbon
baeyer-villiger.why: The product is an ester, and almost nothing else in the course touches that bond.

baeyer-villiger.q: What reagent performs it?
baeyer-villiger.why: The same reagent that epoxidizes alkenes.

baeyer-villiger.q: What is the tetrahedral intermediate called?
baeyer-villiger.why: It collapses by migration, with a carboxylate leaving.

baeyer-villiger.q: What kind of step is the migration?
baeyer-villiger.why: The same motion that rearranges a carbocation, running on a neutral intermediate.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does the migrating group take with it?
baeyer-villiger.why: Which is why it never exists as a free species and never loses its configuration.

baeyer-villiger.q: What happens to a migrating stereocenter?
baeyer-villiger.why: The bond never fully breaks, so the other three bonds are undisturbed.

baeyer-villiger.q: What is the migratory aptitude order?
baeyer-villiger.why: Which is carbocation stability arriving from a different direction.

baeyer-villiger.q: Why does the more substituted group migrate?
baeyer-villiger.why: Whatever stabilizes a carbocation stabilizes this transition state.

baeyer-villiger.q: What migrates in a methyl ketone?
baeyer-villiger.why: Methyl is last in the series, which makes methyl ketones the predictable substrates.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does a methyl ketone give?
options: The acetate ester of the other group
Methyl ester of the other group
baeyer-villiger.why: The oxygen goes between the carbonyl and the migrating group.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does a cyclic ketone give?
baeyer-villiger.why: The migration is intramolecular, so the ring expands rather than opening.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does cyclohexanone give with mCPBA?
baeyer-villiger.why: Six carbons plus the inserted oxygen.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does cyclopentanone give with mCPBA?
baeyer-villiger.why: Ring expansion by exactly one atom, every time.

baeyer-villiger.q: What is a lactone?
baeyer-villiger.why: A cyclic amide would be a lactam.

baeyer-villiger.q: What happens if the substrate also has an alkene?
baeyer-villiger.why: Epoxidation is faster, so the alkene has to be dealt with before the ketone.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does acetophenone give with mCPBA?
baeyer-villiger.why: The phenyl migrates, so the oxygen ends up between it and the carbonyl.

baeyer-villiger.q: What does phenyl acetate tell you about aryl migration?
baeyer-villiger.why: An aryl group stabilizes adjacent positive charge through its pi system.

baeyer-villiger.q: What breaks during the collapse of the Criegee intermediate?
baeyer-villiger.why: And a carboxylate leaves as the migration happens.

baeyer-villiger.q: What leaves in a Baeyer-Villiger?
baeyer-villiger.why: The peroxyacid's other half, which is what makes the O-O bond a good place to break.

baeyer-villiger.q: Which other reaction uses the same reagent?
baeyer-villiger.why: A peroxyacid's O-O bond with a good leaving group is what both exploit.

baeyer-villiger.q: Where does the inserted oxygen end up?
options: Between the carbonyl and the migrating group
baeyer-villiger.why: Which is how you read a product backwards to find what migrated.

baeyer-villiger.q: How do you tell which group migrated from the product?
options: It is attached to the carbonyl
It is past the new oxygen
baeyer-villiger.why: Find the inserted oxygen and look at which side each group is on.

baeyer-villiger.q: Why is this reaction usable on a chiral center?
baeyer-villiger.why: One of very few reactions at this level where a stereocenter survives a bond change intact.

baeyer-villiger.q: What class of compound is the product?
baeyer-villiger.why: Which you already know how to hydrolyze, so the reaction slots into longer routes.

baeyer-villiger.q: Which is the worst migrator?
baeyer-villiger.why: Which is the fact that makes methyl ketones worth choosing as substrates.

baeyer-villiger.q: What kind of ring expansion is this?
baeyer-villiger.why: One of the few reliable ring expansions at this level, and the only one adding oxygen.

baeyer-villiger.q: Is the Criegee intermediate charged?
baeyer-villiger.why: Which is what makes the 1,2-shift here unusual: it runs without a carbocation.

baeyer-villiger.q: Which bond does the oxygen go into?
baeyer-villiger.why: One of the two bonds from the carbonyl carbon to its substituents.

baeyer-villiger.q: Which retrosynthetic clue suggests a Baeyer-Villiger?
options: An ester with a methyl on oxygen
baeyer-villiger.why: Esterifying a tertiary alcohol is hard; migrating a tertiary group is the easiest case.

baeyer-villiger.q: How many groups on the carbonyl carbon migrate?
baeyer-villiger.why: Which is why the whole reaction reduces to a question about aptitude.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Why will chlorobenzene not undergo SN2?
options: Its backside is shielded by the ring
Chloride is a poor leaving group
It is sterically hindered by hydrogens
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The carbon is sp2 and the trajectory a nucleophile needs does not exist.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Why will chlorobenzene not undergo SN1?
options: The ring stabilizes the substrate too well
An aryl cation is badly unstable
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The positive charge would sit in an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, with no way to delocalize.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What order of steps does SNAr follow?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The opposite order from every substitution before it.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What is the SNAr intermediate called?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Negatively charged and not aromatic, which is what the withdrawing groups pay for.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What does SNAr need on the ring?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Only ortho and para can reach the negative charge by resonance.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Why does a meta nitro group fail to activate for SNAr?
options: It is too far to withdraw at all
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The intermediate's charge lands ortho and para to the attack, never meta.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which is the best leaving group in SNAr?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The reverse of every other substitution, because attack is the slow step.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Why is fluorine best in SNAr?
options: It makes that carbon most electrophilic
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The C-X bond is not breaking in the rate-determining step, so electronegativity decides.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What is lost in the SNAr intermediate?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: And restored when the leaving group finally departs.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: How many products does SNAr give?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The nucleophile arrives exactly where the leaving group was.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What conditions produce benzyne from chlorobenzene?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: A very strong base is needed to remove a ring hydrogen.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What order of steps does the benzyne route follow?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The mirror image of SNAr.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What is benzyne's extra bond made from?
options: Two sp2 orbitals in the ring plane
Two p orbitals above the ring
An sp3 and a p orbital
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: They point away from each other rather than overlapping properly, which is why it is strained.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: How many products does the benzyne route give?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The triple bond is symmetric, so the nucleophile can attack either carbon.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What does the benzyne route need on the ring?
options: A hydrogen ortho to the halide
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: That hydrogen is what the base removes in the first step.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What proved benzyne exists?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: No direct displacement could put the nucleophile on a carbon that never bore the leaving group.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Can 2-bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene form a benzyne?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: There is no ortho hydrogen to eliminate.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What does 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene plus methoxide give?
options: The methyl ether at the chlorine's position
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Nitro groups ortho and para make this an SNAr, which gives one product.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which nucleophile is used in the classic benzyne reaction?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The base and the nucleophile are the same species here.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Why is the Meisenheimer complex stable enough to form?
options: Nitro groups take the charge onto their oxygens
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Delocalization onto the substituents is what makes losing aromaticity affordable.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which substitution has the C-X bond breaking in its slow step?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Which is exactly why the leaving group order inverts for SNAr.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What kind of intermediate is benzyne?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: It lasts only long enough to be attacked.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which ring is unreactive to both routes?
options: A plain benzene ring with NaNH2
One with two ortho nitro groups
One with a para nitro group
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: No activation rules out SNAr, and no ortho hydrogen rules out benzyne.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What does para-chlorotoluene plus NaNH2 give?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Amide can attack either carbon of the benzyne, and the two are not equivalent.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Does SNAr rearrange?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: The nucleophile adds where the leaving group already is.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which chapter's reaction also puts a nucleophile on an aryl carbon?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: A third route, and the one that needs neither activation nor a brutal base.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What makes losing aromaticity affordable in SNAr?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Without them the intermediate is too high in energy to form.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which positions carry the negative charge in a Meisenheimer complex?
options: Ortho and para to the attack
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Which is exactly why only ortho and para substituents help.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: What happens to the ring after the halide leaves in SNAr?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Which is the thermodynamic payoff for the whole sequence.

nucleophilic-aromatic.q: Which halide is worst for SNAr?
nucleophilic-aromatic.why: Iodine is the least electronegative of the four, so it activates the carbon least.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What is the benzylic position?
options: The carbon attached to the ring
The carbon two away from the ring
benzylic-reactivity.why: It is not part of the ring, and it behaves unlike any other sp3 carbon.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is a benzylic cation stabilized?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The charge spreads over the benzylic carbon plus both ortho and the para positions.

benzylic-reactivity.q: How many carbons share a benzylic charge?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The benzylic carbon plus the two ortho and one para ring positions.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which other position uses the same argument?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Allylic delocalization spreads over three carbons; benzylic over four.

benzylic-reactivity.q: A benzylic halide is good at which mechanisms?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Rare, and it is why benzyl bromide is used as an alkylating agent everywhere.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is a primary benzylic halide good at SN1?
benzylic-reactivity.why: It sits roughly where a tertiary alkyl halide does.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is a benzylic halide also good at SN2?
options: The halide is a better leaving group
The ring stabilizes the transition state
benzylic-reactivity.why: And a benzylic carbon is usually unhindered, which helps as well.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which reagent brominates the benzylic position?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Light means radicals, and the benzylic radical is by far the most stable.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is NBS used rather than Br2?
options: It is a stronger brominating agent
It is a radical initiator itself
It keeps the Br2 concentration low
benzylic-reactivity.why: Low Br2 suppresses the ionic addition that would attack any alkene present.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What other position does NBS brominate?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Same reagent, same mechanism, and a selectivity problem if a molecule has both.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does hot KMnO4 do to toluene?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The side chain is cut back to one carbon and oxidized to the carboxyl.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does hot KMnO4 do to propylbenzene?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Chain length makes no difference; everything past the benzylic carbon is cut away.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does hot KMnO4 do to tert-butylbenzene?
benzylic-reactivity.why: There is no benzylic hydrogen, so the reaction cannot start.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What does the tert-butylbenzene result reveal?
options: The reaction starts at a benzylic C-H
benzylic-reactivity.why: The one exception that shows what the mechanism requires.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Does hot KMnO4 attack the benzene ring?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Aromatic stabilization keeps the ring inert to conditions that destroy alkenes.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why does a radical abstract the benzylic hydrogen preferentially?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Stability of the radical formed is what selectivity tracks.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What should a benzoic acid suggest retrosynthetically?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Oxidation converts any alkyl chain to a carboxyl, so the chain identity is free.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which alkylbenzene will not oxidize?
benzylic-reactivity.why: No benzylic hydrogen means no starting point.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What is benzyl bromide used for?
benzylic-reactivity.why: It appears in malonic ester and enamine chemistry for exactly this reason.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Is a benzylic anion stabilized?
options: Only if the ring is substituted
benzylic-reactivity.why: The same resonance that stabilizes the cation and the radical.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What comparison does benzylic stabilization most resemble?
benzylic-reactivity.why: One alkene replaced by a whole ring, so the charge spreads further.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which intermediate is NOT stabilized at a benzylic position?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Cation, radical and anion are all delocalized by the same resonance.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What conditions does benzylic bromination need?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Ionic conditions would brominate the ring instead.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why can an alkyl group be put on a ring and then oxidized?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Electrophilic substitution cannot deliver a carboxyl group directly.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What happens to the carbons beyond the benzylic one in KMnO4 oxidation?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Which is why chain length is irrelevant to the product.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which product comes from isopropylbenzene and hot KMnO4?
benzylic-reactivity.why: One benzylic hydrogen is enough, and both methyls go with the rest of the chain.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Does Friedel-Crafts alkylation give a benzylic carbon?
benzylic-reactivity.why: Any carbon attached directly to the ring is benzylic by definition.

benzylic-reactivity.q: What limits selectivity if a molecule is both allylic and benzylic?
benzylic-reactivity.why: One reagent and one mechanism means it cannot tell them apart.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Why is the benzylic C-H weaker than an ordinary alkane C-H?
options: The radical it forms is stabilized
benzylic-reactivity.why: Bond strength tracks the stability of the fragments it gives.

benzylic-reactivity.q: Which position does an aromatic ring make reactive without being reactive itself?
benzylic-reactivity.why: The ring supplies the stabilization and stays intact.

phenols.q: What is a phenol?
options: An OH attached directly to a ring
An OH on a carbon next to a ring
phenols.why: An OH on a carbon next to the ring is a benzylic alcohol, which behaves quite differently.

phenols.q: What is phenol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Six orders of magnitude more acidic than ethanol.

phenols.q: What is ethanol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Its conjugate base has the charge on one oxygen with nowhere to go.

phenols.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
phenols.why: Acidity is about the stability of the conjugate base, not the bond that breaks.

phenols.q: Where does the phenoxide charge go?
phenols.why: Which is also why only ortho and para substituents affect the acidity much.

phenols.q: Which base deprotonates a phenol?
phenols.why: Bicarbonate is not strong enough, which is what makes it useful as a discriminator.

phenols.q: Which base deprotonates a carboxylic acid but not a phenol?
phenols.why: Carbonic acid at pKa 6.4 sits between the two.

phenols.q: How do you separate a phenol from a carboxylic acid?
phenols.why: The acid leaves as its water-soluble salt and the phenol stays behind.

phenols.q: What is carbonic acid's pKa?
phenols.why: Between a phenol at 10 and a carboxylic acid at 4.8, which is the whole basis of the separation.

phenols.q: What is 4-nitrophenol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Nitro withdraws by resonance from para, taking the charge onto its own oxygens.

phenols.q: What is picric acid's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, more acidic than most carboxylic acids.

phenols.q: Why is 4-nitrophenol more acidic than 3-nitrophenol?
options: Para is closer to the OH
phenols.why: From meta only induction is available, which is the smaller effect.

phenols.q: What kind of substituent makes a phenol more acidic?
phenols.why: Anything that stabilizes the phenoxide strengthens the acid.

phenols.q: Which positions matter most for a substituent's effect?
phenols.why: Only those can reach the negative charge by resonance.

phenols.q: Is OH an activator or deactivator on a ring?
phenols.why: The same lone pair that stabilizes the anion also donates into the ring.

phenols.q: Is OH ortho/para or meta directing?
phenols.why: Donation reaches the ortho and para positions, which is where the substitution goes.

phenols.q: What does phenol plus bromine water give?
phenols.why: No Lewis acid catalyst is needed, and all three activated positions react at once.

phenols.q: Why does phenol brominate without a catalyst?
phenols.why: A Lewis acid is needed only for rings that are not already electron-rich.

phenols.q: Can a phenol undergo SN2 at its C-O bond?
phenols.why: The backside is behind the ring, which rules the trajectory out entirely.

phenols.q: In a Williamson ether synthesis with a phenol, what is the nucleophile?
phenols.why: The aryl carbon can never be the electrophile in a substitution.

phenols.q: What does oxidizing a phenol give?
phenols.why: Not aromatic any more, which is why quinones are colored.

phenols.q: Why are quinones colored?
options: They are conjugated and not aromatic
phenols.why: A long conjugated system with a small HOMO-LUMO gap absorbs visible light.

phenols.q: Can a phenol be dehydrated like an alcohol?
phenols.why: Nothing that needs SN1 or SN2 at that carbon works.

phenols.q: How are phenols usually made?
phenols.why: Warm water on an aryl diazonium salt is the standard route.

phenols.q: What does a phenol plus an acyl chloride give?
phenols.why: Aspirin is one of these.

phenols.q: What is 2,4-dinitrophenol's approximate pKa?
phenols.why: Two nitro groups in resonance-capable positions, and now as acidic as a carboxylic acid.

phenols.q: Why is a methyl group on a phenol slightly deactivating toward acidity?
phenols.why: Donating electron density destabilizes the anion, which weakens the acid.

phenols.q: Which compound is least acidic?
phenols.why: An ordinary alcohol has no way to spread the charge at all.

phenols.q: Which is more acidic, phenol or acetic acid?
phenols.why: 4.8 against 10, because a carboxylate spreads charge over two equivalent oxygens.

phenols.q: Why does a carboxylate beat a phenoxide at stabilizing charge?
options: Charge sits on two electronegative oxygens
phenols.why: A phenoxide spreads charge onto carbons, which hold it less well than oxygen does.

birch-reduction.q: What does a Birch reduction produce from benzene?
birch-reduction.why: The unconjugated isomer, which is the less stable of the two dienes.

birch-reduction.q: What are the Birch conditions?
options: Na or Li in liquid NH3 with an alcohol
birch-reduction.why: A dissolving-metal reduction rather than a catalytic one.

birch-reduction.q: What does the deep blue color indicate?
birch-reduction.why: The reducing agent is a free electron in solution.

birch-reduction.q: What is the sequence of steps?
birch-reduction.why: Alternating, which is what makes the intermediates controllable.

birch-reduction.q: What is the first intermediate?
birch-reduction.why: One electron added to the ring.

birch-reduction.q: What does the alcohol do?
birch-reduction.why: The electrons come from the metal and the solvent is ammonia.

birch-reduction.q: Why is the 1,4-diene formed rather than the 1,3?
birch-reduction.why: Protonation happens where charge density is highest, not where stability is greatest.

birch-reduction.q: Which isomer is more stable?
birch-reduction.why: And it is not what forms, which is how you know stability is not deciding.

birch-reduction.q: With a donating group, where does the substituted carbon end up?
birch-reduction.why: A donor destabilizes charge on its own carbon, so the carbanion goes elsewhere.

birch-reduction.q: With a withdrawing group, where does the substituted carbon end up?
birch-reduction.why: A withdrawing group holds the charge on its own carbon, so that carbon is protonated.

birch-reduction.q: What does anisole give on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: Methoxy is donating, so its carbon stays on a double bond.

birch-reduction.q: What does benzoic acid give on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: Carboxyl is withdrawing, so its carbon ends up sp3.

birch-reduction.q: What single question answers both substituent rules?
options: Where is the carbanion most stable
birch-reduction.why: That carbon gets protonated and comes out saturated.

birch-reduction.q: Which reaction uses the same electron-then-proton pattern?
birch-reduction.why: Both are dissolving-metal reductions running on solvated electrons, and both give the opposite outcome from catalytic hydrogenation on the same substrate.

birch-reduction.q: What does catalytic hydrogenation give from benzene?
birch-reduction.why: It either leaves the ring alone or reduces it completely; there is no halfway.

birch-reduction.q: Why is the Birch useful?
birch-reduction.why: An unconjugated diene is a handle nothing else in the course provides.

birch-reduction.q: What does a Birch-derived enol ether give on mild acid hydrolysis?
birch-reduction.why: Which is the standard route into a substituted cyclohexenone from a flat ring.

birch-reduction.q: Which starting material gives an enol ether on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: The methoxy stays on a double bond, and a C=C with an OR on it is an enol ether.

birch-reduction.q: Why can an unconjugated diene be functionalized selectively?
options: Its two double bonds are independent
birch-reduction.why: A conjugated diene reacts as one system, which makes single-site chemistry harder.

birch-reduction.q: What kind of control does the Birch operate under?
birch-reduction.why: The product that forms fastest, rather than the one that is most stable.

birch-reduction.q: Which metal is used besides sodium?
birch-reduction.why: Both dissolve in liquid ammonia to give solvated electrons.

birch-reduction.q: How many electrons are added in total?
birch-reduction.why: Two electrons and two protons, alternating.

birch-reduction.q: What is the solvent?
birch-reduction.why: It solvates the electrons, which is what makes the blue solution.

birch-reduction.q: Does a Birch reduction touch an isolated alkene?
birch-reduction.why: Which is the opposite selectivity from catalytic hydrogenation.

birch-reduction.q: Why does a withdrawing group put its carbon sp3?
birch-reduction.why: The carbanion sits where the substituent lets it, and that carbon gets the proton.

birch-reduction.q: What is a radical anion?
options: A species with an unpaired electron and a charge
birch-reduction.why: One electron added to a neutral molecule gives both at once.

birch-reduction.q: Which position is protonated second?
options: Where the carbanion's charge is highest
birch-reduction.why: Which is what sets the 1,4 relationship in the product.

birch-reduction.q: What does toluene give on Birch reduction?
birch-reduction.why: Methyl is a weak donor, and direction rather than strength decides the outcome.

birch-reduction.q: Why does the Birch not over-reduce to cyclohexane?
options: The diene is not aromatic and resists further electron addition
birch-reduction.why: Adding an electron to an isolated alkene is far harder than to an aromatic ring.

birch-reduction.q: What makes a dissolving-metal reduction different from hydrogenation?
options: It adds electrons, not surface hydrogens
birch-reduction.why: Which is why it can stop where a surface reaction cannot.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the formula of an aryl diazonium ion?
diazonium-chemistry.why: And it leaves as N2 gas, which is what makes it so useful.

diazonium-chemistry.q: How is a diazonium salt made?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Cold, because the salt decomposes above about 5 degrees.

diazonium-chemistry.q: At what temperature is diazotization run?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Warmer and the salt loses nitrogen before you can use it.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why is N2+ such a good leaving group?
options: It leaves as stable N2 gas
diazonium-chemistry.why: A gas that escapes the solution and cannot come back.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What are the three steps to reach a diazonium salt from benzene?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The first two are reactions the course already covered.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What reduces a nitro group to an amine?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Or H2 with a catalyst, which does the same job.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does CuCl do to a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: A Sandmeyer reaction.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does CuCN do to a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: A group electrophilic substitution cannot install at all.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does KI do to a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: No copper salt is needed for the iodide.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does HBF4 then heat give?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The Schiemann reaction, and effectively the only route to an aryl fluoride.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does warm water give?
options: The aryl alcohol on the side chain
diazonium-chemistry.why: The standard way phenols are made, since no substitution works at that C-O bond.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does H3PO2 give?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Which is the most useful row on the menu once you see what it is for.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which groups can diazonium chemistry install that EAS cannot?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Four groups no electrophilic substitution reaches.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the point of replacing N2+ with H?
options: The amine directed a previous step and is no longer needed
diazonium-chemistry.why: A substituent installed to control a step and then deleted.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What does NH2 do as a substituent on a ring?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Which is why it is worth installing purely to direct.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is the aromatic analogue of a protecting group here?
options: An amine installed to direct, then removed
diazonium-chemistry.why: Same idea as the second carbonyl of a malonic ester synthesis.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which other group is used reversibly to block a position?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Sulfonation is reversible, so the group can be removed afterwards.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What is azo coupling?
options: A diazonium salt attacking an activated ring
diazonium-chemistry.why: The diazonium acts as a weak electrophile here rather than as a substrate.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Which rings will couple with a diazonium salt?
diazonium-chemistry.why: The diazonium is too weak an electrophile for anything less activated.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Where does azo coupling occur?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Ortho/para directors send it there, and para is less hindered.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why are azo compounds colored?
options: A long conjugated system absorbs visible light
diazonium-chemistry.why: Two rings joined by a conjugated N=N bridge gives a small HOMO-LUMO gap.

diazonium-chemistry.q: What industry did azo chemistry create?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Methyl orange is one of these compounds.

diazonium-chemistry.q: Why can 1,3,5-tribromobenzene not be made by direct bromination?
diazonium-chemistry.why: Each bromine sends the next one ortho or para, so 1,3,5 is unreachable.
